California Masonic Memorial Temple - San Francisco

W ILLIAM FARLEY STOVALL
William F. Stovall was born and raised in Long Beach , California, where
he graduated from the public schools. He attended Long Beach City College until
his stud ies were interrupted by the Korean War. After his discharge from the
United States Air Force, he returned to complete an Associate of Arts degree in
Business Administration. He continued his education at California State
University, Long Beach, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Public
Administration, followed by a Master of Arts Degree in Public Administration
from the University of Southern California. In addition, he is a graduate of the
Delinquency Control Institute at the University of Southern California, and a
graduate of the National Academy of the Federal Bureau of Investigation at
Quantico, Virginia. He taught for nine years in the History and Government
Department of Long Beach City College.
Professionally, Most Worshipful Brother Stovall served thirty years with
the Long Beach Police Department, retiring in 1987 as Deputy Chief of Police. In
addition, he also served as Assistant Fire Chief and City Personnel Services Officer
during his career with the Long Beach Police Department. In 1989 he was listed
in " Who's Who in California," and in 1990 he was honored as "Chief of Police of
the Year" by the International Union of Police Associations, AFL-CIO.
He was raised on September 16, 1967, in Queen Beach Lodge No. 540,
which his father had served as Master in 1944. He served as Master of that Lodge
in 1972, and again in 1976, and was officers' coach for many years. He also served
as Inspector of the 622nd Masonic District in Long Beach for nine years ..
In 1977 tie was appointed Grand Standard Bearer by Most Worshipful
Donald B. McCaw, and Grand Marshal in 1980 by Most Worshipful H. Douglas
Lemons. In October, 1991 he was elected Junior Grand Warden, and progressed
through the Grand Lodge Line until his election and installation as Grand Master
in October, 1994. During this time he served as a Trustee of the Masonic Homes
of California, the California Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic Memorial
Temple, and as a Founding Director of the Nob Hill Masonic Management
Corporation. He also served on the Wardens' Retreat Committee, and as a Director
of the National Masonic Foundation for Children, in Washington, D.C.
Grand Master Stovall served as Venerable Master of the Long Beach
Lodge of Perfection in 1981, and in 1983, was coroneted a Thirty-Third Degree
Inspector-General Honorary in the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, Southern
Masonic Jurisdiction of the United States of America. He served as the Personal
Representative of the Sovereign Grand Inspector-General for California in the
Valley of Long Beach, and was Vice President of the Childhood Language
Disorders Center in Long Beach, as well as President of the Board of Directors for

the Long Beach Scottish Rite Cathedral. He was a.. Director for the California
Scottish Rite Foundation, and Director of the Honors Ritual for the Scottish Rite
in California.
A member of El Bekal Shrine Temple in Anaheim, he served on the Board
of Governors of the Shriners' Hospital for Crippled Children in Los Angeles. He
was President of the Signal Hill High Twelve Club, the Long Beach Masonic
Service Bureau, and was a member of the Long Beach Past Masters' Club. He is
also a member of the York Rite Bodies in Long Beach, the Royal Order of
Scotland, Allied Masonic Degrees, National Sojourners, the Southern California
Past Masters' Association, Southern California Research Lodge, and the Royal
Order of Jesters. In addition, he served as Sovereign of St. Croix Conc lave of the
Knights of the Red Cross of Constantine.
Most Worshipful Bro. Stovall is a Senior DeMolay, with a Life
Membership in Long Beach Searchlight Chapter, Order of DeMolay. He holds the
Active Legion of Honor.
In his civic activities, he served as president of the Long Beach Optimist
Club, President of the Community Rehabilitation Industries, president and
Chainnan of the Board of the Travelers' Aid Society of Southern Los Angeles and
Orange Counties, and was an officer of the Coordinating Council of the PTA. He
served on the Board of Governors of the Downtown Long Beach YMCA, of the
Los Altos Hospital of Long Beach, and of Doctors' Hospital of Lakewood. He also
served as Vice President of the Retired Police and Fire Association of America, and
is a life member of American Legion Post No. 496.
He is married to Beverly Stovall, and they have two sons, two daughters
and a foster daughter, fourteen grandchildren, and three great-grandchild ren as of
the close of his term of office. His theme as Grand Master was " Freemasonry: For
God, For Country, For Family," and he was responsible for bringing to California
the " Masonic Model Student Assistance Training Program," sponsored by the
California Masonic Foundation, and providing training for public school teachers
in the early identi fication of substance abuse and other dysfunctional behavior in
children. This program exemplified his theme, because this highl y successful
program helped teachers rescue school children before their lives were ruined by
substance abuse, g ang involvement, and other devastating behaviors.

PUBLIC OPENING CEREMONY

Sunday, October 8, 1995
2:30 p.m.
The Public Opening Ceremony of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California began at 2:30 p.m. in the
Masonic Auditorium of the California Masonic Memorial Temple in San Francisco.
With trumpet fanfare and organ, Most Worshipful William F. Stovall led the
1994/95 Grand Lodge Officers into the auditorium to begin the ceremonies. Grand
Lodge was raised by Bro. Edwin Clarke, Executive Officer of the Jurisdiction of
Northern California, and Bro. Gaylord Roten, Executive Officer of the Jurisdiction
of Southern California, Order of DeMolay. They used two gavels, one presented
to the Grand Master by his wife and children upon his installation as Master of
Queen Beach Lodge No. 540 in 1972 and in 1976, and presented to him again upon
his installation as Grand Master in 1994. The other gavel had originally been
presented to his father by his mother, his sister, and by M:. W:. Bro. Stovall, in
1944, when his father was installed as Master of Queen Beach Lodge No. 540.
The Grand Master asked the Grand Marshal to retire and present the Flag
of Our Country, and upon entrance, the Flag was preceded by the flags of all fifty
states carried by the Sanger High School Naval Junior Reserve Officer Training
Corps Fifty State Flag Team. Following the American Flag were members of the
Heroes of '76 of the National Sojourners, who carried the flags of the five anned
services of the u·nited States: the United States Navy, the United States Marine
Corps, the United States Anny, the United States Air Force, and the United States
Coast Guard. The American Flag presented at the Altar was a flag flown over the
U.S.S. Arizona Memorial at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on the Grand Master' s birthday,
December 26, 1994. In receiving this special flag, the Grand Master commented:
'The Flag of the United States of America which was escorted by our
Grand Marshal, was presented to me at a reception at the Valley of Santa
Ana Scottish Rite this year, and was flown over the battleship U .S.S.
Arizona on my birthday, December 26, 1994.
This battleship, now resting in 38 feet of water at the bottom of Pearl
Harbor, is a national memorial, and fli es our national ensign from a
flagpole mounted aboard it from 8:00 a.m. to sunset daily in tribute to the
brave American fighting men killed during the attack on Pearl Harbor on
the morning of December 7, 1941.

thunder ceases to roar, we can walk together toward a new tomorrow, one that is
better than all the yesterdays that we have ever known." Today, " that lightening"
has struck, and its accompanying thunder has ceased, and has ushered in a new
message of accomplishments, hope and prosperity by which both of our Grand
Bodies can embrace the 2 1st century.
During the past several years, the Prince Hall Grand Lodge and the Grand
Lodge of California have developed a cooperative spirit of mutual respect and
understanding. We of the Prince Hall Family believe in our Grand Master' s
guiding principle, which is "together we achieve more", and to that end we are
committed. Both Grand Bodies have taken action on the issue of mutual
"recognition", and as the resu lt of the deliberations of wise, just and upright men,
they having developed a mutual re spect for one another, and seeing beyond the
darkness of fear, were able to create a bright and prosperous vision for the future
of our Grand Bodies. The Grand Lodge of California and the Prince Hall Grand
Lodge have jointly demonstrated the true spirit of Freemasonry, and have done
what is right and have done what is j ust. Masonry was designed to be a
brotherhood of man, which need not be an idle dream in the great State of
California.
Therefore, it is with immense anticipation that I wait for the approaching
time when we will sit in Lodge together on the level, as men and as Masons.
We of the Prince Hall Family are confident that the true workers in the
quarries of Masonry will always prevail. Because Masonry in the final analysis,
is a theory of living, and a philosophy of truth, a way of life.
Therefore, our Masonry must manifest itself in our daily contacts with
each other, and it is not what the tongue proclaims, but what the heart contains that
defines a man as a Mason.
As we seek the real meaning of Masonry for ourselves, I'm rem inded of
the story of Pygmalion and h is statue of Galatea. Pygmalion was an ancient kin g
of Cyprus. The king's business in those days didn 't require a great deal oftime.
There was no Monday Night Football, Six O'Clock News, no golf courses to
absorb idle hours, and no Masonic meeting to attend .
So Pygmalion, who must have been an artist of considerable note in his
day, ch iseled his statue of Galatea from ivory. It was a th ing of such beau ty and
so life-like that Pygmalion fell madly in love with it and prayed that the statue
might come to life. The Goddess Aphrodite, so the story goes, responded to the
prayer and gave being to the beautiful Galatea. The Masonic lesson which may be
drawn from this story, speaks to the fabric of Masonry being as beautiful as the
statue of Galatea, to which Pygmalion gave his best as a sculptor, and finally his
love and devotion, th at resulted in the cold ivory becoming a live, and warm,
human creature.

GRAND LODGE O F C A LIFORNIA

Masonry can only be something cold and inanimate as chiseled ivory, to
those who admire its beauty in a detached kind of way. But, it can become warm
alive and filled with love, through the devotion due from those that believe in th~
great light of her ideals and of her laudable principles.

O NE H UN DRED FORTY-SIXTH

We must never forget that Masons Jive by the bright rays of a great light
produced more than twenty centuries ago. And those who follow us will be a0 uided
b~ that same lig~t. They will see what we have done, and they will judge us by the

EULOGY
BURTON MEYER, JR.
Master Mason
Born: February 12, 1921 in Minneapolis, Minnesota
Entered into Rest : April 25, 1995 in Sun City West, Arizona

Far away, there in the sunshine, are my highest aspirations. I
may not reach them, but 1 can look up and see their beauty,
believe in them and try to follow where they lead.
With these words, Burt began his service as Grand Master of Masons in
California during the !25th year of this Grand Lodge. For men of fa ith , hope and
charity, aspirations challenge them to hone character and ability, chiseling away a t
personal imperfections to better enable them to fit as living stones of human
society.
For special men, as with Burt, aspirations also challenge them to lead
others to that same noble end. They strive not just for self-improvement but fo r the
improvement which they can inspire in others. They challenge us w ith
encouraging wor~s and determination of action to do good and be better as well.
Leaders do not always agree on the evolving shape of that 'house not made
with hands', whether in the world at large or within our fraterni ty. Some become
discouraged when construction turns in an unintended direction. It is then when
we must pause and reflect on our true mission. It is not to achieve our own will but
to challenge others to work together and strive for the best that we can become
together. And, in this leadership, Burt excelled.
Burt inspired many men with his encouraging words and his determ ination
of action. He served his country in the United States Coast Guard during the
Second World War and was a spokesman for the War Bo nd drive, both in person
and on the radio. His business career started as a young man on a paper route and
ended as the owner of a successful printing company.
He became a Mason in 1945 in Golden State Lodge No. 358, now
Metropolitan No. 352, and was Golden State's Master in 1960. He was a District
Inspector, an Assistant Grand Lecturer and the Grand Orator before his election as
Junior Grand Warden. He was an Inspector-General Honorary of the Scott ish Rite
and a Past Venerable Master in the Valley of Los Angeles. He served on the Board
for the Los Angeles Unit ofShriners Hospitals. He belonged to all of the York Rite
bodies, the Shrine, Red Cross of Constantine and Royal Order of Scotland.

EULOGY
CHESTER RIDDOCH MacPHEE
Grand Master 1969-1970
Born: June 5, 1905
Entered into Rest: August 9, 1995
Hear the revised words of a poem first written by Leigh Hunt:
Chester MacPhee. may his tribe increase ,
A woke one night from a deep dream of peace,
And saw within the moonli ght in his room,
Making it rich and like a lily in bloom.
An angel writing in a book of gold Exceeding peace had made Chester bold,
And to the presence in the room he said,
" What writest thou?" The Vision raised its head,
And with a look made all of sweet accord,
Answered, "The names of those who love the Lord."
"And is mine one?'· asked Chet. ·'Nay, not so,"
Replied the Angel. Chet spoke low,
But cheerily still and said, "I pray thee then,
Write me as one who loves his fellow man."
The angel wrote, and vanished. The next night
It came again with a great awaken ing light,
And showed the names of those whom love of God had blest,
And lo. Chet MacPh ee's name led all the rest.

CHESTER RlDDOCH MACP HEE
PAST GRAN D MAST ER
June 5, 1905 - August 9, I 995

Chester Riddoch MacPhee was a man who not only loved the Lord,
but
his fellow man, his native land, and his Masonic Fraternity. When judged
by every
standard, Chet MacPhee earned the never ending fondness. admiration,
and respect
of thousands of people.

24

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

. I am sure that most of us would like to leave behind words of hope and
consolation rather than the customary last will and testament bestowing our worldly
goods. Most of us would like to be remembered and exalted when we leave these
earthly bounds. Chester Riddoch MacPhee was honored by a most unusual tribute,
unusual because the tribute was so rare and so beautiful. It was manifested in a
book published by his wife Marjorie on June 5, 1990, and titled ''My Chet". Listen
to h~r wo.rds written ~bout her husband of 63 years: " If you ask me to give you
Chet s ph1los.ophy o~ hfe, ~would say it is a life of giving of himself in the many
areas of service to his farnily, and yes, service to all mankind . .. he lived by the
words, ' Real happiness is something we must give to others before it comes back
to us."'
Our Past Grand Master was born in San Francisco on June 5, 1905. He
travele.d to the land fr~m whose boume no traveler returns on August 9, 1995.
Maso~1c me~onal services were held in the California Scottish Rite Temple in San
Francisco with Past Grand Masters Donald B. McCaw officiating and Warren J.
Blomseth delivering the eulogy.

Ch~st~r MacPhee became a Mason in 1940 in Golden West Lodge No.
455, no': M_iss1on ~o. 169, and its Master in 1949. His vital interest in Masonry
resulted i.n his appomon~nt to numerous Grand Lodge committees and trusteeships.
After being elected Junior Grand Warden in 1967, he served as Grand Master of
Masons in California and Hawaii in 1969-1970. His Masonic activities extended
to_ the Yor~ Rite and Scottish Rite Bodies and by election of the Supreme Council
of the Ancienr and Accepted Scottish Rite he was coroneted a 33° Mason. He was
a member of Islam Shrine Temple and the Royal Order of Scotland. As evidence
of the high regard the Fraternity held for him, after serving as Grand Master, he
was elected Grand Treasurer and served with distinction for ten years. In 1986 Past
Grand Master John W. Driskell recognized Chet MacPhee's devoted Masonic
s~rvice by bestowing up~n him the appellation ..Mason of the Year". Based upon
his many years of experience as a Trustee, Board President, and Treasurer of the
Mason~c Homes he wro~e and published the resourceful and valuable history of the
Masonic Homes of Cahfom ia under the title, 'The Greatest of These is Charity".
Any vita of Chester MacPhee must include his joining DeMolay at age 16.
It was at a DeMolay event that he and his beloved Marge first met. His service to
DeMolay contimred for.the next 75 years. He demonstrated his support for youth
as Grand Master, as director of the Red Shield Youth Center treasurer of San
Francisco Boys Club, founder and chainnan of the San 'Francisco Youth
Association, and director of the Y.M.C.A.
While I believe this remembrance of Past Grand Master Chester MacPhee
should include a report of all of his outstanding and noteworthy contributions to the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

25

community of San Francisco, I have chosen to highlight only a limited number to
demonstrate their quality and goodness.
Chester MacPhee served as a Supervisor of the City and County of San
Francisco from 1941 to 1953 and as its Chief Administrative Officer. From 1953
to 1958 he was Director of the United States Customs Service. He was Past
President of the San Francisco Rotary Club and trustee of the Rotary Foundation.
One of his most outstanding and productive endeavors was his founding
in 1944 of the San Francisco Bible Breakfast Club for which he acted as moderator.
He was a member of the State Real Estate Commission, Past President of
the Cancer Society, Council of Churches, Mission Y.M.C.A., and San Francisco
Youth Association. He was senior Past President of the San Francisco Real Estate
Board, and Director and Treasurer for 15 years of the San Francisco Boys and Girls
Club, and an honorary member of Novato Youth Center.
He was founder, chainnan of the board, and trustee of the Western
Investme nt Real Estate Trust. He was president and trustee of Olivet Memorial
Park as well as serving as member of the President's Council of the Dominican
College of San Rafael. He was a director of the Associates' Council of the
California Institute of Technology of Pasadena.
I met Chester MacPhee for the first time when we both became Trustees
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple in 1968 and from that moment on our
fellowship began.to tum into a friendship that was to endure for the next twentyseven years. r became the beneficiary of his wisdom, his wise counsel and
encouragement. He sent me inspirational articles for the California Freemason.
Thus I feel entitled to contemplate on what his last message would be to you, his
brother Masons, were he present at this moment. But I don't have to ponder long.
He spoke to you twenty-five years ago this week and I believe his message would
be the same today as it was in October 1970. This is what he said:
" Had I but the power of the ages, it would be to spread the cement of
Brotherly Love and affection among all men. To those in our great Fraternity who
may have excuses for not doing so, I would urge a more considered study to their
Masonic responsibilities. Let us remember always that a Mason must be the first
to demonstrate Brotherly Love, to extend kindly considerations to others at all
times, and that it is only by personal forgiving that we are forgiven.
To all of you I most sincerely urge a greater study of the depth and
breadth of Freemasonry. For our relationship to God, for our homes and our
families, for our country, for the betterment of all mankind - let us learn, let us
understand, let us each live responsibly in those ways our obligations indicate and,
My Brethren, let us always act as Master Masons."

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

146TH ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Good morning brethren,

APPENDIX A

Section I 060 of the California Masonic Code requires the Grand Master
to deliver to the Grand Lodge at each Annual Communication a written message
setting forth first, all his official acts for the year; secondly, the general condition
of Masonry within the jurisdiction; and thirdly, recommending suc h legislation as
he deems necessary or expedient for the welfare of the craft. I have delivered a
copy of my message to the Grand Secretary, and it will be printed in full in the
Proceedings of this Annual Communication. This afternoon I will present to you
my decision and recommendations, all of which were previously mailed to each
lodge in this jurisdiction.
Just a brief twelve months ago, Columbus Day, 1994, I knelt here in your
presence, at this altar as a humble servant before my God, seeking His inspiration
and guidance in the great and important undertaking that your sufferage had called
upon me to assume.
That morning I pledged to you my singular goal to work to awaken our
Fraternity to the opportunities and challenges in front of us as a Fraternity; the
opportunity to rekindle the fire of charity and community involvement in our
lodges and members and thus, reaffirm the goodness of our institution in the eyes
of alJ who view us. And I hoped to keep focused on this goal with the adoption of
the theme, FREEMASONRY: FOR GOD, FOR COUNTRY, AND FOR FAMILY .
The hour of accounting for my stewardship is now upon me, and I present
myself to you with a wide range of emotions as I discharge one of the fina l duties
that devolves upon all Grand Masters, according to our law.
The office of Grand Master would be a hollow title without the strong
support of our lodges, lodge officers, committeemen, Inspectors, Grand Lodge
Officers and Past Grand Masters, and I have a profound gratitude to all of you for
demonstrating that support to me throughout the year.
Every lodge that I have called upon with a request has demonstrated a
fraternal eagerness to support their Grand Master. The hospitality that you have
extended to my wife, to me, and to our Grand Lodge Officers in more than 21 0
activities, ceremonies and events as we traveled throughout this jurisdiction has
been a source of great pride and comfort to your Grand Lodge Family and I thank
you so much for that fraternal Jove that you shared with us.

State of the Craft
There is yet a continuing decline in the membership rolls of our lodges
that looms as an ever-increasing burden on their ability to generate the financial
resources to support new programs and activities in their communities. This
decline has been expected and has been inevitable because we have not attracted
younger members in the numbers necessary to replace our ever-advancing age of
membership. And indicative of that point, your Grand Lodge had the priv;lege of
presenting thirteen (13) 75-year Veterans' Awards this year including one such
award to Worshipful Abner F. Thompson, the 98 year old Master of Alcatraz
Lodge No. 244, who had served his lodge as Master the first time 50 years ago.
There is, howeve r, evidence that some lodges are doing the right things.
I have observed that the lodges that involve their younger members as
committeemen and officers invariably attract more younger members. For
example, the young Master of my own lodge hosted a Masonic Information Night
and invited the young men from the Greek Letter Fraternities at his University to
attend. He had a remarkable turnout of very interested young men who were
relentless in their questions who showed a serious membership interest.
Our decline in membership this year is less than predicted, with 50 of our
lodges either maintaining the same, or increasing their membership, and with I 2
of them having done so for the second year.
I am encouraged with the growing interest I see in our lodges to become
more involved in community activities and more involved in working to support
community needs. This doesn't just happen, it takes initiative and hard work,
something that has been replaced with so much apathy in our society today. But,
this is an important function of Freemasonry, one which was evidenced by the
Masons who were the principals in the founding of our Country, our States and our
cities, and it should ever be the focus of the Fraternity. I am convinced that our
society needs Freemasons, as the men who have a timeless system of ethics and
morality that should be carried into every level of our government.
There is yet much work to be done to move us into the relevance we once
held among everyone, that relevance that invariably attracts those who are
searching for like-minded men to associate with, and who will become the
foundation and the leaders of our furure Fraternity.

I want to thank our Grand Treasurer, V:.W:. Herb Wilkins, our Chief
Financial Officer, Brother Doug Scott, our Investment Committee and all of you
who have worked so diligently with me to control our financia l profile.
Dues and Fees
I am concerned with an attitude that seems to prevail in our craft that any
attempt to raise the dues and fees in a lodge is somehow unfair and prejudicial to
our Brothers. I view just the opposite to be true.
Without solid operating funds your lodges and your Grand Lodge will
soon dry up and wither away. New programs and community invol vement cannot
be initiated without the finances to support them. If we continue on the same
course, business as usual, repeatedly resisting the realities of this world's financial
life, the inevitable result will be lodges with no one sitting on the sidelines, with
no degrees to work in, with no exciting ideas, with no new activities, and with no
community recognition, lodges doing absolutely nothing to attract the attention of
the young, ambitious men out there today who wou ld join our lodges, those men
who would be the life-blood of tomorrow's Freemasonry.

Financial

It is disturbing to realize that the annual dues of my own lodge barely
exceeds the monthly cost of my service club. We can afford more. in fact, we
can't afford not to pay more.

Last year I presented to you a budget which was reduced from the
previous year, and I pledged that I would keep all of the ceremonial and operational
expenses of our Grand Lodge within that budget.

My challenge to you is this: set your membership and dues structure
commensurate to the value of your organization. If your lodge is of little value to
you, then low dues and membership fees would be appropriate. Of course, if it's

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

This project bears no Grand Master's name because its importance to our
schools, our Fraternity and to our society is far too great for such a limited identity.
I believe it is the mechanism that will push our Fraternity into the forefront of the
most important issue facing our communities today, that of the safety of our
communities and our children. And the vanguard of this project is the Masonic
Model Student Assistance Trainin~ Program, our new partnerhisp between
California Masons and our Public Schools. This program is one that gives our
educators the tools to help build good kids today to ensure a bener and safer
tomorrow for our children, our grandchildren and for all of us.
The outstanding response, from both the schools and our members, to this
intervention training program is absolutely overwhelming. We began this program
last November 30th with little money and great apprehension. I told you at my
installation that we planned to hold five sessions for the year and that we expected
to provide the training to over 250 educators. Those expectations have been met,
and in the five classes which were completed this last May, we have trained 258
educators representing 60 schools from all over the state. The preliminary reports
are just coming in. From the first two sessions alone, December and January, there
have been 673 at-risk children referred to our intervention teams with 418 children
in actual treatment.
And your financial support has enabled us to contract for 13 more classes.
All six classes planned for this present school year (95-96) are now full, with 330
educators enrolled, and the seven classes for the following year which will
accommodate 385 educators are now building a waiting list.
My sincere appreciation for causing the success of the student assistance
training program goes to the M:.W : Roy J. Renville, President of the California
Masonic Homes Board and his Board Members for the use of the Covina facility
and its support services, to the Wor. Frank Russell, President of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple Board and his Board Members for their direct and
unhesitating assistance, to Wor. David Decker, President of the California Masonic
Foundation Board, Wor. Michael Stovall, the Chairman of the Board' s Student
Assistance Training Committee, and to all members of the Foundation Board, and
to each and every Mason and lodge among you who has so generously given of
your time and money to support this outstanding program, a program that will put
the word Freemason on the lips of every educator in the state and on the tongue of
every parent whose child has been helped by the generosity of the Masons of
California.
As you may recall, I had asked that you consider any gifts to the Grand
Master this year to be a donation to the Student Assistance Program in lieu of any
other gifts. Your acceptance of that idea has given me an additional 47 thousand
dollars to add to the support of this fine program.

Appreciation

My heartfelt appreciation goes to my Grand Lodge Officers and their
wives who nuly melded into a cohesive Masonic Family and worked long, hard
and diligently to represent each and every one of you up and down the length and
breadth of this state this past year.
They have been so supportive of Bev and me that our job was not only
made easier, but our lives were greatly enriched with their encouragement, support
and love. There are no words adequate to express our appreciation to these
outstanding Masons and their wives whom we' ve come to regard as our own
extended family.
We are forever greatful for the continued support and understanding of
our children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, who missed us for four years
at all the birthdays, holidays and special occasions that we had never before missed.
I might add that in this time we have added four great grandchildren to our family
who want to meet their great grandparents.
And lastly, this journey would not have been possible without my love,
my soulmate, my wife at my side. For four years she has encouraged me, inspired
me, tolerated my impatience, and put all the household chores on an extended
leave, all the while being the smiling, gracious and loving person that she is. She
made this rough and rugged road the smooth highway that it was, and to her my
undying gratitude bums eternal.
Where Do We Go from Here?

There is an excitement in the air... we must nurture it - expand upon it and
spread it throughout our entire jurisdiction. Masonry is good, we need to act like
it is. Our lodges should become so involved in meeting community needs that
every city, town and neighborhood will know what we stand for and respects us for
what we teach and what we do, because it is what we do that we will be judged by,
and not by what we say.
I said at my installation, we are all riding that merry-go-round of life,
looking for that gold ring on each tum of the carousel. We must grab every ring
that we can reach, knowing full well that one of them will be the gold one. And we
must grab every opportunity presented to us to talk Freemasonry, to write about
Freemasonry and to show-off Freemasonry and if that opportunity is not presented
to us we should create that opportunity every chance that we can.
We are a premier organiz.ation, and we must demonstrate to the world
what we are, that Freemasonry is good, that Freemasonry truly does stand for God,
for Country and for Family.

year.

Several events of historic import were conducted by our Grand Lodge this

On May 13, 1995, the Grand Lodge was convened in a special session in
the hall of Hornitos Lodge No. 98, Hornitos, to conduct a dedication ceremony and
to affix a bronze State Historical Marker to the exterior of the building. This lodge
building is the oldest, single story lodge building in the State of California, and was
operating as a lodge during the gold rush period much in the same character that
it now operates. The State Historical Committe e selected this lodge to be
recognized as another important location significant to the early developm ent of
California .
Grand Lodge was opened in ample form in this small lodge room, scarcely
22-feet by 35-feet, with nearly 100 Master Masons and Grand Lodge Officers
present. All Masons then assembled in the community building a block away with
their fami!ies, friends and interested citizens of the area for a special ceremony of
dedication of the historical marker to be affixed to the building. After the
ceremony the lodge members served a barbecue for over 400 persons in attendance.

New Perspectiv es on Charitable Giving
I have observed that, with the exception of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Contributions, the level of participation with our Masonic Foundation
has steadily declined in the past several years. The Homes contributio ns appear to
maintain activity through the repeated request envelopes which are sent by the
lodges during the annual dues collection process and by a diligence of the lodge
secretaries. The amounts collected, however, are far below their potential.

moment for reading and understanding that would otherwise have caused the mail
tc have been discarded without another thought.
Acting on this infonnation our California Masonic Foundation decided to
adopt the Student Assistance Training Program as one which is easily recognized
as well worthwhile to all communities in California. In developing funding
strategies, they undertook new and untried methods of program recognition and
fundraising for California Masons. A return address label program was initiated
as a trial. There was such an outstanding, even overwhelming response to this kind
of request that coUiage to further experiment was found.

50

Similar requests by Grand Mastt.:s on behalf of our Foundation have not
experienced the same degree of response as those of the Homes. I attribute this to
two main reasons :
The programs and activities supported by the Foundation were
l.
not widely known and seemed to lack a relevance to our
members. There may even have been a lack of confidence in the
Foundation ' s activities which was borne out of that lack of
knowledge.
Our general society has literally been bombarded with written
requests for charitable giving from every quarter and has become
desensitized to the request mailing approach. This has carried
over into our Masonic Charities, and results in such requests
being generally ignored.
This was no better demonstrat ed than our Grand Master's request to
lodges and members for earthquake relief contributions in 1994. More funds were
received from Grand Lodges outside of California than from all the members and
lodges of California combined. I don 't believe it was the ''hard heart" of our
California members which we saw, but rather a clear evidence that written requests
alone for worthy funds are no longer a viable way to raise those funds.
With our general funds so dear, and with little hope for general fund relief
in the near future, new programs and activities which will be so necessary for our
future organizational health, need to be sculptured to fit the charitable activities
model, and to meet the mission of our California Masonic Foundation .
2.

It does appear that our members have an open pocketbook for the support
of a worthwhile charity which they understand , but they have little tolerance for a
plea to increase (gdge dues and Grand Lodge per capita levels.
Armed with this understanding, I undertook an examinatio n of the
successful methods offundrais ing used by other Grand Lod~es in this country. I
found that, with respect to charitable giving, Masons will stop to read a plea for
funds and respond to it if that plea has something tangible either sent with it or
involved as a collateral to it. But, the request must be made for an activity that the
member strongly feels is worthwhile . The tangible item seems to provide a

They tried marketing a Grandfather Clock and a Hamilton Wristwatch
offer. These offers were presented in a package which included the mailing of our
California Freemason publication . Not only did we raise considerable funds for
the Foundation, but we saved over thirty thousand dollars on mailing costs alone
from our general funds.
And lastly, the membership will be given an opportunity to have a credit
card which carries the logo of our Grand Lodge and which use will raise funds for
the Foundation in a simple aqd painless way.
The responses to these new fundraising approaches speak for themselves.
In the past year nearly $900,000.0 0 in gross dollars was raised strictly from our
membership. A new and exciting type of charity fundraising has established itself
as acceptable by our members and worthwhile and beneficial to the charitable
programs of the Grand Lodge of California.
This is just the beginning ... we cannot stop here if we are to survive. I
suggest that if we sit passively by while other charities are actively prospecting our
members we will not just stand still, we will slip back into oblivion. Our Masonic
Homes and Masonic Foundation are not in competition with one another, they are
in direct competitio n with all other charities whose pleas are searching out the
dollars of our members.
The handwritin g is on the wall. The future of all charities now lies in
wills, bequests and gifts. Many of our members and their widows now leave vast
sums to other, non-Masonic charities because we don 't actively market those of our
own Gr.and Lo~ge._ This condition must change. We are in a time demanding
chang~ _m organiza~1ons to survive. This includes changing the traditional practice
of wa1tmg for chanty donations to appear on our doorstep.
It would be a great service to our members, their widows and to our
if
charities we vigorously pursue a "giving option" in a serious marketing effort to
be offered for the benefit of our craft.

REDEDICATION
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
TUESDAY, JUNE 13, 1995
Grand Master: Brethren and friends, from ancient times the history of
man has recorded the ceremonies of rededication, or the affirming again, of one's
devotion to something sacred, or the setting aside of something for a special
purpose.
For example, God commanded the children of Israel to observe the Feast
of the Tabernacles beginning on the 15th day of the 7th month (or Tishri) each
year, as a rededication of their obedience and love for Him who brought them out
of the land of Egypt and out of bondage over 3,000 years ago. And the Eucharist,
or Ceremony of Communion is a symbolic but solemn oath of a Christian's
renewal, or rededication, of his pledge to his Lord.
It is not uncommon today for a man and wife of many years to rededicate
themselves to one another by repeating those solemn wedding vows first taken
years before, thus pledging themselves anew to their bonds of love and devotion.
And so we too, recognizing the values of this ancient rite of mankind,
have assembled here today with joy and solemnity to rededicate this beautiful
Masonic Memorial Temple to our heroic dead, that the cause of freedom for which
they died shall be the sacred trust of their Brethren and Freemasons yet unborn.
It is fitting that we celebrate the rededication of the Memorial Temple at
this time because it is the time of the 50th Anniversary of the defeat of the tyrants
and despots of all humanity in World War 11, wherein our freedoms were paid for
with the lives of so many. And it is also the time to observe the 50th Anniversary
of that noble experiment of men, the formation of the United Nations, that
organization which was formed on the heels of World War II, whose main purposes
are to "save the succeeding generations from the scourge of war," to develop
friendly relations among states; to cooperate in solving international economic,
social, cultural and humanitarian problems; and to promote respect for human
rights and fundamental freedoms.
Though the United Nations has been the object of considerable scorn
because of its seeming inability to deal with political crisis, the easing of the EastWest tensions have led to a significant increase in its effectiveness. It is not a
perfect tool, but it has had remarkable success in helping to resolve many of the
world's crises.
This Temple stands today as a remembrance of the costs of American lives
laid down in the name of freedom,

Over 290,000 lives in World War II
Over 23 ,000 lives in the Korean Conflict
Over 58,000 lives in Viet Nam

and hundreds of thousands more who were injured and maimed in battle.
It was Monday, September 29, 1958, at I :50 p.m., during the afternoon
session of the 109th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California, that
the dedication ceremony of the new California Masonic Memorial Temple was
performed. The dedication was a closed ceremony, performed b y the Most
Worshipful Leo E. Anderson, Grand Master, according to ancient form and usage
in the ritual of this Grand Jurisdiction.
There was a world-wide attendance of distinguished Masonic leaders
including the Grand Masters of:
•
•
•
•

+
•

•

The United Grand Lodge of England
The Grand Lodge of France
The Philippines
El Salvador
Canada, the Province of Ontario
·British Columbia
Alberta
Saskatchewan
21 of our Sister Jurisdictions

as well as representatives of Grand Masters throughout the world.
It was a glorious event which began with Past Grand Master Edward H.
Siems, as President of the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple,
presenting a review of the history of the Memorial Temple program and finally
requesting the Grand Master to dedicate the Temple.
Our Brothers did their work well, and today we have a true jewel set atop
the crown of Nob Hill which is the envy of the world and a beacon which shines
its light for the memory of all those fallen heroes who have guaranteed our
freedoms for tomorrow.
It gives us great pleasure to discharge the important and interesting duty
which devolves upon us. I express to the Brethren and guests here assembled our
hearty appreciation for j oining with us to recognize those brave souls and
enterprising spirits which inspired the completion of this Memorial Temple, which
is not only a credit to the Fraternity, but an ornament to this community. In

PROCLAMATION

PROCLAMATION

P l !BI IC SCHOO! S WEEK. 1995

"FR.EE PUBLIC £DUCA TION ··AMERICA 'S CREA TEST FREEDOM"

YOUTH ORDERS MONTH

WHEREAS, the three Youth Orders of the Masonic Family have been. and will continue
to be, the future of our Country; and
WHEREAS, the oldest of the three Youth Orders, the Order of DeMolay, was founded
during the month of March, 1919; and
WHEREAS, the International Order of Job's Daughters is celebrating its Seventy-Fifth
Anniversary during 1995.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, WILLIAM F. STOVALL. GRAND MASTER OF MASONS IN
CALIFORNIA, DO HEREBY PROCLAIM THE MONTH OF MARCH 1995 TO BE:

PROCLAMATION
Two hundred and eight years ago on September 17, 1787, the Constitution of the United States of
America was born. 1ne Philadelphia Convention had completed rts wor1<. in preparing a Constitution for
our new nation and the final draft was signed off by 39 of the 55 delegates to the Convention. The new
Constitution was relatively short and can be described as a model of simplicity. It provided for a strong
central govemment, while it guaranteed the sovereignty of the thirtee,. ir ,..;;..,;..:uc.i states of the Union.
1ne doclJment endeavored to solve the many problems that beset our fledgling nation, but still assured
the independenca and unity that American patriots had fought so valiantly to achieve. It began with a
clear and concise pronouncement to the world, which so aptly describes the character and the
f\.odamental goals of our nation ... "We, the People ... do ordain and establish this Constitution for the
United States of America.·

APPENDIXB

As Freemasons, we have a vested interest in our Constitution. Freemasons not only participated in the
Constitution's preparation, but were prominent figures in all of the events that preceded it - the
Declaration lndependenca, the Revolutionary War and the Constitutional Convention, itself. Today,
Freemasons have a special responsibility to insure that the great legacy that our Masonic forefathers
have left us is preserved and maintained. Public education and awareness are critical factors in this
eflort To that end, Califomia Freemasons have a special responsibility to insure that our members, our
families and our communities lXlderstand the importance of the United States Constitution . This should
be accomplished through a variety local programs. patriotic events, articles and public opinion letters
focusing on the history and importanca or our Constitution.

or

or

I therefore proclaim the entire month of September 1995 to be
US CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH
and direct every lodge in California to commemorate the 208th Anniversary of the U.S. Constitution
within each lodge and our communities.
I f\61tl8r direct this Proclamation be read at the August and September meetings of each lodge and that
a formal program focusing on the Constitution be presented within each lodge and local community.
Dated: July 7. 1995
Fraternally,

William F. Stovall , Grand Master

REPORT OF THE SENIOR GRAND WARDE N

Per Capita Recomm endation s for 1996-97
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

APPE NDIX C

Legislatic n adopted at our 1993 Annual Commun ication charges the
Deputy Grand Master with the preparation of a budget covering his anticipated year
as Grand Master. Of necessity , this preparation must begin during his year as
Senior Grand Warden, as the per capita which you act upon at this Annual
Communication will be for our 1996-97 Grand Lodge year. Preliminary work on
the 1996-97 budget was begun several months ago.
As you know from the communication sent to your Lodges by our Deputy
Grand Master we are again supporting a 4% increase in the per capita for the 199697, with a portion of that increase to be allocated to our publication, The California
Freemason. Rising costs, particularly the virtually certain increase in postal rates,
makes it impossible to avoid increasing the allocation to that publication.
As was also stated in our Deputy Grand Master's communi cation to you,
this will leave our Grand Lodge with a smaller operating revenue than for the
previous year. Your Executive Committee pledges itself to continuing the concept
of shared sacrifice. Therefore , although the per capita increases, it will be
matched, as it has been for the past several years, by reductions in the operating
costs of your Grand Lodge equal to the revenue lost by declining membership.
This will continue to be accomplished by careful oversight and tight control of all
Grand Lodge expenditures.
After consultation with representation of the Grand Lodge Finance
Committee, who will present this to you for adoption in their report, we ask for a
total per capita for the 1996-97 Grand Lodge year of $16.1 1, of which $1.16 will
be allocated to the California Freemason.
I might add that the increase for the California Freemason is not likely to
cover the anticipated increased costs, but the California Freemason w ill probably
have to be subsidized by allocation from operating revenue. This has already been
considered in the prelimina ry budget planning.

APPENDIXD

The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting to the
members of this Grand Lodge on the financial condition of Grand Lodge and its
entities, which include the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the California Masonic Foundation, and the Nob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc. (please refer to the opinion leners attached hereto by your
auditors).
The reports and comments of the Grand Treasure r are based on the official
examinations and statements of our Certified Public Accountants whose reports are
an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most
recently ended and contain a complete record of income and expenses for the
period.
The de legates to the Annual Communication are, in effect, the
stockholders of the entities of Grand Lodge and you are encouraged, and it is
recommended, that you read and review this report. Your observations are
appreciated.
Both the Grand Lodge and each of its re lated entities are in sound
financial condition. The extent and size of our charitable activities were fi nancially
possible inlarge measure due to the generosity of prior generations. To assure the
future of these fine programs we must continue our Masonic tradition of financial
support.
Respectfully submined,
Henry H.P. Wilkins, Grand Treasurer

ORGANIZATION AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Organir.ation - Masonic Homes of California ("Masonic Homes"), a California nonprofit corporation

~sters a home for adults at Union City, California, and a home for adults and children at Covina'.

Cal~fonua .•The homes are supported by The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of

Califonua ( Grand Lodge") and members of the Masonic Fraternity in California.

The adult residents who enter Masonic Homes.~ Rquiml by a life care agreement to assign all their
assets to Masoni~ ~omes m exchange for contmumg care for the remainder of the resident's life. In the
event that a contmumg care contract_is cancelled by the resident through withdrawal within the first ninety
da~ of residency, the resident 1s entitled to a pro rata refund of all their assigned assets. Assigned assets
subject to refund at June 30, 199S were approximately $28S,600. The majority of these assets are
recorded as deferred revenue from ass~ assets. Based on historical experience, management believes
no accrual for refundable assigned assets 1s Rquired.

lnvatments in marketable securities are stated at fair market value. Gains or losses that result from
market fluctuations are recogni2al in the period such fluctuations occur. Realized gains or losses
resulting from sales or maturities of securities are calculated on an adjusted cost basis. Adjusted cost is
the market value of the security at the beginning of the year, or the cost if purchased during the year.
Proputy and eq11ip-nt are carried at cost and are depreciated on the straight-line method over the
following estimated lives:

A.um lreld for sale consist primarily of tangible property, including real estate, received from residents

which are held for sale. Assets are recorded at appraised value on date of assignment.

Othu assets consist primarily of resident assigned assets awaiting liquidation, life insurance policies on
residents, and fine art at the two homes.
Life insurance policies are recorded at their actuarially determined present values. Other assigned assets
are recorded at fair market value on date of assignment. Fine art is recorded at appraised value at date of
donation.
Deferred Rever11e from A.ssiped Assets - The fair market value of real and personal property assigned
to Masonic Homes by residents entering into a continuing care contract is deferred and amortized over the

actuarially determined individual or joint and last survivor life expectancy (using straight-line method
based on the State of California Department of Social Services life expectancy table) with any
unamortized balance recogni2a1 as income upon death of the individual or last survivor.

Reven11e Recognilion - Contributions and memorials are recognized as revenue when received. Bequests
are recogni2al as revenue when title is established and the proceeds are measurable. Pensions of residents
whicb are assigned to Masonic Homes are recognized over the life of the resident.

California Franchise Tax Board.

ORGANIZATION AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Organization - Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc ("Nob Hill"), a for-profit c orporation, is a wholly
o"1led subsidiary of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California ("Grand

operates the California Masonic Memorial Temple auditorium, parking garage, exhibit hall, and various
rencal properties under the terms of an operating lease with the California Masonic Memorial Temple (the
"Temple"), an affiliated entity. The financial scatements of Nob Hill are not necessarily indicative of
financial position and results of operations had Nob Hill operated without its affiliation with the Temple .
btvt!stmt!nt st!curilit!s availahlt!for salt! are carried at fair value in accordance with Sratement of
Financial Accounting Standards No. 115 ("SFAS 115"), Accounting for Certain lnvestmen1s in De/11 and
Equity Securities. SFAS 115 escablishcs classification of investments into three categories: held to
maturity, trading, and available for sale. Net unrealized gains and losses a.re excluded from earnings and
reported net of applicable income caxc:s as a separate compcnent of equity until realized. Gains or losses
on sales of securities arc recorded in earnings at the time of sale and are determined by the difference
between the net sales proceeds and the cost of the investment. using the specific identification method.
Nob Hill did not have any investment securities at June 30, 1995 .

Equipmmt, which consists of an automobile, is carried at cost and is depreciated on the straight-line
method over five years.

pension plan (the "Plan") that covers all employees. Benefits are to be paid to eligible employees at

to the Plan reflect benefits attributed to employees' services to date, as well as services expected to be
provided in the future. Plan assets consist primarily of common and preferred stock, investment-grade
corporate bonds, and U.S. government obligations .

INDEPENDENT AUDITORS' REPORT
California Masonic Retirement Plan
We have audited the accompanying Statements of net assets available for benefits of the California
Masonic Retirement Plan (the "Plan") as of December 31, 1994 and 1993, and the related statements of
changes in net assets available for benefits for the years then ended. These financial statements are the
responsibility of the Plan's management Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial
statements based on our audits.
We conducted our audits in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those standards
require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial
statements are free of material misstatement An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence
supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the
accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the
overall financial statement presentation. We believe that our audits provide a reasonable basis for our
opinion.
In our opinion, such financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, information regarding
the Plan's net assets available for benefits at December 31, 1994 and 1993, and the changes therein for
the years then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
Our audits were conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements taken
as a whole. The additional information listed in the Table of Contents is presented for the purpose of
additional analysis and is not a required part of the basic financial statements, but is supplementary
information required by the Department of Labor's Rules and Regulations for Reporting and Disclosure
under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. This additional information is the
responsibility of the Plan's management. Such additional information has been subjected to the auditing
procedures applied in our audit of Ute basic 1994 financial statements and, in our opinion, is fairly stated
in all material respects when considered in relation to the basic financial statements taken as a whole.

DESCRIPTION OF THE PLAN AND SUMMARY OF
SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Gerrua/ - 1lie California Masonic Retirement Plan (the "Pl;111") is a defined benefit plan that pro\ ides
retirement benefits for substantially all employees of Masonic Homes of California., Masonic. Grand
Lodge and Component Organizations (collectively, "Grand Lodge") who have reached the age of 21 and
completed one year of service. It is subject to the provisions of the Employee Retirement Income Secumy
Act of 1974 ("ERISA"). Participants should refer to the Plan documents for a more complete descnption
of the Plan

Employees with five or more years of SCl"Vlce arc entitled to annual pension benefits bcginntng at normal
retirement age (65). For service prior to January I, 1990. the annual reurcment benefit at normal
retirement is equal to 2% of the average annual compensation earned during the five calendar years prior
to January 1, 1989 times years of service through 1990. For sel"Vlce after Dcccmber 31, 1989 the annual
retirement benefit at normal retirement is equal to 2 ~. of the compensation earned in c:ich full and partial
year of service. The Plan was amended effective January 1, 1993 and changes the Plan's method of
calculating the benefit formula. For service prior to January I , 1993, the annual retirement benefit at
normal retirement is equal to 2% of the average annual compensation earned during the five calendar
years priorto January I, 1993 . For service after fanuary 1. 1993 the aruiual retirement benefit at normal
retirement is equa1 to 2% of the compensation earned 10 c;ich full and partial year of service. In addiuon.
the revision cscablishcs an hour requirement of at least 50 I hours of service to be credited with a year of
service for these purposes.
The Plan pennits early retirement at ages 55 to 64 for participants with a minimum often years of
service. Married employees may elect to receive their pension benefits in the form of a joint and survivor
annuity. If employees terminate before rendering five )'ealS of service, they forfeit the right to receive the
portion of their accumulated plan benefits anributable to the Grand Lodge's contributions.
If an active employee dies at age 55 or older, a death benefit equal to the value of the employee's
accumulated required contributions is paid to the employee's beneficiary A death benefit will also be
payable to an employee who dies after accumulaung five years of SCl"VICe Active employees who become
disabled and totally incapacitated may receive an aruiual disabahty benefit that is equal to the normal
retirement benefits they have accumulated as of the tame they become duabled, reduced for early
"1tbdrawal. Disability bcocfits arc paid until normal retirement age, at \\lucb umc disabled participants
bcg.m receiving normal retircmcot benefits.

The assets of the Plan arc m;llntaincd in a b'ust established pursuant to a trust agreement between the
Grand Lodge and Wells Fargo Bank. N.A
Basis of Acco"ntilrg - Tbc: financial statements of the Plan arc prq>ared under the accrual basis of
accounting.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. o/California:

My Brethren:

APPENDIXE

This is the fourth time that I have had the privilege of addressing you as
Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge. The 1994/95 Grand Lodge Year has been
an eventful one for the Grand Lodge Office, and each year progress is made toward
providing greater services to our constituent Lodges at less cost. This is also the
first year of operation without an Assistant Grand Secretary as an employee on the
staff. The operations of the office have changed, and hopefully improved, as the
restructuring has taken place.
Electronic Communication
This is the age of communication, and several major steps·were taken this
year in making the Grand Lodge Office more responsive to the constituent Lodges.
The biggest of these steps was the installation of a fax/modem bulletin board with
a dedicated " 800" number, for use by Secretaries. The increasing availability of
fax machines and computers with both modems and fax boards, made this next step
inevitable. Secn;taries now can send in their Activity Reports (formerly the
" monthly reports") via fax or modem, as well as mailing them to the Grand Lodge
Office. Reports are sent to the Grand Lodge Office only if there is an activity to
report. If there is no activity, then no report is due or expected. This is intended
to reduce unnecessary paperwork, and allow Lodges to concentrate on sending in
relevant information when necessary rather than filing unnecessary reports
monthly.
Secretaries are encouraged to send in changes of address as soon as they
are received at the local Lodge, and the fax/modem system, with the " 800" number
makes this an easy task. The savings to Grand Lodge in returned mail alone far
outweighs the cost of the " 800" number.
Secretaries' Workshops
This year two all-day workshops for Lodge Secretaries were held. The
first was held on March 4, 1995, in San Diego, and the second was held on June 10,
1995, in Sacramento. These workshops proved to be highly successful, and six are
planned for 1996. The focus ofthe workshops was the role of the Secretary as the
chief administrative officer of the Lodge, just as the Master is the chief executive
officer. The working sessions were designed along the same lines as the Wardens '

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

194

Retreats, and placed an emphasis on the Secretary as a part of the Lodge
Leadership Team .
Secretaries' Associations
An effort was made in mid-year to revive the secretaries' associations,
some of which had discontinued meeting as a result of the loss of the position of
Assistant Grand Secretary at the Grand Lodge Office as an employee available to
meet with these associations on a regular basis. These associations are valuable to
our Grand Lodge, and the Grand Secretary took over the fonner role of the
Assistant Grand Secretary in meeting regularly with these associations. Meetings
were held in Redding, Long Beach, Redlands, Oakland, Sacramento, and San
Diego. Future meetings are now scheduled on a regular basis, and other
associations are being revived as well. The ability to devote this time to local
secretaries' associations was made available by a new arrangement with the several
boards and committees which the Grand Secretary serves as Secretary of Record.
Most of them selected a trustee to record the minutes at their meetings, freeing the
Grand Secretary from the responsibility of attending each of their several meetings
each year. The resultant time that was made available could be devoted to meeting
with Lodge Secretaries, both in the workshops and in the secretaries' associations.
Computerization of Grand Lodge Information Systems
This year saw the completion of a two-year project to completely organize
all the complex infonnation that flows through the Grand Lodge Office into a
system of Jogs so that infonnation can be tracked and monitored. This has enabled
the Grand Lodge Office to provide a better flow of work in the office, and to
establish time lines for the completion of tasks. These systems included charter
amendments, by-law amendments, dispensations, consolidations, Roster changes,
address changes, out-of-state communications, fifty and seventy-five year pin
presentation, Hiram Awards, and general communication and mail distribution.
Multiple Roles of the Grand Secretary
The Grand Secretary is expected to perfonn many roles on behalf of the
Grand Lodge of California, and its constituent Lodges. Among these are the
following:

Finally, thanks must also go to the Brethren who work with the Grand
Lodge Office as . well as discharging their own significant responsibilities as
president or chainnan of major boards and committees: Roy J. Hen ville, President
of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees; Frank Russell, President of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees; Donald B. McCaw,
President of Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc., Board of Directors; David C .
Decker, President of the California Masonic Foundation Board of Trustees; and
other important chainnen of various Grand Lodge Committees. And above all,
thanks must go to Most Worshipful William F. Stovall for his support this year, and
for that of the Executive Committee. They set high expectations for the Grand
Lodge Office, and our employees have labored long and hard to fulfi ll those
expectations. Our goal is to provide quality service for those who depend upon us
to do the right job, and to do the j ob right.
Respectfully submitted,
John L. Cooper III, PM, Grand Secretary

The Grand Lodge of California maintains fraternal relations with other
Grand Lodges throughout the world. A current listing of those that we recognize
is printed in the General Appendix of the Proceedings each year.
Until 1992 the Committee on Recognition recommended to the Grand
Master the recognition of new Grand Lodges. If interim recognition was granted
by the Grand Master, it was laid before Grand Lodge at the following Annual
Communication for approval. Recognition then became permanent, unless
subsequently revoked by Grand Lodge. In 1992 the Committee on Recognition
was dissolved, and these duties were transferred to the Grand Secretary.
In 1994/95 Grand Master William F. Stovall took the following actions
with respect to the establishment of recognition of Grand Lodges:
( 1)

Grand Lodge of Rondonia. in Brazil :
Interim recognition was given to the Grand Lodge of Rondonia
in Brazil, which had requested such recognition from our Grand
Lodge. This Grand Lodge meets all the criteria established by
the Commission on Recognition of the Conference of Grand
Masters of Masons in North America for recognition.

(2)

Grand Lodge Yugoslavia:
The "Grand Lodge Yugoslavia" c.hanged its name to the
"Regular Grand Lodge Yugoslavia," and the Commission on
Recognition of the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in
N orth America recommended acceptance of this name change.
Confirmation of this name change was granted by the Grand
Master.

For the complete report of the Trial Review Committee on the above
Trials, please refer to Appendix "K" of these Proceedings.

(3)

Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile:
The Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile asked for recogntion from the
Grand Lodge of California. After review, the Grand Master
decline to grant recognition. His decision was based on the the
1993 Recognition Report issued by the Commission on
Recognition of the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in
North America, which recommended against the recognition of
any Grand Lodge in Exile.

REPORT OF THE GR.\ND LECTURER

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F& A.M. of California:
Brethren - in just a little less than three days, this Grand Lodge year will
become another page in the history of our Grand Lodge.

APPENDIXF

At the outset, I take this opportunity to express my sincerest ''Thank You"
for the privilege to serve this jurisdiction as its Grand Lecturer.
Excellence in ritual continues to be our strongest resolve - it has been most
rewarding for me to observe the concentration of effort which is applied at all
levels of our ritual instructional system. From the Grand Lecturer and the Assistant
Grand Lecturers, to the Inspectors, Coaches, Officers and Brethren. Literally
thousands of hours are spent studying, teaching, trying to perfect the ritual, yet the
demand for more effort on the part of all of us, continues to be ever with us.
Fifteen seminars were conducted throughout the jurisdiction this Grand
Lodge year. The program continues to be growing more popular, with a greater
number in attendance at almost all of them. The enthusiasm is ever-present and I
thank you for making the effort to be there.
On Saturday, September 23rd of this year, I visited Maya Lodge No. 793.
They were conferring the third degree for the first time in the Spanish language.
I do not speak no·r understand the Spanish language. Nevertheless, I was impressed
with the floor work and the dignified manner in which the degree was conferred.
I have now witnessed all three degrees and have the assurance of the Inspector,
Worshipful James Paden, who speaks Spanish, and the translators, that the ritual
has been accurately translated. With the above qualifications and assurances, I am
pleased to certify that the Spanish language is now officially a part of this
jurisdiction.
To Worshipful James Paden, Inspector of the 334th District, to the
translators, to the officers and members of Maya Lodge No. 793 , to Worshipful
Arthur Hernandez, Inspector of the 328th District, who also assisted, please accept
my heartfelt congratulations for bringing your dream into fruition - mis herrnanos,
los felicito, gracias.
In closing, my personal thanks to our Grand Master and his wife, Beverly,
for all the courtesies extended to me throughout the year, along with the warmth
of their friendship. To the rest of the "team" who have acquitted themselves so
ably in our ceremonies, and for their everlasting friendship, my thank you.
To our Candidates' and Officers' Coaches, your efforts are always deeply
appreciated. To our Inspectors, and to those who have served in that capacity who

222

are leaving or have left us during the year, no expression of gratitude can be
adequate. To my colleagues on the committee, your efforts, strength and support
are and have always been appreciated, thank you . To the Grand Secretary and his
entire staff for the ir continued and val uable assistance, thank you.
Again, to you, my brethren, for allowing me the privilege to serve our
fraternity, thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos, Grand Lecturer
