GRAND CHAPLAIN'S MESSAGE
Donald W. Lindenau. Grand Chaplain
Sunday, October 8, 1995

APPENDIXG

In April 1912, the largest, most luxurious vessel every built set out upon
her maiden voyage across the North Atlantic. The eyes of the world were upon her
and such high hopes were held for her by her builders. This magn ifice nt creation
was greater than the sum of all the parts and people involved in her building. She
was immense and so richly appointed. Every im aginable service was ava ilable.
She was so big and so safe that she was believed by all to be indestructible. The
passengers were busily leading the good life and having such a good time. They
were secure and wann and cozy and well fed. They were being waited upon by the
crew and their every need was being met. They were oblivious to the course and
speed being taken by the captain and - we all know what happened to the Titanic
on the night of April 14th when she was driven onto that which destroyed her along
with most of those aboard.
The people of this country have , what I call, the ''Titanic Mentality."
What makes America so great? We cannot deny that the land itse lf has
helped. One of our most moving and patriotic hymns cites the beauty of America,
Katherine Lee Bates stood atop Pike's Peak and scanned the sweep of the land then
wrote of the "Puri>le Mountains Majesties" and the ''Amber Waves of Grain." She
concluded that God had shed his Grace on this land, a vast and rich wilderness that
in a short time grew into a great nation and spread " From Sea to Shining Sea." But
a nation is made great not by just its fruitful acres but by the spirit and the character
of the men who cultivate them.
Alex De Tocqueville, the great French political philosopher of the 19th
century, visited this country for the purpose of discovering the secret of her
greatness. He traveled from town to town talking with people. He exam ined our
young national government, our schools and our centers of business. But not until
he visited the churches o f this land, which he described as "Aflame w ith
Righteoi..1sness" did he feel that he had found the secret of our greatness. Returning
to France he summarized his findings by stating simply. "America is great because
America has put God at the center of its life. And if America ever fails to do so,
America will cease to be great."
Their French revolution had been very anti-Christian and it was almost as
dangerous to be religious as it was to be royalty. In a very few short years
Napoleon proclaimed himself as Emperor and the French revolution was lost.
The Ru ssian revolution was a Godless gathering of ruthl ess thugs who
recognized no power but their own. The bounty of the country along with all rights

226

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and privileges were dispensed according to political loyalty and - were guaranteed
to no one.
All ofour Founding Documents from the Mayflower Compact. to the New
England Charter. to the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution - all have
evidence that our Nation was founded on a commitment to God and the principles
of his Holy Word.
We have al I read the profound and eloquent statements of the Founding
Fathers as they acknowledge the role of God in the formation of our country. They
profess faith in a Creator who works in and governs the affairs of men in
establishing absolute standards and to which men are held accountable. For the
protection of its religious people they provided for the separation of the State from
the Church. But. should God be eliminated from government. their answer would
be "Never."
In its 200 plus years of existence our country has known the stinging
reality of conflict. There have been wars, assass inations, inj ustices, catastrophes
and plagues of disease. But our country has endured for its moral fabric has been
woven with the durable threads of spiritual and scriptural truths.
But as the children of Israel did from time to time. Americans have
forgotten their spiritual and religious heritage. In Israel's case God always sent
prophets to forestall final judgement. But us? We are still sailing full speed ahead
through the fog.
You have all heard the story of the two men who were talking and one
asked the other, " What do you think are the two most important things that are
wrong with the people of this country." His friend replied, " Look - I don 't know
and I don ' t care." The man replied. "You got them both right." Although our
nation is rotting from the inside and there are those at work to undennine our
freedom s, too many people are either not aware or they just don't care.
The new politically correct word for atheism is secularism. which we hear
a lot about and which rejects and is opposed to all fonns of religion. The
dangerous thing about secularism is that it has been adopted by segments of our
government and the courts who are all working to eliminate religion from any
meaningful participation in our society. They believe that man has evolved to
perfection and is now qualified to replace God' s law with man 's law.
God, along with any reference to his Laws or Commandments has been
driven from our schools. Neither the Golden Rule nor any of our virtues or values
can be taught because they are religious in origin. All religious expression has
been eliminated from public places and with government intruding itself into more
and more aspects of our lives, there are few places outside the home or church
where we can display or engage in religious activity. They legislate immorality

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

227

and we endorse it with our silence. And where is God in our personal lives? He
is locked up in the attic with crazy Aunt Hattie. We let him out for weddings and
funerals. Political philosophers today assure us that we have gone beyond the need
for religion and are already referring to this time in our lives as "The Post Christian
Era."
The consequence of this is that all the rights and freedoms which we enjoy
are being separated from their historical base and their religious roots. When the
day is reached that we all believe that we crawled out of some slime pool in the
dark distant past and that we have evolved into what we are today, then that
eliminates the Creator from the political equation. All of those high sounding
phrases in our Founding Documents that say we are endowed by our Creator with
certain unalienable rights among which are the right to life, to liberty and to the
pursuit of happiness, they all go out the window. If there was no Creator then it
follows that he could not have endowed us with any rights. No Creator - no rights.
Without God, our Creator, standing in the center of our lives, when you remove
Him, that leaves only man as the measurer and the judge of all things. Man will
decide what is good for you and will be the bestower, the giver and taker of all
rights and privileges - and they will be guaranteed to no one.
The Israelites in their time also opted for the "new morality". They were
as enthusiastic as many of our present thinkers are about situational ethics. We
read in Judges that "In those days there was no King in Israel and every man did
what was right in ~is own eyes." But, as the Israelites learned time and time again
that it was only by submission to the Laws of the God of their Fathers that they
could survive and prosper. But us, we are still heading for that big chunk of ice out
there.
But, not to worry - not to worry. This country is so immense, so diverse,
so richly endowed. The eyes of the world are upon us and such high hopes are held
for us. America is so big and so safe that certainly we are indestructible. We are
leading such a good life, so warm and secure and so well fed. Certainly we can
survive and overcome anything. Who cares on what course the Captain is taking
us. This is the Titanic mentality.
Will God send a prophet to forestall our final judgement? Will we, while
we are cozy and leading the good life allow our country to continue on the reckless
course that it is on? Or will we, like the children of Israel, realize in time that it is
only by submitting to the Laws of the God of our Fathers that we can survive and
prosper as a nation.
Collectively we can make a difference. But in order to make a difference
collectively we must act and make a difference as individuals. lfthis government
of the people, by the people and for the people is to function, then every citizen has
a responsibility to participate. This is not an option but rather a mandate as a

228

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

citizen and a Mason. Ifwe are to save our Faith, our Families and our Freedoms
then we must register, be infonned, vote and actively influence others.
This is what makes Masonry so fundamentally important to this country.
Masonry compliments and does not contradict religious beliefs. It is supporting
of morality and virtue. It is a supplement to the leading of a good life. It gives
another dimensio n to living and is a fonn of dedication to God, to Country and to
Family. We endeavor to keep our moral standards at a high level and to pass them
behind so that others will benefit. And we finnly believe that it is only under God
that this Nation, or any nation, can remain free.
Only man is capable of religion. It is our ability to have religious feelings
and religious faith that elevates us above the animals. So - without religion - what
are we? Although God has placed us above the animals, certainly there are those
who have qualities which inspire us.
Our Grand Master is an admirer of the American Eagle and it is most
appropriate that this should be so. For thousands of years the eagle has been
admired for its grandeur, for its grace in flight and its great size and awesome
power. The soaring eagle is also a stirring picture of the true meaning of Masonry.
Assisted by his powerful wings the eagle glides effortlessly to altitudes of over
2,400 feet and is capable of using his powerful wings to carry other eagles to
safety. Turbulent winds only cause him to fly higher and faster. The eagles keen
eyesight enables him to be sensitive to approaching danger and to protect himself
and his family. The eagle displays the sense of responsibility that is a companion
to genuine liberty. He mates for life and returns to the same nest each year. He
takes an active role in providing for his family and in teaching his young to fly. In
so many ways the eagle illustrates the life, the victory, the power and the freedom
that God gives to those of us who put our Faith in Him.
God Bless You Everyone.

Who is Tampering With the Soul of America?

·I

J

229

In reflecting upon the Grand Master's Theme for 1995, "freemasonry for
God, for Country and for Family'', I found that I was unable to think of them as
separate entities and for me, God, Country and Family are inseparable. The family,
with faith in God sufficient to obey His Commandments is the "Little Platoon"
upon which our country runs. This family makes up and constitutes what our
country is. To me - they are all one.
History tells us that there has been no society which has not sought to give
meaning and order to life through some fonn of religion. Out of religion flows the
Higher Law principle which was so central to our Founding Fathers and upon
which the entire history of British and American constitutional law is based. Out
of religion, with all its hopes and fears, arises our cultural values, our standards for
both public and private moral discipline. From it we develop a sense of family
commitment and personal responsibility. Religion has participated in education
and has been a strong character building institution for both young and old alike.
From it we learn to have Faith, Hope, Charity and love for our fellow man.
Religious beliefs 1ead to moral absolutes, that some things are always the right
thing to do and other are always wrong. And above all, we have believed that
arising from and beyond our conduct, there are eternal consequences for our soul.
Our very system of government has worked because of the sacred aura
surrounding our founding documents. The frequent reference to God, our Creator,
establish that these were more than legal documents. They were a covenant, an
oath between the American people and before God.
Prior to 1962 our courts subscribed to the idea that a government of the
people ought to reflect the values of the people it governed. That the Constitution
was all about placing restraints upon the federal government, which was only
empowered to perfonn a few specific tasks, none of which included interfering in
the lives of its religious people. The First Amendment was specifically to protect
a religious people from government. And this was the kind of Nation we were for
most of our 200 plus years. However, in 1962, with a new make-up of the court,
all this changed.
Madeline Murray O'Hare objected to her son hearing a school prayer each
day, which resulted in the Supreme Court ruling that the practice of prayer in
school was unconstitutional and ordered that it be discontinued in all public schools
in the land. Mrs O'Hare's son has since become a Christian Minister and has

231

disassociated himself from his mother who he describes as an unmitigated atheist
and communist. But regardless, she had accomplished her purpose.

he could not be relied upon to leave religion out of his speech. A_ teach.er was
suspended for having a Bible on his school desk, and another fo~ m.clud 1~g the

him to draw. There are over 30 years worth of stories just like these.

Alexander Solzhenitsyn tells us in his writings that to destroy a people you
must first sever them from their roots, and if you want to change things, you have
to start with the children.
The school prayer issue has since gone far beyond both school and prayer,
and although there is no direct mention of either school or prayer in the
Constitution, we have come to learn that what the Constitution says and what the
law is whatever 5 members of the Supreme Court say that it is. Ever since its 1962
ruling the Supreme Court has used the supposed menace ofreligion as a launching
pad for broader attacks in order to eradicate all religious expression or reference
from our institutions and from Americas's public life. And ever since l 962 we
have seen a growing influence and acceptance in our schools and in our public life
of a doctrine identified as secular pluralism.
Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary describes a Secularist as "One who
rejects every fonn of religious faith and who believes that education and
government should be without religious element." Pluralism is the doctrine that
there is more than one kind of ultimate reality. Pluralists reject the idea of moral
absolutes as being too confrontational, too authoritarian, too dogmatic. They
substitute a live and let live, fuzzy kind of morality where everyone is allowed to
feel good. Their doctrine releases man from the constraints placed on him by
religion and makes him and his intellect the measurer of all things. Their common
and constant refrains are, "Don't impose your values on me - who are you to judge
me? and who is to say what is right or wrong?" This doctrine has been very
attractive to a segment of our young people because it gives them everything they
want and nothing that they need. If this doctrine continues as it is, unchecked, then
eventually everyone will be living by their own set of rules and we will look a long
time before we find a man who will give the right answer when asked, "In whom
do you put your trust."
In 1985 the High Court ruled that a State authorized moment of silence at
the beginning of the school day was unconstitutional because some students might
take it as encouragement to use that moment for silent prayer. Many school
administrators, fearing costly litigation at the hands of secular civil liberty lawyers,
joined the courts in becoming adversaries of religion and hostile toward the
feelings of religious parents.
In St. Louis a 4th grader was placed in 3 days detention for bowing her
head and whispering a prayer over her lunch in the school cafeteria. Another suit
involved an I I year old Oklahoma girl who used her recess time to discuss religion
with her class mates. The senior class president of a Georgia high school was not
pennitted to make the farewell address to which his grades entitled him - because

And so - here we are. What are the consequences of all this? Do you thin.k

The efforts of the family and the home and the church to perform their
sacred duty of passing to the next generation a high sense of values has been
demeaned and undermined and held up to ridicule to the point where many of our
young people simply go their own way - and we are paying the price for that. The
character building institutions home, family, church and school do not exist in little
vacuums, separate and apart from each other. There has to be a free flow between
them of all that is uplifting. challenging, inspiring - and they must supplement and
support the efforts of each other. Above all, any one of our character building
institutions should not be hostile towards nor attempt to subvert the efforts of the
others.

One of the decisions handed down by the Supreme Court on the very last
day of its 1994/95 session dealt with the Church State issue and it ruled in favor of
the students. The Court stated that, in the case before them, the school's
suppression of the student's religious expression constituted a violation of the
student's right of free speech, which is a beginning. In a recent interview of a
Supreme Court Justice he explained that when the Court goes off in a new
direction, that they watch it for a while and if it doesn't seem to be working - they
make an adjustment. It isn't working. It hasn't been working - not for us.
However, there are signs of a reawakening and 1 believe that, in our time, we will
see a spiritual element and values that are the fruit of the religious tree returned to
our institutions - including our schools. I believe that there is a growing National
Will to do this, and as Masons we should work to encourage and strengthen that
National Will. There are those who say you can't tum the clock back. I say you
can. We do it all the time. When the clock is wrong we set it back. We must work
to insure that our next generation of children are raised in an atmosphere less
hostile toward religion. And we can not allow our value system and our code of
moral conduct to be rejected and abandoned because they are religious in origin.

A reading of Robert Rourke's book, "Something of Value" should have
alerted us to the consequences of what we were doing to our children. Although
he was writing of the people of Kenya, since man is a spiritual being wherever he
is found, the same applies to us. Mr Rourke writes that if a people are cut off from
there source of spiritual life that gives meaning and purpose and maintains order
in their lives, then a void is created. And if this void is not soon filled with
something of equal value, then it will be filled with something destructive and it is
only a matter of time until there erupts an explosion of violence. We are living
through our explosion of violence now.
During this past June the California State Assembly Select Committee on
Children held hearings in Sacramento to determine the condition of California's 8.9
million children. Young people from around the state were invited to testify and
following the hearings newspapers around the state carried stories like this - this
from the Stockton Record. '' ST A TE FAILING TEENS'' cries the headline.
" California needs to find a way to teach youngsters to believe in themselves and to
have faith in the future." The anicle goes on to say, "They have lost hope in
everything, they lack motivation." All this in the most prosperous country in the
world, with the most freedom to be the best that you can be, and the country to
which people come from all over the world because of the boundless opportunities
to be found here. To believe, to have faith , to have hope, these are all spiritual
qualities that they are looking for and which they expect to receive from the State.
Well, they are looking in the wrong place. God did not create the State, man did
that.
For faith and hope and for all things spiritual they must look to the being
that is within themselves and - to their Creator. The State can't teach them to
believe in themselves, but what the State can do is to get out of the way and stop
interfering with the effons of the family and their churches who are endeavoring
to instill all those spiritual qualities which our youth complain that they are lacking
and - for which they appear to be searching.

We must remember that our children are messengers that we are sending
into a time that we will not sec. And so how important it is that the message they
carry include God's Laws and His Eternal Truths - and a knowledge of and a love
for their Creator.
Earlier this year your Grand Lodge performed a Cornerstone Laying
Ceremony at the Mary Peacock Elementary School in Crescent City. The first new
school built there in over 40 years. Two men who were instrumental in
accomplishing this were speakers at the ceremony. One was a member of the
Board of Education and the other was a member of the County Board of
Supervisors, and both wore the apron of a Master Mason. An example, my
Brethren, worthy of all imitation.
We speak with pride of our Masonic leaders and heroes of the past. We
are the Masonic leaders of today and we have to wonder what the Masons of the
future will say of us. I believe that the Masons of the 90's have a mission and a
future. That mission is to build a better tomorrow by helping to build a better child
today through our suppon of the Masonic Model Student Assistance Training
Program. We can't salvage them all. We know that we are going to have to
continue to pay the price for all those who have already gone over the edge. But
for everyone that is lost there is one who has a void in his life, who has unm et and
previously unrecognized physical or spiritual needs. California Masons should
support the Masonic Model program because it is a sound investment in the future
of our community and in the future of Freemasonry. We will take great pride in
what it will accomplish and I believe history will treat us well.

GRAND ORATION

Auri Spigelman, Grand Orator
"What Came You Here To Do?"

APPENDIX H

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters, Grand
Lodge Officers, visiting dignitaries and my brethren all:
Can a Grand Oration really make a difference to you? Could it modify
your intentions and decisions at this Communication, so to characterize them as
courageous and frame breaking? These are the imperatives of my message to you
today.
Permit me. first. to set the stage with a history of the Grand Orator's
office. and let us learn something of the rich heritage of wisdom and grace le ft by
my predecessors, since the lessons of the past can teach us to adapt our actions to
the demands of the present. With a complete set of the Proceedings of our Annual
Communications at my disposal, I sequentially read all of the past Grand Orations.
I discovered that it was not until 1856, at the 7th Annual Communication, that
Grand Master William H. Howard appointed John F. Morse the first Grand Orator;
that in I 857 authorization was obtained "to procure su itable jewels and regalia for
the Grand Orator''; and that the I 859 revision of the Grand Lodge Constitution was
the first to list the Grand Orator among other Grand Lodge Officers. Then, as still
defined today, the Grand Orator's function was "to deliver at each Annual
Communication an address to the Grand Lodge, upon maners appertaining to the
Craft."
My 128 predecessors were very capable. even exceptional, men. ten of
whom served in the position twice, and 32 of whom eventually became Grand
Master. The only Past Grand Master to assume the office was James A. Foshay,
in 191 2. Two former Grand Orators are presently standing for Grand Line election
(Charles Alexander and Melville Nahin). These highly-educated men spoke with
inspiring, and often sermonic, eloquence. Many were politicians, professionals and
clergymen. Those of the legal profession have predominated, and distinguished
statesmen from among them have included a Governor and several Senators,
Congressmen, and Judges. Only in a dream could my skills emulate the h igh
oratorical standards set by such brilliant and talented brethren as Thomas Starr
King, John Felton, Jacob Voorsanger, Francis Baker, James Foshay, Will iam
Rhodes Hervey. Samuel Burke, Ellsworth Meyer, Leo Anderson and many of the
former Grand Orators sitting here with us today. As Antony explained in " Ju lius
Caesar" (Act III, Scene 2):

238

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

religion and to politics. They chafed at, and passionately protested, the
unwarranted and insidious accusations that were occasionally leveled against the
Craft. In the 1920s and 1930s they seemed to be over concerned, perhaps to
obsession, that Masons be perceived as loyal citizens of this country. They
repeatedly expressed opposition to labor unrest, gangsterism, and the many other
" -isms" of the day, such as socialism, communism, Nazism, agnosticism and
atheism.

"I am no orator, as Brutus is.
For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth,
Action, nor utterance, nor the power of speech
To stir men' s blood. I only speak right on."
Reading these Orations was an ocular challenge, as well, for until the turn
of the century they were printed in seven point type, with little space between the
lines. Only in recent years have they been enlarged to ten point type. The
browning and brittle paper of older volumes was another hindrance. The Orations
often ran to 14 or 18 pages, which, if delivered as such, probably required an hour
or more.
James L. English authored the first published Grand Oration, in 1859. Of
the subsequent 126 printed Grand Orations, that of 1900 was only a summary. Five
were delivered ex tempore, and their manuscripts were never submitted for
publication (1873, 1891, 1905, 1908 and 1928). Apparently, six Orations were
never given (1857, 1858, 1864, 1870 and 1945), and there is always some lore
about such occurrences. For example, Grand Orator James H. Hardy was not
permitted to speak in 1870. During the course of the year, the charter of his lodge
had been revoked by the Grand Master "for good and sufficient reason." Never
citing that reason, Hardy' s personal membership was restored at the Annual
Communication of 1871 . Speeches, printed in the Proceedings but not considered
Grand Orations, were delivered at the cornerstone dedications of the Grand Lodge
Temple in San Francisco in 1860, and the Decoto Masonic Home in 1896.
"Operative or Speculative" was the first titled Grand Oration, given by Brother
Benjamin Bledsoe in 1909; but it was not until after 1935 that titles appeared more
routinely.
These Orations constitute an exceptional Masonic education, and I suggest
that for the purpose of study and discussion, they be published as a collection.
Within them is interwoven a panoply of Masonic information and American
history: from the Revolutionary to Civil Wars, through the bereavement of
President Garfield ' s assassination, through the terrible anguish of the two World
Wars, to the anxieties of the Depression years, and to the mounting concerns about
the rapid and radical changes that pervade contemporary society. The emotional
impact of the Orator's stories was often electrifying.
Throughout most of the 19th century, the Grand Orators eloquently
portrayed several theories of Masonic origin. In what were attempts, perhaps, to
justify Masonry' s existence, they repeatedly expounded on its purposes and
principles. They defined Masonic culture as the advancement of high moral and
intellectual forces in an environment of ha rmonious social interaction. They
opined on " what it means to be a Mason" and on the relationships of Masonry to

239

\

1'

It was not until the mid- l 880s that organizational problems began to
surface, and by the 1890s reproach became a more frequent Oration tactic. In
1892, Grand Orator Reuben Lloyd discussed some very familiar-sounding practical
problems of the day. Why was lodge attendance decreasing? Education lacking?
Social programs poor? Admission standards inconsistent? As to why only 1110 to
117 of lodge memberships were attending meetings, he cited business pressures;
lack of interest, boredom and unfriendliness; self-serving motives; non-adherenc e
to Masonic principles outside the lodge; poor ritual performance; no educational
discussion groups; and the attractiveness of the social activities of other societies.
Through the years, the exposition of problems became a dominant theme of the
Orations, accompanied by a litany of suggestions that " we should" , " we ought to"
and "we must" adopt, at least theoretically. Solutions and schemes for their
implementation were poorly defined, however, and it would not be until the late
1980s that the deliberations of the Long Range Planning Committee would set the
stage for Masonic Renewal efforts.
What was Grand Orator Eugene N. Dueprey' s focus of concern in 1895,
exactly 100 years ago? Interestingly, Masonic education! He mentioned that the
expression "knowledge is power" was well known even to ancient civilizations
and that the development of mind, so-called " enlightenment", was a paramoun~
ambition among them. Symbols of moral principle were clothed in " mysteries",
in order to indelibly impress their lessons upon initiates to the philosophical orders.
For similar purposes, Freemasonry 's ritual has preserved the essence of these
elegant traditions. Beyond the candidate level, however, it became a brother' s duty
to continually study and reflect and teach, not only Masonic history and
philosophy, but also the liberal arts and sciences. Dueprey challenged the brethren
to proudly discourse on Freemasonry ' s mission as an instrument of friendship,
benevolence and compassion toward others; as a model for man' s plans, purposes,
hopes and strivings to be better; and as a platform to strengthen and express a belief
and devotion to God. Such are the tenets of brotherly love, relief and truth! In his
concluding remarks, Dueprey stated that consonant with the Masonic ideal, "the
true purpo~e of education is to cherish and unfold the seed of immortality already
sown within us; to develop to their fullest extent the capacities of every kind with
which the God who made us has endowed us."

What shall we do? How often I've smiled during the second section of the
third degree, when the triad ofFellowcrafts simultaneously exclaim "What shall we
do?" They exemplify the importance of fraternal caring and concern, and promote
their dependence upon one another in collective effort. But, as conversation
proceeds, they remind us that ultimately we are accountable for our actions and
must report to a higher authority. "Agreed!" The degree then teaches us the
importance of independent thought and action. "Hold! Before we return and
report, let us separate", ostensibly for individual experiences. But, " let us keep
within hailing distance" , that is, within the same context, so we may once again
"meet and consult should any important discovery be made."
What shall we do? We have a Masonic Renewal Task Force that is
composed of some of the brightest and most creative brethren in this jurisdiction.
They have consulted and deliberated, and discovered a:
VISION FOR FREEMASONRY IN CALIFORNIA:
Freemasonry in California will be a preeminent fraternal organization of quality
men, selected without regard to race, religion or creed.
Freemasonry will be dedicated to charity, true fellowship and brotherly love under
the Fatherhood of God.
Freemasonry will embrace and spiritually enrich its members with an ethical value
system that will contribute substantially to their personal happiness and
satisfaction.
Freemasonry will be a relevant organization, dedicated to delighting, involving and
educating members and their families; where the lodge will be a vibrant,
respected, and contributing part of its community.
Freemasonry will be well led, financially secure, and distinguished from other
organizations by the quality of the experiences it provides its members,
in an environment of shared fellowship.

242

PROCEEDrNGS OF THE

Freemasonry will be actively involved with youth in ways that guide and improve
their lives as ethical and productive members of society.
A man who becomes a Mason in California will be proud of his membership and
will radiate enthusiasm about his organization that makes a difference.
A man who is active in Masonry in California will find his lodge a place to learn
and to lead, to respect and be respected, and to contribute in a way that
brings him personal growth.
The Renewal Task Force understands that " life is made up of effort and
results", and that "the strength of the effort is the measure of the result." It realizes
that attainment of its vision for the lodges and their members will require a
proactive, even aggressive, stance. It intends to learn from both the successes and
failures of the past. Consultants need to be hired, products must be created, and
experimental programs authorized. Excellent publications and practical seminars,
besides our successful Wardens' Retreats, must be created to guide our lodge
officers in administrative, educational, financial , membership, family, public
relations and community programs. A modem "Table Lodge" protocol, Masonic
plays, and other meaningful materials must be written for the brethren to enjoy.
We need to harness the technological revolution for our benefit: audio and
videotapes, cable television, computers, CD-ROMs, and what is now known as
" Masonic Cyberspace" on the Internet. To capture interest, we need to create
interactive Masonic education courses and even Masonic video games; we might
even explore "virtual reality." The Masonic Information Services Team has been
established not only to formulate this information and these products, but also to
efficiently distribute them. Internal marketing and communications among our
brethren will be improved. Our community image and reputation will be polished
brightly. The process to ena ble this vision has begun ; the educational tools for the
renewal solution are understood .
What came you here to do? To guarantee the future of this Fraternity.
First, there are several economic realities for you to consider:
l.
Inflation has priced goods at 15 to 20 times that of 35 to 40 year
ago.
2.
Lodge dues have barely increased in that period; certainly not
commensurate with the value of Masonry.
3.
This is a time of diminishing membership and diminishing
revenues.
4.
Efficiency measures recently adopted by Grand Lodge have
drastically cut operating expenses and committee budgets.

Although our Foundation and Endowment Funds are successful
for their specific functions, we are severely constrained to enact
any proposed new programs.

If there is any hope for successful Masonic renewal in California, you
must be financially responsible to the process. My brethren, be cognizant of
Cassius' admonition:
" Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world
Like a Collossus, and we petty men
Walk under his huge legs and peep about
To find ourselves dishonorable graves.
Men at some time are masters of their fates.
The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars,
But in ourselves, that we are underlings."
(Julius Caesar: Act I, Scene 2)
At this critical juncture of spiritual and financial crisis, we cannot behave
as petty men, unable to govern the fate of our Craft and its extraordinary mission.
"Talk to me not of time, p lace or patience." I had three acquaintances
who talked like that. They were petty men, victims of time and circumstance, who
did irreparable hann to their task by demanding their rewards inappropriately.
The fauft, indeed, will be in ourselves if we do not act with insight and
courage during our deliberations at this Annual Communication. We must
continue to build and renew, to conquer the ruffians of our day. We can actuate the
words of Henry David Thoreau:

"If you've built castles in the air, your work need not be lost, for
that is where they should be. Now put the foundation under
them."
Most Worshipful, thank you for the honor and the opportunities that have
been afforded me during the past year. It has been a pleasure to travel with you
and our wonderful Grand Lodge Family, visiting many remarkable places and
meeting many devoted brethren. Each one of us may take a fall, sooner or later,
as I did from the lodge stage in Ione. But, inspired by your firm, yet compassionate
style of leadership I was able to overcome the adversity, get up, brush myself off,
ascend the podium, quip a bit, and deliver the message. On that basis, and with the
blessings of God, so may we recover the beauties and lessons of our Craft and
translate them to make Masonic Renewal a reality for all good men .

Recomm endation No. I
Changes Number of Petaluma - Hamilton Lodge No. 180
In 1898, Petaluma Lodge No. 77 consolida ted with Arcturas Lodge No.
180 and became Petaluma Lodge No. 180, adopting the higher number. Petaluma
Lodge No. 180 consolidated with Hamilton Lodge No. 751 in 1986 and became
Petaluma-Hamilton Lodge No. 180. There is now a strong desire by the brethren
of Petaluma-Hamilton Lodge to have restored the original number of Petaluma
Lodge No. 11. Under Section 14090 of the California Masonic Code, the name and
number of a Lodge can be changed only by Grand Lodge.
I find no policy reason why a Lodge should not be assigned a number
which had been surrendered by one of its predecessors during a consolidation if the
brethren of the Lodge so desire. No. 77 is vacant on the list of Lodges of our
Grand Lodge and has been so since 1898 when the number was surrender ed by a
predecessor of Petaluma-Hamilton Lodge. I therefore recommend that this request
be granted.

Recomme ndation WITHDR AWN at the request of the Lodge.
Recomm endation No. 2
Reorgani zes Commerc ialism Rules
Our Grand Lodge rules on commercialism have developed over the years
in a haphazard ly fashion . Many of the current provision s in our law were added
to address a then current concern. No anempt was made to place the
commerc ialism rules in logical order nor make them mutually consistent. The
legislation proposed by this recommendation would do that. It would also address
some other concerns which we have had in this Grand Lodge over the past years
with respect to financial support of our fraternal and charitable activ ities. Finally,
it would make permanen t the special grant of authority which was given in 1992
to the Masonic Organizations other than constitue nt Lodges with respect to public
fund-raising.
If you adopt this recommendation, the current Article XV of Part II of the
California Masonic Code will be redesignated as Article XVI and a new Article XV
will be added to Part II of the Code to read as follows:

Recommendation No. 3
Increases Limits on Temple Association Improvements
Without Grand Lodge Consent
For many years, our California Masonic Code contained a bothersome
provision. One set of roles applied if work at a Masonic Hall was a repair, and a
different set of rules applied if the work was an improvement. Grand Master's
spent too much time arbitrating the difference. This problem was eliminated some
years ago. Unfortunately, recent changes to Section 6050 of the Code reintroduced
the problem. Now, repairs in excess of$15,000 must be approved by the Grand
Lodge Temple Properties and Taxation Committee but any improvement in excess
of $7,500 requires this approval. I propose that we return to the more recent
practice of disregarding the distinction between repair and improvement and use
$15,000 for both.

If you adopt this recommendation, Section 6050 of the California Masonic
Code will be amended as marked:

§6050. TEMPLE PROPERTIES AND TAXATION.
The Committee on Temple Properties shall examine and approve all
details regarding any contract involving a Lodge, Temple Association,
committee, partnership or corporation or other entity representing itself
to be Masonic in character, or operating for the benefit of a Lodge or
Lodges in this Jurisdiction for:

Recommendation No. 4
Adds The Grand Wardens to The
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board
For many years, the Deputy Grand Master and each of the Grand Wardens
have been ex-officio members of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of
California. Because our Homes are such an important part of our Grand Lodge
operations, this three year membership on the Homes Board recognized the
contribution which the progressive Grand Lodge officers could make to the Board's
deliberations. It also recognized that a three year membership helped prepare the
Grand Master to deal with the important issues which arise from time to time at our
Homes.
In recent years, our California Masonic Memorial Temple operations have
increased in importance as we have assumed management of the garage and
increased auditorium rentals. I believe that each incoming Grand Master should
have a similar three year experience on the Memorial Temple Board, and your
current Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens agree. At present, only the
Deputy Grand Master serves on the Memorial Temple Board. It is my
recommendation that the Grand Wardens also serve as ex-officio members of this
Board.
If you adopt this recommendation, the Deputy Grand Master has indicated
that he will, if installed Grand Master, cause the Bylaws of Nob Hill Masonic
Management, the manager of this building, to be amended to make the Deputy
Grand Master and Grand Wardens ex-officio members of that Board also. At
present, only the Junior Grand Warden serves on the Nob Hill Board. This
amendment will not require any Grand Lodge action.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 10020 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended as marked:

§10020. COMPOSITION OF BOARD.
The Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple shall be~
in number. The Deputy Grand Master. Sepjor Grand War<len and
Jypjor Grapd Waaleo shall W be a Trustee ex-officio. The other six

m

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

263

Trustees shall be appointed by the Grand Master for terms of three years
each. The terms of one-third of the appointed Trustees shall expire at the
close of each Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. When a vacancy
occurs, the appointee shall serve the remainder of the unexpired term.
The Grand Master may remove a Trustee at any time, upon request of
two-thirds of the Trustees, and appoint another.

If a member shall have served for nine consecutive years, including
service as a Chairman, he shall be ineligible for reappointment until the
lapse of one year.
Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Recommendation seeks to add the Grand Wardens to the California
Masonic Memorial Temple Board as ex-officio members. Because our California
Masonic Memorial Temple operations have increased in magnitude and complexity
over the years, this additional experience will prepare each Grand Warden to deal
with any important issues regarding the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
Section I 0020 would change the number of trustees to nine with the
Senior and Junior Grand Wardens along with Deputy Grand Master acting as
trustee ex-officio.
This Recommendation is consistent with current Grand Lodge policy.

Recommendation No. 5
Permits Licensed Caterers to Serve and Sell
Alcoholic Beverages at Lodge Events
At the 1989 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge adopted more
liberal rules with respect to the use of alcoholic beverages at the activities of
Lodges and Masonic Organizations and by other groups when on Masonic
property. In 1990 and again in 1993, the Grand Master promulgated Guidelines to
help Lodges and Masonic Organizations interpret these rules.
We have now had five years experience with these rules, and one of them
has proven bothersome. Under Section 15050 of our Code, Lodges, Temple
Associations and other Masonic Organizations may rent or lease their land or
buildings to non-Masonic tenants other than business establishments who serve
alcoholic beverages, if alcoholic beverages are not sold. Under this rule, you may
rent your building for a wedding reception or similar activity where alcoholic

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDrNGS OF THE

264

serving or selling alcoholic beverages, whether in, on, or away
from premises owned, leased, or rented by either of them;

beverages will be served but may not be sold by the sponsor or caterer, even if the
sponsor or caterer is properly licensed to sell drinks. In addition, Lodges, Temple
Associations and other Masonic Organizations may not have catered events on
Masonic property where alcoholic beverages are sold by the caterer, even if the
caterer is properly licensed.

F.

It does not seem to me that these restrictions are required by the spirit of
the 1989 legislation. I therefore recommend that licensed caterers be permitted to
serve and sell alcoholic beverages at all Masonic events and at non-Masonic events
held on Masonic property, if all applicable California laws are followed. I also
recommend that you be pennitted to rent your building to non-Masonic tenants for
a wedding reception or similar activity where alcoholic beverages may be served,
consumed and sold by the sponsor, ifthe sponsor is properly licensed.

G.

If you adopt this recommendation, Section 15050 of the California
Masonic Code will be repealed and replaced with the following:

GUIDELINES FOR USE OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES
BY MASONIC LODGES AND MASONIC ORGANIZATIONS

§15050. ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES.

Questions frequently arise with respect to permissible use of alcoholic
beverages in Lodge halls, on other property owned by ~r le'.15ed to a ~asonic body
and at Masonic activities held elsewhere. These guidelines explam the Grand
Lodge rules applicable to such use . Thes~ guid~lines appl~ to Lodges, Temple
Associations the Scottish Rite, the York Rite bodies, the Shrme, Eastern Star and
all other pre;equisite organizations and their Temple Associations.

Alcoholic beverages may be sold, served, and consumed on property
owned by or leased to a Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization and at Masonic activities held elsewhere if the following
requirements are observed:
Alcoholic beverages may not be sold, served, or consumed in a
Lodge room or in a room in which Masonic ceremonies are
normally conducted except when such room serves a dual
purpose as a ceremonial room and social room;

B.

A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization may not maintain, on a regular or permanent basis,
a bar stocked with alcoholic beverages;

C.

The funds of a Masonic Lodge or Temple Association may not
be used to purchase alcoholic beverages;

D.

Alcoholic beverages may not be served, consumed, or sold
during the course of a meeting of a Masonic Lodge, Temple
Association, or Masonic Organization;

E.

A Masonic Lodge or Temple Associatiou may not directly or
indirectly apply for, assume title to, or operate under any
government license or permit for the purpose of consuming,

A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization may not rent or lease property in whi~h it has ~n
ownership interest to business establishments wherem alcoh~hc
beverages are served, consumed or sold unless such se~1ce,
consumption, and sale are incident to and not the primary
purpose of the business; and
Any sale, service, or consumption of alcoholic beverages
pursuant to this section must comply with all applicable laws of
the State of California.

Finally, I propose that Section 15050 be rewritten to make it easier to
follow than the current version of it.

A.

265

These guidelines address only the policy and reg~lations of.the Grand
Lodge. Your use of alcoholic beverages also must comply with the apph~able laws
of the State of California and the rules established by your Masonic Temple
Association or other landlord.
A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association and other Masonic O~ganization
may allow alcoholic beverages to be. served on M~sonic property to their m~mbe~s
and invited guests, with one exception. Alcoholic beverages are not perm1~ed m
the room where a Lodge or a Masonic Organization meets unless that room 1s also

\

the regular social hall.
Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masoni~ Organizations may
maintain a bar on Masonic property so long as alcohohc beverages are not
regularly or permanently stored in the bar. Alcohol should not be stored elsewhere
on Masonic property either.
Lodges and Temple Associations may not use f~nds from the Lodge's or
the Temple Association's treasury to purchase alcoholic beverages. However,

266

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDING S OF THE

funds collected by a committee of the Lodge for social purposes are not Lodge
funds. Therefore, if a committee of the Lodge plans a Lodge activity where
alcoholic beverages are served, the committee may use the money collected from
ticket sales to purchase alcoholic beverages. The excess ticket sale proceeds may
not be given to the Lodge until after the reimbursement has been made. No Lodge
or Temple Association funds may be used to reimburse anyone who has purchased
alcoholic beverages. These restrictions apply only to Lodges and Temple
Associations. The Scottish Rite, the York Rite bodies, the Shrine, Eastern Star and
other Masonic Organizations may reimburse the purchase of alcoholic beverages
from their treasuries, iftheir regulations so permit.
Alcoholic beverages may not be served, consumed, or sold during the
course of a meeting of a Masonic Lodge, Temple Association, or Masonic
Organization. Any alcoholic beverages must be removed from the meeting room
prior to beginning the meeting. The meeting may be opened and called to
refreshment, after which alcoholic beverages may be served, but the alcoholic
beverages must be removed from the meeting room prior to calling back to labor.
Lodges and Masonic Organizations may hold tiled meetings and social
events on non-Masonic properties where there is a permanent bar, such as a hotel
or restaurant, provided that no alcoholic beverages are present during any meeting.
Any bar located elsewhere in the building may remain open during the meeting.
Licensed caterers are permitted to serve and sell alcoholic beverages at all
Masonic events held by any Lodge, Temple Association or Masonic Organization
on or away from Masonic property, if all applicable California laws are followed .
No Lodge or Temple Association may directly or indirectly apply for,
assume title to or operate under any governmental license or permit for the purpose
of consuming, serving or selling alcoholic beverages, whether in, on or away from
premises owned, leased or rented by a Masonic Lodge or Temple Association.
Therefore, if alcoholic beverages are not sold and served by a licensed caterer.
there are certain restrictions on the event which must be observed because the event
has not been licensed. As a general rule, no license or permit is required if
alcoholic beverages are not sold and the premises are not open to the general public
when alcoholic beverages are being served or consumed.
•
If alcoholic beverages cannot be sold, you cannot have a cash bar or sell
drink tickets or tokens to be exchanged for alcoholic beverages. You may
charge for the meal or other event at which alcoholic beverages are
served, so long as everyone pays the same price, regardless of whether
they will be served an alcoholic beverage. Alternatively, members and
guests may bring their own alcohol if alcoholic beverages are not sold.
•
Under no circumstances may the general public be present when alcoholic
beverages are served without a license. You may not advertise to the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Recommendation No. 7
Modifies Rules on Balloting
Too often, good men are denied admission to Masonry because one biased
or angry member objects. Most of us probably know of at least one instance where
an applicant was rejected for no valid and Masonic reason. We have considered
this problem in the past but have not yet found the appropriate solution. We
considered a three black cube proposal but many believed that this would only
encourage a malcontent to recruit two more objectors. We cannot solve the
problem unless the Lodge can discuss dispassionately the cause of the objection but
we have been reluctant to require a Mason to divulge his reasons for objecting to
an applicant's election.
I propose that we adopt an approach to the problem which is already in
our law. If an objection is made to the advancement of an Entered Apprentice or
a Fellow Craft, the Master appoints a committee to investigate the objection and
report to the Lodge. The Lodge then determines by a two-thirds vote whether the
objection to advancement is valid and Masonic. If two-thirds vote to advance the
man despite the objection, he advances. Otherwise, he does not advance.
I propose that we adopt the same procedure for objections made before
initiation. If an objection is made to the Master before a man's initiation or if one
or more black cubes appear in the ballot box, the Master would appoint a
committee to investigate the objection. While the committee would be available
to hear and discuss the cause of any objection, no one would be required to present
his objections to the committee. After its investigation of any sources available to
it, the committee would report to the Lodge. The Lodge would consider the report
and then vote on whether the objection is valid and Masonic. If two-thirds vote to
elect the man despite the objection, he is elected. Otherwise, he stands rejected.
I believe that this approach will protect innocent applicants from rejection
for improper reasons yet protect the anonymity of those who choose not to come
forward with reasons for their objections.
If you adopt this recommendation, Sections 26190, 26200, 26210, 26220,
26230, 26240, 26250, 26260 and 26270 of the California Masonic Code will be
amended and a new Section 26245 will be added to the Code as marked:

§26245. RESOLUTION OF OBJECTIONS BEFORE INITIA TlON.
The Committee appointed to resolve any objection before initiation shall
meet at the time and place fixed . The Master shall be a non-voting
member and chainnan of the Committee. The Secretary. or a Brother
appointed in his place. shall record the proceedings. The Committee may
receive the statements of Masons or non-Masons in such manner as it
determines. Any oral statements made shall be taken down jn narrative
or other form by the Secretary or. at the Master's option. by a stenographic
reporter qualified as provided for elsewhere in this Code. The Committee
may adjourn from time to time and shall have complete charge of the
investigation. It may hear the statements privately or in the presence of
the objector and aoplicant or either of them. Neither shall be allowed any
objection to the Committee or its methods.
The Committee shall report at the next Stated Meeting unless further time
be given by the Master or the Lodge. stating fully the cause of objection
and its conclusions thereon. The statements upon which the report is
based shall be read in the Lodge. if required. After receiving the repo.rt
from the Committee appointed to resolve the objection. the Lodge shall
vote by ballot on whether or not the objection is valid and Masonic.
If in the opinion of two-thirds of the members present. the objection is not
a valid and Masonic one. the applicant shall be elected without further
ballot. The Master shall not allow the same objection to be made a second
time. The decision is final and may not be reconsidered and no appeal
may be taken. If the objection is found to be valid and Masonic. the
applicant stands rejected and a reballot cannot. thereafte r. be had on the
same application without obtaining a dispensation.

§26260. COMMITIEE TO RESOLVE OBJECTION AFTER

The Committee appointed to resolve an objection after initiation shall
meet at the time and place fixed. The Master shall be a non-voting

receive the statements of Masons or non-Masons in such manner as it
detennines. Any oral statements made shall be taken down in narrative
or other form by the Secretary or, at the Master's option, by a stenographic
reporter qualified as provided for elsewhere in this Code. The Committee

§26270. DECISION OF LODGE ON OBJECTION AFTER
INITIATION.
After receiving the report from the Committee appointed to resolve the
objection, the Lodge shall vote by ballot on whether or not the objection
is valid and Masonic. If in the opinion of two-thirds of the members
present, the objection is not a valid and Masonic one, the Lodge may
confer the degree in the same manner as if no objection had been made,
and the Master shall not allow the same objection to be made a second
time. The decision is final and may not be reconsidered and no appeal
may be taken.
If the objection is found to be valid and Masonic, the contributions and
that part of the fee for the degree or degrees not taken by the applicant
shall be returned to him. The candidate denied advancement shall have
the status of one rejected for the unconferred degrees. His status shall be
reported to the Grand Secretary, and the time interval applying to other
rejections of an application must elapse before a new application may be

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

This Recommendation seeks to modify the rules on balloting to ensure
that an applicant has not been rejected for an invalid and/or non-Masonic reason.
This new approach extends the procedure currently in place for objections
raised after an election for the degrees of Masonry to apply also to any instance in
which an unexpected anonymous objection, in the fonn of one or more black
cubes, occurs at the time of balloting. In the event that such a ballot occurs, the
Master of the Lodge must appoint a committee to investigate such an objection.
After the investigation of any and all sources available to it regarding the applicant,
including anonymous statements, the committee would report to the Lodge. A twothirds vote by the lodge would detennine whether the objection is valid and, if not,
the applicant would continue despite the objection.
lt is a policy of Grand Lodge that all men of good character be afforded
the opportunity to become Masons. It is also a policy of Grand Lodge that each
individual Mason be accorded the privilege of exercising his personal judgment
with the protection of anonymity. Inherent in this latter policy is the assumption
that this exercise of personal judgment will be one of good faith, based on Masonic
principles. However, occasional episodes have occurred in which the personal
judgments were based on less lofty concerns, including anger or bias. Hence, the
current balloting practice is occasionally inconsistent with our Grand Lodge policy.
By changing our current procedure so that any objection made has to have validity,
this recommendation will make the balloting process more consistent with our
policy.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
This legislation was supported last year by the Ritual Committee, and we
support it again this year.
Our reasons for supporting this legislation are as follows:
An examination of a visitor to see if he is qualified to sit in Lodge is an
l.
important safeguard for the ritual as we have received it. A visitor to a
Lodge must be able to prove that he is a Mason and entitled to sit in
Lodge. Coaching him under these circumstances is not appropriate, and
can lead to the admission of an unqualified person. This proposal would

2.

prevent such admission.
This legislation does not prevent the presentation by the Lodge of a
"Rusty Brother Night" . In such circumstances, the Master of the Lodge
has satisfied himself that those invited are indeed Masons, and entitled to
be present. The "coaching" that takes place on such occasions is simply
a "refresher course" for those invited to be present. It is not "private
coaching" to enable a person to sit in Lodge who cannot otherwise prove
that he is a Mason. The adoption of this legislation would not interfere
with a "Rusty Brother Night", and indeed the Ritual Committee
encourages the use of such a program.
The Ritual Committee therefore supports Grand Master Blomseth' s

Recommendation No. 8, and urges its adoption.

our Masonic trials, your Trial Review Committee recommends a "Yes" vote.

Masonic trials are not criminal trials. They are more nearly like civil trials

more nearly approximates how our Masonic law works.

Recommendation NOT ADOPTED.
Grand Master Blomseth's
Recommendation No. 10
Changes Requirements For Ritual Changes
The California Masonic Code presently contains an archaic and inaccurate
statement about our Ritual. It states that the Ritual can be changed, but can only
be changed to "restore" it to the Ritual that has existed from time immemorial. But
no one can clearly demonstrate today what that Ritual is. Masonic Ritual has been
in a constant state of evolution for as long as we have any evidence for it. The
Code Revision Committee has therefore recommended to me that I propose a
change in the law to reflect historical accuracy. This section would require that our
Ritual be changed the same way that other laws are changed, which is in fact what
we have always done. The proposed revision would clear up an inaccuracy in our
written law, and clarify what is now an ambiguity.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 26310 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended to read as follows:

If you adopt this recommendation, the following paragraph will be added
to the end of Section 32320 of the California Masonic Code:
The accuser has the burden of proving by a preoonderance of the evidence
all of the facts necessarv to establish the existence of unmasonjc conduct
on. the part of the accused. "Preponderance of the evidence" means
ev~dence .t hat has more convincing force than that opposed to it. If the
ev1den_ce 1s so evenly balanced that one is unable to say that the evidence
on an issue meponderates. the burden has not been met.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Blomseth recommended that in Masonic trials the evidence
necessary to convict a Mason of a Masonic offense be reduced to "preponderance
of evidence" from "beyond a reasonable doubt".
Such evidentiary proof is simpler and less convincing than in a criminal
trial. It the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes that this
change m the burden of proof in Masonic trials is well founded and proper, and the
proposed recommendation is consistent with Grand Lodge policy.

§26310. CH.ANGE OF RITUAL.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
As Grand Master Blomseth noted, Masonic ritual 1s m a state of
continuous evolution. Practically speaking, any changes in our ritual have to be
adopted by a formal vote of Grand Lodge. Grand Master Blomseth is seeking to
clarify this legislative function by rewording Section 26310.
We have no record of what the original ritual was. California Masonic
Code Section 26310, only allows Grand Lodge to authorize change in the ritual,

286

.

"for the purpose of having it remain as it was handed down from time
immemorial". This creates an ambiguous directive. For example, we have recently
seen changes in the position of the candidate's seating for lecture; originally, he
presumably sat either between the East and the Altar, or between the West and the
Altar. Which is correct? At the most, only one of these alternatives can be that
correct location, but it can never be known which one it is.
If, at any time, the then-current ritual is considered to be that which was
handed down from time immemorial, then any change must deviate from that
original version. As the candidate' s seating example so clearly illustrates, any
change to the ritual becomes logically inconsistent with Section 26310 as it is
currently written. The lack of knowledge of the original ritual permanently fixes
this area of confusion in our statutes.
A purpose of Grand Lodge is to make Masonry as free from ambiguity
and confusion as possible. Section 26310, as it is currently written, is contrary to
this purpose.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Grand Master Blomseth ' s Recommendation No. 10 would eliminate an
inaccurate statement presently in our California Masonic Code as it relates to the
Ritual of this Grand Lodge. It re-emphasizes that the Grand Lodge alone has the
power to change the Ritual, and that changes must have the same majority as any
other major changes in our law. It deletes the inaccurate and obsolete phrase about
"changing it for the purpose of having it remain as it was handed down from time
immemorial". Such a statement is not accurate; and is actually an embarrassment.
We support this Recommendation for the following reasons:
1.

2.

The Grand Lecturer is the Custodian of the Ritual for the Grand Lodge of
California. He is responsible for maintaining the accuracy of the Ritual
as we have received it. His predecessors in office have had the same
responsibility, continuing all the way back to the first Ritual adopted by
this Grand Lodge when it came into existence.
The Ritual as we have received it has historically been changed from time
to ti.me by action of Grand Lodge. Each such change has been a change
away from the original Ritual, and has reflected the needs of the time in
which the change was made. In the l 920's, Grand Lodge permitted the
omission of the Long Form of the Third Degree Lecture when so desired
by the Lodge; and in more recent times, we made the Long Form of the
First Degree Lecture similarly optional with the Lodge. These changes
were not " restorations" of the Ritual to an earlier form . They were

287

changes in the Ritual deemed important for the future, and adopted by
Grand Lodge.
3.

Obsolete and meaningless language in the California Masonic Code leads
to " confusion in the Temple". We need to mean what we say, and say
what we mean. The Ritual Committee supports this Recommendation.

Grand Master Blomseth's
Recommendation No. 13
Permits Lodges to Have Roving Charters
Section 16050 of the California Masonic Code requires a Lodge to hold
its Stated Meeting in a location as fixed in its Charter. Section 16110 provides that
a Lodge may change this meeting place temporarily, or permanently, by following
certain procedures. However, there appears to be no provision for a Lodge to
regularly hold its Stated Meeting at more than one location. If a Lodge were
permitted to do so, it would have what is commonly termed a roving charter,
although it more accurately might be described as a charter with more than one
location.
In the past, Lodges in some jurisdictions have held such charters,
particularly military Lodges. However, California has apparently never had this
practice. Some Masonic Organizations pennit roving charters. For example, the
Grand Council of Cryptic Masons in California specifically permits such charters.
There are Lodges in California that would like to meet regularly in more
than one location. Sometimes this is the result of a consolidation of two Lodges
who wish to maintain the Masonic identity in two communities. Sometimes this
is the result of the desire to preserve a historic meeting place.
It is therefore my recommendation that our law be amended to permit a
Lodge to hold its Stated Meetings in more than one location, if due notice is given
to the members in writing of the location of each Stated Meeting through the usual
means of communication, such as the Lodge trestleboard.

If you adopt this recommendation, a new Section 16115 will be added to
the California Masonic Code to read as follows:
§16115. MULTIPLE MEETING PLACES.
A Lodge may hold its Stated Meetings in locations other than the
approved building in the place (city. town or community) fixed by its

Grand Maste r Blomseth's
Recommendation No. 14
Permits Stated Meetings in The First Degre e
As an historic perspective, it is duly ackno wledg ed that,
throug hout the
formative years of Freemasonry , Entere d Appre ntices
made up the bulk of the

Mason s were rare. In the
I 840's many Grand Lodges in the United States revise
d their rules to require
Lodges to hold Stated Meetings only in Lodges of Maste
r Masons. Originally done
to encourage all Mason s to become Master Mason s, it
eventu ally resulted in the
exclus ion of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from
the core life of their
Lodges. ContempPrary Masonic experience teaches us the

§23090. ENTE RED APPR ENTI CES AND FELL OW CRAF

GRAN D LODGE OF CALIF ORNIA

TS.

Entere d Apprentices and Fellow Crafts have only the right
to sit in the
Lodge in which they received the degree or degrees
when open in a
degree taken by them, and the right to advan cemen
t therein after
satisfactorily passing a strict examination in open Lodge.
They may, with
the consent of the Master, visit another Lodge worki ng
in a degree taken
by them, if accompanied by a Master Mason who witnes
sed the initiation
or advancement of the visitor.
They are not required to pay dues and are not entitled to
vote or speak in
Lodge. exs;ept as provided for elsewhere in this Code.
They may be
buried with Masonic honors upon the request of their family
and with the
permission of the Maste r or, in his absence, a Warden.
Neither they nor
their widows or orphans are entitled to relief from the Lodge
. They shall
not exercise any control over Lodge funds for charity
, or for other
purposes. except as provided for elsewhere in this Code.

Repor t ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Bloms eth's Recom menda tion No. 14 propos
es that most
Stated Meetings should be open to Entered Apprentices and
Fellowcrafts, with only
balloti ng and election of officers reserved for Maste r Mason
s.
Similar proposals have been presented in the form of Resolu
tions in 1984,
1987, 1991 and 1992. All were rejected by this Grand Lodge
.
We have been taught that Masonry is a progre ssive moral
scienc e taught
by degrees only. Upon compl etion of the three degree s,
the candidate becom es a
Maste r Mason and we inform him that he is now entitle
d to all the rights and
privileges. Until that time California Masonic Code Sectio
n 23090 states that the
candid ate does not pay dues and is not entitled to vote or
speak in the Lodge .
It is desirable for candid ates to learn as much as they
can about the
Fraternity and participate in the social affairs of the
Lodge while he is still
progressing through the degrees. These objectives can be
met without sitting in a
Stated Meeting. In many Lodges, the candidates attend the
Stated Meeting dinners
and other Lodge functions and spend time with their
coaches while the Stated
Meeti ng or other meetings are in progress. There is certain
ly no restriction on
Entere d Apprentices attending social functions.
A part of this Recommendation also gives the Lodge the
option of voting
for it, and then later, reverting back to the original practic
e of meetin gs as Master
Masons. However, this could result in different Lodges
having different practices.

293

Since one of the streng ths of this Grand Lodge is its consis
tent practic es
and policies throughout th is jurisdiction, this recommenda
tion has the potent ial o f
erodin g this strength.
The propo sed chang e is inconsistent with present Grand
Lodge policy .

The Ritual Comm ittee is opposed to Grand Maste
r Bloms eth' s
Recommendation No. 14 for the following reason s:
1.

The Ritual Committee has consistently suppo rted unifor
mity of work on
our Grand Lodge . Options lead to confusion, and
we prefer that
uni form ity of work be the standard practice in th is jurisdi
ction.

2.

It is difficult for our officers to becom e proficient in the
Ritual under the
best of circum stance s. To add to this a responsibility
to run a stated
meeting in the First Degree, while reserving certain voting
privileges for
Master Masons present, simply adds to the difficulty. We
might suppo rt
such legisla tion at some time in the future if our presen
t problems with
learning the Ritual had been overcome. But until we
are satisfied that
Lodge s have no difficulty in learning the present Ritual,
we canno t
suppo rt adding anythi ng to this burden.
Your Comm ittee on Ritual recommends a "No" vote.
