§25120. INSTALLATION.

Resolution 94-10
Modifies Installation Service to Allow
for Joint Installations
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the Installation Service to allow
for the joint installation of Lodge officers.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. ofCalifornia:
WHEREAS, it is the Master's duty to provide for the installation of his
successor in the manner prescribed by Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, it may be the Master's desire to hold a joint installation with
another Lodge for fraternal, financial or civic reasons; and
WHEREAS, there is no definitive prohibition of joint installations in the
Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, there exists a ninety-four year history of continuous joint
installations recorded in minute books with the Grand Master of Masons in
California presiding as Installing Officer for twenty-five of those years, the Grand
Lecturer presiding as Installing Officer for two of those years, other Grand Lodge
Officers presiding as Installing Officer for nineteen of those years and the Grand
Lecturer acting as Master of Ceremonies for nineteen of those years; and
WHEREAS, the current installation service is written for a single Lodge
only; and
WHEREAS, the installation service has been altered through revisions in
the past; and
WHEREAS, the current Ritual Committee has failed to see the merit of
allowing exemptions for joint installation requests.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that two Lodges may
participate in a joint installation of officers and that the Installation Service be
amended to provide for said joint installation, as follows: (I) the instructions shall
pennit singular words be made plural when circumstances require, (2) where one
Lodge is currently identified by name, both Lodges shall be identified, (3) the line
of march for a joint installation shall provide for the Master of Ceremonies to walk
between the Tilers with the officers of each Lodge following single file behind their
respective Tiler, (4) the officers ofone Lodge shall be se~ted on one leg of the "V"
facing their counterparts on the other leg, and (5) the Installing Officer shall install
the officers from both Lodges concurrently for each chair.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 25120 of the California·
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

"

The officers, including incumbents, shall be installed in the manner
prescribed by Grand Lodge, as soon as practical after their election or
appointment, and shall hold their respective offices until their successors
have been duly elected or appointed and installed.
The installation may be performed by the Master or, by invitation of the
Master, by any qualified Past Master of any jurisdiction. It is not the
privilege of the Master-elect to select the Installing Officer or in any way
interfere with the duties and privileges of the office of Master. If
performed by a Past Master, the Master or a Warden of the Lodge must
be present. There can be no installation by proxy. Installation may be
private or public. Two Lodges may particjpate in a joint installation.
The Certificates required for installation, endorsed by the Installing
Officer, shall be forwarded to the Grand Secretary.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California Masonic
Code and the Installation Service to allow for the joint installation of Lodge
Officers from two Lodges. this amendment would codify formally a practice that
has existed between two Lodges for 94 years.
As currently written, the California Masonic Code calls for the installation
of officers "in the manner prescribed by Grand Lodge". The official Installation
Service is clearly written in the singular, implying that, that "manner" is intended
to be for a "one Lodge" installation.
However, it must be noted that, on numerous occasions, these joint
installations have been presided over by a sitting Grand Master, acting as the
Installing Officer. The fact that a Grand Master was the Installing Officer at such
an installation implies that joint installations are acceptable practices.
Throughout the jurisdiction, each of the individual Lodges has developed
its own unique traditions. In fact, these traditions are often responsible for a
particular member developing a sense of loyalty and personal involvement in his
own Lodge. As long as these traditions are consistent with Grand Lodge policy and
procedures, Grand Lodge has not insisted that they be abandoned. It would
probably be detrimental both to the individual Lodge and to Grand Lodge to make
such demands.
For over 94 years, two Lodges have held joint installations as part of their
tradition, believing in good faith that they were acting in concert with Grand Lodge
policy. When a similar resolution was presented to Grand Lodge in 1993, concerns
were raised by both the Ritual Committee and your Committee on Policy and

300

PROCEEDlNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Gener al Purposes that joint installations could detract
from the authority of the
outgo ing Master and the honor of the incoming Maste
r. Obviously, these two
lodges have overcome these problems in the past; perhap
s they have seen value in
having individuals relinquish some of their personal gratifi
cation for the greate r
good of the Lodges. The Lodge s must wish to continue
this tradition, as they are
making the effort to obtain Grand Lodge sanction. The
amendment, as proposed,
does not require joint installations, it only allows them
if Lodges choose to hold
them.

1995 RESO LUTI ONS

Report of the Commiflee on Ritual:
The published Installation ritual, which specifies the wordin
g and floor
work for all Craft Lodge installations , is written in
the singular, obviously
intend ing each Lodge to condu ct its own installation.
This Resolution seeks to
chang e that concept. We believe that the drafters of the
cerem ony put it in the
singular for good reasons, and we should consider them
before changing it.
The retiring Maste r is responsible for all issues
concerning this
installation. This includes the form, the installing office
rs, the amount and
selection of music, etc. Although these decisions are
usually deferred to the
incoming Master, the retiring Master still has the last word.
We can easily foresee
disput es arising among the Masters, both retiring and
incoming, with Lodges
involved in joint installations .
The retiring Master should deem it an honor and privile
ge to install his
succes sor. Obviously, there can be only one Installing
Officer. I know I would
deeply resent being deprived that opportunity because
tradition dictates a joint
installation for my Lodge. I also know that any Master who
breaks with tradition
for personal reasons is going to subject himself to a Jot of
discontented grumbling.
Rewriting the installation to accommodate two or more
Lodges will
indeed be difficult, particularly in delivering the floor work.
For example, how
would 39 or 52 chairs be arranged in the semi-circle? How
would you distribute
rods to, and escort to their seats, six or eight Deacons?
Many, if not most, of the
Lodges have one fixed chair for each Warden and Maste
r. How would you seat
three or four of them?
We rarely see an installation which is correct in every
respect. We
hesitate to encourage a condition which can only lead
to increased error and
confusion, and recommend a "No" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

WHEREAS, during World War II there were 16,354,000 personnel on
active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces of which 405,399 were killed in action or
died in service, 291,557 were battle deaths (KIA), 113,842 other deaths in service,
and 670,846 wounded in action;
WHEREAS, seventy-three percent of these members of the U.S. Anned
Forces during World War II served overseas with an average overseas tour of 16.2
months;
WHEREAS, the annual rate of pay of the U.S. Armed Forces during
World War II for officers was $2,442.00 and enlisted men $856.00;
WHEREAS, the United States government and the State of California
have passed specific legislation in an attempt to compensate these Veterans of the
U.S. Anned Forces during World War II by passing the GI Education Benefits Bill,
the Veterans Administration Home Loans, the California Veterans Home and
Business Loans, and the California Veterans Education Grants and Loans;
WHEREAS, this Resolution succinctly is intended to demonstrate the
reasons why the Grand Lodge of California should recognize the grave hardships
endured by our Masonic Brothers during World War II as well as the arduous duty
performed during the numerous battles and campaigns around the world;
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California should recognize this
honorable service in the United States Anned Forces and authorize the granting of
honorable time for service during World War II for the conferral of the Golden
Veterans Award t1rior to their being raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason;
and
WHEREAS, under this proposed change to Section 23150 of the
California Masonic Code, a brother who served honorably in the U.S. Armed
Forces during the full period of World War II could claim and be granted five years
and 24 days or any part thereof as good times toward the conferral of the Golden
Veterans Award.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 23150 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
§23150. GOLDEN VETERAN AWARD.
The Grand Lodge, upon request, shall provide a Golden Veteran's Award
to members of this Jurisdiction who have been in good standing for a total
of 50 years or more, presentation being made by the Grand Master,
District Inspector, or their representative with appropriate ceremony.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The. proponents of this Resolution seek to reward a man for serving
his
Countr y dunng World War II. This in itself is a laudable and
noble cause
However, ~ey are seeking to couple it to the Golden Veterans Award.
These tw~
have nothmg to do with each other.
The Golden Veterans Award is given for membe rship in, and service
to
the craft f~r 50 years. It is beyond dispute that many men were called
into that
great conflict before they could join our great Fraternity. It is also a fact
that a man
wh~ was "over there" would not be eligible to receive
his Golden Veterans Award
until he had accumulated his full 50 years in Masonry. By the same

m~y.ofthe 405,399 men who paid the supreme sacrifice. And did not hav~ time

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Resolution No. 2 has been referred to the Ritual Commi ttee by Grand
Master Stovall, and we are opposed to it for the following reasons:
1.
The Golden Veteran ' s Award is an award for Masonic membership in
this
Fraternity for at least Fifty Years. To count any years spent before a
man
became a Master Mason is false advertising. There may have been many
reasons why a man did not seek to become a Mason earlier in his life.
To
single out one event, no matter how major an event, as the sole reasons
,
is inappro priate. Whether or not a man was called to the service of
his
Country during time of war has nothing to do with whether or not
he
sought Masonic membership.
2.
During all wars the lives of men have been disrupted. A man may have
put off becoming a Mason because he was called to serve his Country
.
But many. men who were called to serve their Country did not put it
off.
The Grand Lodge of California recognized this fact during World War
II,
and indeed, still recognizes this fact, by permitting the usual residen
cy
rule to be waived . Section 26240 of the California Masonic Code
specifies that a membe r of any uniformed service of the United States,
whose duty station is in California, may apply for and receive the degrees
of Masonry in any Lodge having jurisdic tion over that duty station,
and
that a dispensation may be obtained when he has been at that duty station
less than six months. For all practical purposes, we made it easy for
a
man to seek to become a Mason during World War II, and all subsequ
ent
wars, despite the fact that he was serving his Country . And we continu
e
to do so today.
For these reasons , the Ritual Committee is opposed to Resolution No.
02.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

312

WHEREAS, current procedure as set by the Masonic Ritual requires the
officers to recite their duties during both opening and closing of the Lodge;
WHEREAS, this procedur e has no apparent historical significance; and
WHEREAS, nothing would be taken away from the overall meaning of
any of the three degrees by reciting officer duties only once during a meeting.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Masonic Ritual be
changed to delete the practice of the officers reciting their duties during closing of
the Lodge.

313

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The Ritual Committee is opposed to the adoption of Resolution No. 95-06.
As with other such proposals, we are, in general, not in favor of changing a practice
that has not proven a burden to the Lodge over the years. The practice of obtaining
the jewel of office from the Master of the Lodge has some symbolic significance,
for it reminds the office holder that it is the Master of the Lodge that continues to
give him the right to wear the jewel of office. It emphasizes the right of the Master
to govern the Lodge over which he is called to preside, and confinns that the
holding of Masonic office is a privilege.
The Ritual Committe e urges a "No" vote on Resolution No. 95-06.

Resolution WITHDRAWN.
Resolution NOT ADOPTE D.
Resolutio n 95-06
Makes Optional the Distribut ion of the
Officers Jewels at the Opening of Lodge
The proponen ts of this Resolution seek to make optional the distribution of the
officers jewels at the opening of a Lodge.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
WHEREAS, current Masonic Ritual requires that the Officers of a Lodge
proceed in procession to receive the jewels of their stations from the Master at the
opening of a Lodge;
WHEREAS, this procedure has no apparent historical significance;
WHEREAS, Grand Lodge Officers, at the Annual Communication, enter
the Lodge room wearing the jewels of their stations and do not go through the
ritualistic procession.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Masonic Ritual shall
be changed to permit a Lodge at its option to eliminate the practice of the Officers
receiving their jewels from the Master at the opening of a Lodge. When opening
in the optional form, the Masonic Ritual is to conform to that currently used by the
Grand Lodge Officers at the opening of the Grand Lodge during the Annual
Communication. Current ritual will remain if a Lodge chooses to receive the
jewels from the Master.

Creates a Permane nt Lire Members hip Card
The proponents of this Resolution seek to create a permanent life membership card.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
WHEREA S, Section 27020 of the California Masonic Code authorizes a
Lodge to adopt a standing resolution which provides for a system of life
members hip which shall forever exempt a member from the payment of dues
therein;
WH EREAS, an increase or decrease of Lodge dues does not affect Life
Membership status;
WHEREAS, the Lodge Secretary spends much wasted time reissuing Life
Member Dues Cards annually;
WHEREAS, the Lodge could save money eliminating postage costs to
mail annual Life Member Dues Cards;
WHEREAS, the requirement for Section 27030 of the California Masonic
no longer be needed; and

for life rather than year-to-year.
NOW, THEREF ORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 27030 of the
California Masonic Code, which presently reads as follows, be repealed :

§20010. CONSOLIDATION.
A.
Two or more Lodges, located near each other, may consolidate
into one Lodge upon such terms as may be agreed between the
Lodges, provided they perform the following in consecutive
order:
I.
Adoption of a written resolution by each Lodge at a
Stated Meeting to the effect that a consolidation is
expedient and that a committee be formed to meet and
arrange terms;
2.
Giving of notice in writing of the adoption of this
resolution to all members of the Lodge without delay;
3.

Agreement by the Committees upon the terms;

Reporting of the terms to their respective Lodges, in
writing, at a Stated Meeting, and acceptance of the
terms by a majority vote of those present; and

5.

Receipt of the signatures of at least three-fourths of the
members of each Lodge to a consent form agreeing to
the proposed terms of the consolidation.

At a Stated Meeting not earlier than the third Stated Meeting
after adoption of the first resolution, the Master of each Lodge
shall examine the consent forms of the members of his Lodge,
and if he finds the required number of valid signatures, he shall
declare the consolidation to be approved by the Lodge.

§16030. STATED MEETINGS.
A Lodge shall hold a Stated Meeting for the transaction of its regular
business once in each calendar month, except that Lodges whose By-Laws
provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall hold a Stated
Meeting each lunar month and Lodges whose By-Laws provide for
quarterly meetings shall hold a Stated Meeting once during each calendar

Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution 95-08
Permits Quarterly Stated Meetings
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit a Lodge the option of holding
quarterly Stated Meetings.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
WHEREAS, there are Lodges in our jurisdiction which are able to conduct
the transaction of business, efficiently and effectively, on a quarterly basis;
WHEREAS, quarterly Stated Meetings would allow additional time for
family, fellowship and community involvement, both by individual Masons and
our Lodges;
WHEREAS, attendance, both at the conferral of degrees and Stated
Meetings, would be enhanced;
WHEREAS, when occasion requires, Lodges may call special meetings
for the transaction of business should an emergent situation arise between Stated
Meetings;

A Lodge may be opened for a Stated Meeting prior to the time fixed in its
By-Laws. No business shall be transacted prior to such time.
The Inspector may grant a dispensation to change the date of a Stated
Meeting, as provided for elsewhere in this Code.
Jn the event that the Master of a Lodge determines that inclement weather,
including ice, snow, and flood conditions, existing on the day established
in the By-Laws of the Lodge for its Stated Meeting, makes it hazardous
for members of the Lodge to attend the meeting, he may, with the consent
of the Inspector of the District to which the Lodge is assigned, postpone
the Stated Meeting to the same day of the week next following the week
scheduled for the Stated Meeting. Upon such postponing, the Master
shall notify, to the extent possible, all members of the Lodge residing
within 50 miles of the meeting place of the Lodge.
Should a Stated Meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed Stated Meeting shall be limited to the reading of the minutes
of the last Stated and subsequent Special Meetings, action thereon,
payment of the invoices of the Lodge, and such other business of an
emergent nature as determined by the Master to require immediate
consideration. No other new business shall be considered.

WHEREAS, this resolution is permissive and does nothing to require
Lodges to adopt quarterly Stated Meetings; and

BE IT FURTHER RE SOLYEO that Article III of Section 19040 of the

to read as follows:

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents wish to pattern their lodge after the English Lodges that
meet quarterly. A proponent states that this has been most effective in bringing a
large percentage of the members to a meeting. The proponents state that the lodge
could meet informally on other months for social events.
This is an interesting concept, however it does have some areas of

concern:
1.

2.
3.

The reception of applications, balloting and degrees could take
several months.
The payment of bills is of notable concern.
November elections as specified in California Masonic Code
Section 25010 might require special dispensation.

Resolution 95-09
Increases the Fees for the Degrees
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the minimum degree fees in the
California Masonic Code to reflect past inflation and to provide for future periodic
adjustments based on changes in the cost of living.
To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, the minimum fees for degrees were established by the Grand
Lodge of California in 1949 at $50 ($75 where Lodges have concurrent
jurisdiction);
WHEREAS, these amounts have not been adjusted in the Code since 1949
to keep pace with inflationary trends;
WHEREAS, according to the 1993 Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, the
current fees range from $50 to $250, the average fees being $106.29;
WHEREAS. the current average fees are far below the calculated
minimum amounts adjusted for inflation since 1949;
WHEREAS, financial limitations result in many Lodges being
handicapped in their efforts to show Freemasonry in its best light;
WHEREAS, the low fees may actually be a deterrent to some potentially
desirable members;
WHEREAS, Freemasonry prides itself on pursuing the principles of
fraternity ;
and
equality
WHEREAS, the standardization of the ritual work in conferring the three
degrees of Masonry is an important goal of the Grand Lodge, thus ensuring that all
members receive essentially the same ceremonial work in the degrees; and
WHEREAS, the fees for degrees should therefore be adequate to carry out
the mission of the fraternity and should be unifonn throughout the jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of California .
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 26100 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

Resolution 95-IO
Increases Minimum Dues for Membership
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the ~inimum dues in t~e
California Masonic Code to reflect past inflation and to provide for future penod1c
adjustments based on changes in the cost of living.

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the minimum annual dues for membership were established
by the Grand Lodge of California in 1953 at $12;
WHEREAS, these amounts have not been adjusted since 1953 to keep
pace with inflationary trends;

323

WHEREAS, according to the 1993 Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, the
current dues range from $12 to $100, the average dues being $38. 74;
WHEREAS, the current average dues are far below the calculated
minimum amounts adjusted for inflation since 1953;
WHEREAS, financial limitations result in many Lodges being
handicapped in their efforts to show Freemasonry in its best light;
WHEREAS, the low dues may actually be a deterrent to some potentially
desirable members;
WHEREAS, Freemasonry prides itself on pursuing the principles of
equality and fraternity;
WHEREAS, the financial participation of the Constituent Lodges in the
affairs of the Grand Lodge of California should be equally distributed among the
Lodges of the Jurisdiction;
WHEREAS, the basic dues for membership in a Lodge in the jurisdiction
of the Grand Lodge of California should therefore be uniform; and
WHEREAS, each Lodge may require additional dues from its members
to maintain its property and support its programs, as deemed appropriate by a vote
of its membership.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Sections 270 I 0 and 27020
of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

.

§27010. MINIMUM.
The minimum annual dues are $12 through December 31. 1995.
Beginning on January I. 1996. the minimum annual dues are $80. This
$80 minimum annual dues amount shall be adjusted by the Grand
Treasurer every two years thereafter based on chan~es jn the Consumer
Price Index. Dues shall commence with the first day of the month next
following the conferring of the Master Mason Degree or as provided for
elsewhere in this Code.
Lod~es may impose additional dues with the consent of the brethren of
the Lodge.
§27020. LIFE MEMBERSH IP.
A Lodge may adopt a standing resolution providing for a system of life
membership, which shall forever exempt a member from the payment of
dues therein. The resolution or any amendment shall not be acted on at
the Stated Meeting at which it is introduced, or until notice in writing has

§23020. MULTIPLE.
Dual membership is membership in Lodges of different Grand
Jurisdictions. Plural membership in two or more Lodges in the same
Grand Jurisdiction. A multiple membership is either dual or plural
membership.
This Grand Lodge recognizes and authorizes multiple membership under
the following conditions:
A member of a Lodge of this Jurisdiction residing in the
A.
Jurisdiction of another Grand Lodge which allows dual
membership may affiliate with one or more Lodges in that
Jurisdiction while retaining his membership in this Jurisdiction.
He becomes a dual member.
B.

A member of a Lodge of any other Grand Jurisdiction which
allows dual membership may affiliate with one or more Lodges
under this Grand Lodge while retaining his membership in such
other Jurisdiction. He becomes a dual member.

A member, in good standing, of a Lodge in this Jurisdiction may
retain such membership and affiliate with any one or more other
Lodges under this Grand Lodge or join in a petition for a
Dispensation for a new Lodge and may present a paid up dues
receipt in lieu of a Dimit or Request for Dimit. He becomes a
plural member.
Upon election of a multiple member or the formation of a new Lodge
containing one or more multiple members, the Secretary shall
immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which each multiple member holds membership. The Grand Secretary
shall provide forms to cover this section.

C.

A plural member shall declare his primary Lodge and shall pay all dues
required by that Lodge. His other Lodge memberships shall be
considered secondary. and he shall be required to pay only that portion of
the secondary Lodge's dues which exceed the per capita sums described
jn Section 13020. A plural member shall declare hjs primary Lodge on
a fonn provjded by Grand Lodge for that pumose.
Except as provided in the preceding paragraph. a -A multiple member shall
pay all dues required by each Lodge wherein membership is held and
shall have all the rights and privileges of membership in each of the
Lodges except that he shall not be Master, Warden or Secretary, or any
combination thereof, of more than one of such Lodges at the same time.
The burden of the relief of a multiple member, his wife, widow and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

327

orphans shall rest on the Lodges in which he holds membership in
proportion to the length of membership in each.
A multiple member may receive a Certificate of Discontinuance of
Multiple Membership as provided in this Code if otherwise entitled to the
same.
Suspension or expulsion of a multiple member by any of his Lodges fo r
other than non-payment of dues, shall forthwith suspend or expel his
membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction, and the Secretary of any
Lodge in this Jurisdiction suspending or expelling such mem ber shall
immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which the multiple member holds membership. Any member who has
been suspended or expelled in any other Grand Jurisdiction for other than
non-payment of dues, and who is subsequently restored to membership
therein, may also be restored to membership in this Jurisdiction in the
same manner as is provided in this Code for members suspended or
expelled by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction initially.
Suspension by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction for non-payment of dues of a
multiple member shall automatically suspend his membership in all
Lodges in this Jurisdiction. The Secretary of any Lodge suspending such
a member shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every
other Lodge in which the multiple member holds membership.
Notificatu:m shall also be given in case of reinstatement by a Lodge in this
Jurisdiction which shall automatically restore him to membership in every
other Lodge of which he was a member in this Jurisdiction, upon payment
of any dues or the performance of any other obligations requ ired for
restoration to membership.
The suspension shall become effective only after a 60 day prior Notice of
Intent to Suspend has been sent to every other Lodge in which the
member holds membership. During this 60 day period the other Lodge
or Lodges may contact the member in an effort to avoid suspension. If
within the 60 day period the member fails to obtain good standing in all
Lodges involved, he shall be suspended. The suspension shall
automatically terminate his membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction.
Suspension by a Lodge in any other Grand Jurisdiction for non-payment
of dues shall automatically suspend his membership in all Lodges in this
Jurisdiction. The suspension and any restoration shall become effective
in the same manner as provided in this section for members suspended by
a Lodge in this Jurisdiction.

Resolution 95-16
Increases Contributions to the Masonic Homes
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the contributions to the Masonic
Homes of California required of Lodges for the degrees to reflect inflationary
trends over the past forty years.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
WHEREAS, Section 13030 of the California Masonic Code requires each
applicant for the degrees and each petitioner to form a new Lodge and each
applicant for affiliation whose Demit or Certificate is from a Lodge of anoth~r
Jurisdiction to make a contribution of $25 for the use and benefit of the Masomc
Homes of California;
WHEREAS, no adjustments for inflation have been made in these
contributions, as appearing in the California Masonic Cc.~-, :ince pre-1956;
WHEREAS, since that time, inflation has increased prices as much as
tenfold;
WHEREAS, the cost of operating the Masonic Homes has also increased
proportionally, and it is therefore appropriate to make some adjustments in these
contributions; and

WHEREAS, periodic review of these contributions should be made by the
Grand Lodge to adjust for inflation.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 13030 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
§13030. MASONIC HOMES CONTRIBUTIONS.
Each applicant for the degrees, each petitioner to form a new Lodge, and
each applicant for affiliation whose Dimit or Certificate is from a Lodge
o~ another ~uri~diction, shall accompany the petition or his application
with a contnbut1on offfi ~for the use and benefit of Masonic Homes
of California, unless he shall have paid such contribution with a former
application to a Lodge of this Jurisdiction.
All contributio~s for Masonic Homes of California collected by a Lodge
shall be transmitted to the Grand Secretary at the time and in the manner
specified on forms provided for that purpose. Before issuance of a
Dispensation to form a new Lodge, petitioners therefor shall transmit the
contributions accompanying their petition to the Grand Secretary.
Immediately upon receipt of contributions the Grand Secretary shall pay
the same over to the Grand Treasurer to be held by him subject to the
order of the Trustees for the use and benefit of the Homes.
If an applicant dies before being raised or is elected to membership in
another. Lodge beyond this Jurisdiction under a Dimit issued by his
Lodge, or is denied advancement by action of the Lodge, that fact shall be
certified to the Grand Secretary by the Secretary of the Lodge. The Grand
Secretary shall cause the contributions for Masonic Homes of California
to be returned to the Lodge, unless forfeited, which shall refund the
payment to the widow or representative of the deceased applicant, or to
the applicant himself.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 95-17 requires Temple Associations to make semi-annual
and annual reports to the Lodge. Currently there is no policy regarding reports to
the Lodge. There is, however, a requirement that Temple Associations report semiannually to the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple Properties.
This Resolution would expand current policy and promote a more
involved lodge membership, in agreement with the general purposes of our
fraternity.

Report of the Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation:
Your Temple Properties and Taxation Committee strongly supports
Resolution 95-17.
Although this Section will require the preparation of an additional report
at mid-year by the Temple Association, the additional report will improve
communication between the Temple Association and the Lodge and its members.
Further, the effect of this resolution will decrease.the barriers, if any may exist,
between the Temple Association and the Lodge.
A standardized form currently exists for reporting, the Form 200, and as
such may be used for compliance with the proposed resolution. As an aside, the
committee has been infonned that the Form 200, the form which is used for
reporting the affairs of the Association to the Grand Lodge, will be added to the
computer forms package which may be purchased by the lodge, and therefore, that
form will be even more readily available to lodges and Temple AssoGlations.

Lastly, by requiring semi-annual reporting of the Temple Association, the
Temple Association presentation will coincide with the timing for presentation of
the lodge's Secretary and Treasurer reports. It will thus be a reminder to the
Temple Association to report to the lodge timely and consistently.
Your Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation urges a "Yes" vote
on this resolution.

Resolution 95-19
Exempts Member Suspended for Nonpayment
Of Dues in One Lodge from Automatic
Suspension in Lodge in Which Holds Life Membership
The proponents of this Resolution seek to exempt a multiple member who has been
suspended in one Lodge for nonpayment of dues from automatic suspension in any
other Lodge in which he holds a life membership.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. o/Ca/ifornia:
WHEREAS, Section 27020 of the California Masonic Code provides for
life membership in Masonry;
WHEREAS, Section 27030 of the California Masonic Code provides for
termination of life membership only if mail is undeliverable for seven years;
WHEREAS, Section 21100 ofthe California Masonic Code provides that
the assets of a life membership fund are to be turned over to the Grand Lodge in
the event of a Lodge dissolution so that the character of life membership is
preserved; and
WHEREAS, suspending a life member from all Lodges under Section
23020 of the California Masonic Code for non-payment of dues is contrary to the
intention of the life membership provisions.

Upon election of a multiple member or the fonnation of a new Lodge
containing one or more multiple members, the Secretary shall
immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which each multiple member holds membership. The Grand Secretary
shall provide fonns to cover this section.
A multiple member shall pay all dues required by each Lodge wherein
membership is held and shall have all the rights and privileges o f
membership in each of the Lodges except that he shall not be Master,
Warden or Secretary, or any combination thereof, of more than one of
such Lodges at the same time. The burden of the relief of a mult iple
member, his wife, widow and orphans shall rest on the Lodges in which
he holds membership in proportion to the length of membership in each.

342

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

A multiple member may receive a Certificate of Discontinuance of
Multiple Membership as provided in this Code if otherwise entitled to the
same.
Suspension or expulsion of a multiple member by any of his Lodges for
other than non-payment of dues, shall forthwith suspend or expel his
membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction, and the Secretary of any
Lodge in this Jurisdiction suspending or expelling such member shall
immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge in
which the multiple member holds membership. Any member who has
been suspended or expelled in any other Grand Jurisdiction for other than
non-payment of dues, and who is subsequently restored to membership
therein, may also be restored to membership in this Jurisdiction in the
same manner as is provided in this Code for members suspended or
expelled by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction initially.
Suspension by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction for non-payment of dues of a
multiple member shall automatically suspend his membership in all
Lodges in this Jurisdiction except the Lodees in which he holds life
memberships. The Secretary of any Lodge suspending such a member
shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary and also every other Lodge
in which the multiple member holds membership. Notification shall also
be given in case of reinstatement by a Lodge in this Jurisdiction which
shall automatically restore him to membership in every other Lodge of
which he was a member in this Jurisdiction, upon payment of any dues or
the performance of any other obligations required for restoration to
membership.
The suspension shall become effective only after a 60 day prior Notice of
Intent to Suspend has been sent to every other Lodge in which the
member holds membership. During this 60 day period the other Lodge
or Lodges may contact the member in an effort to avoid suspension. If
within the 60 day period the member fails to obtain good standing in all
Lodges involved, he shall be suspended. The suspension shall
automatically tenninate his membership in all Lodges in this Jurisdiction
except the Lodees in which he holds life memberships.
Suspension by a Lodge in any other Grand Jurisdiction for non-payment
of dues shall automatically suspend his membership in all Lodges in this
Jurisdiction except the Lodges in which he holds life memberships. The
suspension and any restoration shall become effective in the same manner
as provided in this section for members suspended by a Lodge in this
Jurisdiction.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponents of this Resolution have described what might initially
appear to be a conflict in the California Masonic Code. They note that Section
27020 provides a mechanism whereby a Mason may pay his dues to a particular
lodge for the remainder of his lifetime, by becoming a Life Member of that lodge.
Moreover, Section 23020 creates a mechanism whereby a Mason may become a
member of more than one lodge. Section 27070 requires a lodge to suspend any
member who has not paid his dues for twelve months. Section 15040 requires
another Mason not to have Masonic Communication with a suspended Mason. In
essence, a Mason who became a life member of one lodge and then joined a second
lodge but failed to pay the dues owed to that second lodge, could lose his
membership in the first lodge because of that non-payment of dues. The
proponents perceive this situation as being wrong, and they have drafted this
Resolution to correct it.
A Mason is free to seek membership in as many lodges as he chooses.
However. inherent in membership in any lodge is an obligation to support that
lodge, including the payment of dues. If a member finds it necessary to cease
paying dues, he has the ability to dimit from the lodge. If the reason that the dues
cannot be paid relate to a financial hardship, such dues can even be remitted.
Hence, there is no reason for any Mason to find himself in a state of
having failed to pay his dues to any lodge. Any such failure becomes an act which
is inconsistent w.ith one' s recognized responsibility as a Mason. The penalty for
that fail·:re is suspension from the lodge in question and, subsequently, from other
lodges to which that Mason belongs. It is the opinion of your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes that it is not consistent with current Grand Lodge policy to
allow a man to retain active membership in one lodge simply because he once paid
a life membership, when, for no justifiable reason, he has failed to honor another
Masonic commitment.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

[t has been an honor to serve the Board of Trustees of the California

We continued our policy of meeting in Masonic facilities, including the
Home at Covina and this Grand Lodge, in our continuing effort to reduce

Our Grand Master serves as a Director of the National Masonic
Foundation for Children in Washington, D.C. During this past year. your

runners-up each received a certificate of recognition and a $1 .000 check to be used
at their discretion within their school districts.

special named funds to keep the donors apprised of how their funds are progressing
and the number of scholarships awarded.
Since the inception of the California Masonic Foundation, scholarships
have been a major thrust of our charitable program. Over the years, many changes
have occurred, and 1995 was no exception.

with 850 completed applications being returned to our office. It was detennined
a computerized database was necessary to aid in the selection process. Toward that

Elevator Project
As you can see the first phase of our elevator upgrade program is
complete. The interior of both elevators have been remodeled. They are much
more eye appealing and the lighting is much better. This is extremely important
because so many non-masons use these elevators daily. The project to upgrade the
electronics to make them work smarter has been delayed because the parts were not
available on a timely basis. There is a 6 month plus lead time on just the
electronics. Then each elevator would be down for approximately four to six
weeks. So this next phase is going to take some real smart planning. It was very
difficult just scheduling five days for the interior upgrade.

Admissions Committee
by Victor Howard, Ph.D. and Ernest A. Pooleon, Co-Chairmen
This year the Admissions Committee of the Board of Trustees modified
the previous practice of meeting on the first Tuesday of each month prior to the full
Board Meeting which was on the following Wednesday. The informal meeting, on
Tuesday, was to allow for a free exchange of information about each of the
applicants between the Trustees of the North and the South and the Homes
Administrators, Representatives and Medical Staff. Due to the ability of refining
methods of communication, the committee has been able to conclude all
preliminary business during the meeting of the full Board.
Prior to the full Board Meeting, on the first Wednesday of each month, the
.
eight Trustees who form the Admissions Committee, four from the North and four
from the South, have received and carefully studied the applications for Masonic
assistance. These Trustees evaluate the applications and submit their comments
and vo~es to the two co-chairmen. The co-chairman in charge for that month (the
co-chairmen alternate responsibility) then produces a preliminary Admissions
Committee Report.
Following receipt of the preliminary information from the members of the
Admissions Committee, with input received from the medical staff at the Home
this preliminary Admissions Committee Report may be modified to reflect th~
discussions. The revised Admissions Committee Report is then presented to the

full Board of Trustees at the formal Board Meeting on Wednesday, where the final
decisions are made on each application.
The number of applications handled by the committee for couples,
individuals and children varies from month to month. This past year the high was
nine applications handled in one month for seniors, and six applications in one
month for children.
Because of the need to control admissions due to the reconstruction at the
Union City facility, and because the Skilled Nursing Facility was operating close
to maximum capacity, admissions were restricted to those classified as
"Independent Ambulatory." As was anticipated, this continues to result in an
increase in the number of persons receiving Nonresident Assistance (NRA).
Paralleling this reduction at Union City, the adult section of Covina
continues to operate at maximum capacity; although, at present, we continue to
limit the level of applications we can accept, due to a lack of on-site medical and
nursing facilities, to those classified as " Independent Ambulatory."
The co-chairmen sincerely thank the other Trustee members of the
Admissions Committee who labor long and hard over the applications. All
Trustees try to make a thoughtful judgment as to what is best for the applicant and
the capabilities available within our facilities .
We appreciate the fine support and dedication to the applicants and
Trustees provided by Karla Griffin, Homes Representative North, Carolyn Sage,
Homes Representative South, Kira Reginato, Director of Outreach Services, and
Kitty Teal and Hilma Mautz of Covina who also assisted in the South.
The co-chairmen gratefully acknowledge the hard work and dedication of
the Trustees who are on the Admissions Committee. The members are Warren
Buschmann, Charles Alexander, Allen Gresham, Roy Henville, Richard Wright and
Robert Peters. We also acknowledge the work of the two Administrators, Kelly
Wiest and Dale Ankney, and their staff.

The market availability of earthquake insurance in California continues
to drive rates up and limits our ability to purchase coverage adequate for our needs.
This bas become an escalating problem in our Grand Jurisdiction in recent years
and without significant changes in legislation the situation will continue to
exacerbate.

This is a remarkable perfonnance, particularly when considering the everincreasing cost of health care in general and skilled nursing care in particular.

Coverage available to us has been reduced to approximately one-third
over a three year period while costs have increased. Accordingly, we have agreed
to establish a "self-insured" fund to protect the assets of our Masonic Homes
beginning with the 1995/96 fiscal year. We are pleased the first contribution to this
fund will be $599,013.

shown little acti~ity, has prompted us to seek higher deductibles in exchange for
significant premium savings.
We will continue to review options available to us while maintaining the
"prudent man rule."

Planned Giving Options
The Masonic Homes planned giving program offers various gift-making
options to prospective donors, including the Pooled Income Fund, charitable
remainder annuity trusts, and charitable remainder unitrusts. In addition, individual
wills and living trusts are most popular methods of making planned gifts to the
Masonic Homes. During the year several steps were taken to publicize these
options, including:

A toll-free telephone number, 800-242-0123, was established
exclusively for the planned giving program.
Articles were written for each of the four issues of the California
Freemason.
Assisted the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment
Board revise brochures that now include the toll-free telephone
number.
A letter was sent to the Master of every lodge (over the Grand
Secretary's signature) publicizing my appointment and
availability to make presentations to lodges and Masonic groups
on the Masonic Homes planned giving program. As a result,
two presentations were made and one scheduled for the future.
A "fact sheet" was revised to further elaborate on various
planned giving options.
A database of attorneys with expertise in estate planning was
established for referrals to individuals requesting the need for
such an attorney.
A description of the Masonic Homes was published in "The
Guide to Gifts and Bequests - California: 1995-1997." This
directory of philanthropically supported institutions is sent at no
cost to over 13,000 attorneys, bank trust officers, accountants
and foundation trustees in California and parts of Arizona,
Hawaii and Nevada.

by William W Dickson, Chairman
We had our customary scholarship funding reviews with young people
from our Home. Their individual goals range from business administration, to
teaching and nursing, to international studies.
We are seeing increases in tuition costs and particularly living costs for
the students. The cost of graduate work at a major university, plus housing and
living, cost approximately $27,000 per year per student.
We request that if you have the capability please remember the needs of
our children. However, we also request that any consideration you may make be
as broad in use definition as you can be comfortable with but designated for use in
educating the children of the Home.
With that in mind we and the Administration have been assessing the
futures of all the children and several programs have been initiated.

Real Estate Committee

I.

A particular effort is being made to increase the reading skills of
each child. This is being done by outside services, literary
programs and tutors. Communication ability is paramount.

2.

The computer is becoming more and more important in our lives
and the children should be informed. We have purchased some
computers and engaged an outside teacher in computer science
to help our young people in developing computer skills.

3.

All children at the high school level are being given aptitude and
personal evaluation testing at Human Engineering, an
established foundation. This is in keeping with the old
admonition, "Know Thyself."

4.

The administration is watching more closely each individual
child for clues to interest and aptitude which we will enrich by
outside sources - whether music, art, drama, etc. This is the time
to explore.

by Stanley M Cazneaux, Chairman
The Real Estate Committee of the Masonic Homes of California presently
includes the Chairman and one member, Robert D. Peters.
The Real Estate ~ommittee is charged with the responsibility of disposing
o~ all real estate made available to the Masonic Homes through asset assignment,
wills and bequests, gifts and grants.
During the past year, July I, 1994 through June 30, 1995, we sold twentythre~ (23) pieces of property for a total of$l,038,412. We sold twenty (20) motor
vehicles for a total of$47,729, and home furnishings in the amount of$29.25.
Total sales for 1994/95 equal $1,086,170.25. In addition, payments, including
payoffs, on our "Notes Receivable" amount to a total of$724, 160.24. We continue
to carry thirty-five (35) Notes with a total value of$1 ,789,499.86.
We always have an inventory of unsold properties, due to the Life Care
Contract signed by each new resident of the Home. This affords them a ninety (90)

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
MASONIC HOJ\1E, UNION CITY

and other related Masonic groups visit, tour and conduct degrees and installations
for our residents to anend.

1994-1995

A special thank you to Alameda Lodge No. 167 for sponsoring an
Octoberfest; Tri-Square Lodge No. 551 for hosting a Strawberry Festival; and
Acacia Lodge No. 243 for their summer barbecue.

Since our Annual Communication last year, several resident milestones
have been reached.
Vera Sherman from Columbia Lodge No. 388 celebrated her 106th
birthday.
Lily Wilkinson from John P. Jannan Lodge No. 669 celebrated her I 04th
birthday.
Jesse "Ed" Lacy from San Fernando Lodge No. 343 turned 103 as did
Lillian Garfias of Temple Lodge No. 14.
We also have five residents at the young age of99.
In addition, the following couples celebrated notable wedding
anniversaries:
Joseph and Anna Duch, Chula Vista Lodge No. 626, 66 years.
Max and Pearl Wilson, Atwater Larchmont Lodge No. 614, 65 years.
Loland and Ruby Fowler, Nonna! Heights Lodge No. 632, I year.
As reported last year, our residents continue to enjoy varied entertainment
through activities at the Home as well as monthly trips away from the Home where
they enjoy such events as musical shows, ice skating shows, the circus and the
Oakland A's baseball games.
Our own musical group, the Silver Sonics, consisting of 16 residents,
performed many times for their co-residents, as well as making 8 off-site
perfonnances within the surrounding local communities.
Many of our residents volunteer their services daily to help in the post
office, library, canteen, gift shop, coffee shop, recreational services, and to serve
as tour guides.
Once again, our residents participated in and enjoyed "Jam and Jelly" day.
This is sponsored annually by the East Bay Past Matrons' Association. This year
marked the 91st year the event has been held. The Home is indeed grateful for this
wonderful, caring group of ladies.
Throughout this past year, we had 42 Masonic Lodges, Eastern Star
Chapters, Job 's Daughters Bethels, DeMolay Chapters, Rainbow Girls Assemblies,

ln June of 1995, our facility's four year old Clinical Pastoral Education
Program was granted full accreditation in the Association for clinical Pastor~)
Education, Inc. This program involves student chaplains in our Sunday worship
services, structured pastoral groups, and spiritual guidance to all levels of residents.
Students from all religious backgrounds are involved, including Roman Catholic,
United Methodist, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Pentecostal, and Episcopalian. This
reflects the diversity of religious backgrounds among our residents.
Capital improvements to our facility came in the form of refurbishing our
Medical Speciality Suite for use by our on-site optometrist, ophthalmologist,
audiologist, and podiatrist; a satellite TV dish for additional viewing channels for
the residents; a new nursing lift; a new automated employee time clock system; and
new telephone switching equipment which will allow us to expand telephone
service to resident apartments in the future. In addition, an energy saving light
system was installed in the Sedam Building. This will greatly reduce our electrical
expense. Also, two new electric doors were installed for the ease of residents using
walkers and canes.
Renova•ions were also made to our Masonic Cemetery located near the
Chapel of the Chimes Cemetery at 32992 Mission Boulevard in Hayward. New
brick columns and wrought iron fencing were installed.
Our population statistics show that we currently have 283 residents, with
76 Masons and 207 spouses or widows, including 26 couples. The average age is
87, and there are 170 lodges represented at our Home.
The renovation plan to modernize and improve our facilities, which was
mentioned in last year's report, continues to move forward, with the Wollenberg
construction now underway. Our Skilled Nursing floor on 5-Adams was closed
this past year, and the residents relocated into our Lorber Skilled Nursing Building.
Renovation on the Adams Building is expected to begin in 1996. When
completed, it will accommodate three floors of Assisted Living residents (our
largest and fastest growing group of residents), plus our Recreational Services
Department which includes crafts and ceramics.
Hopefully, this summary report of the past year's events gives you a small
impression of what life is like at this great Masonic Home. However, to really feel
and see the brotherly love that goes on daily, I invite all Brothers to stop by and
visit.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR

to the north. This new arrangement greatly reduces transfer trauma which often

provided by the employment of our own nursing personnel to supplement the care

MASONIC HOME, COVINA

1994-1995
It is an honor to provide the Masonic fraternity with my initial annual

report describing the status of the children, adults and staff who reside and work
at the place we proudly call the Masonic Home at Covina. The 1994-95 period
could best be described as a period of transition for our Home. Not only was I
appointed Administrator of this fine facility, but the two senior managers
responsible for child and adult care-giving were new to their positions as well.
Despite this seemingly tumultuous period, the Masonic Home at Covina continued
to march forward in providing excellent care to those who we lovingly call our
residents.
We are particularly proud of the continuing improvements in the care we
provide the Senior members of our community. As has been reported here before,
the age of the adults who enter our Home continues to advance. The average age
of the senior entering Covina last year was 86. As a result, the health services we
provide are being challenged more than ever before.
In order to meet the challenge of escalating health care demand, our new
Director of Adult Services introduced home health services on our campus
beginning last November. The purpose of this program is to provide quality health
care services in the resident's apartment in order that the resident may comfortably
and safely continue to age in place. The home health program is administered by
our Drrector of Adult Services in coordination with the Visiting Nursing
Association (VNA). Services provided by the VNA include:
Hospice Care
Registered Nursing Services
Medication Auditing and Administration
Home Health Aide Services
Restorative Nurse Aide Services
Despite our continuing efforts to provide our Senior residents with Homebased health services, inevitably, some of our residents require a higher level of
care than we are able to provide. Previously, this meant the resident would be
transferred to our sister facility in Union City which is licensed to provide all levels
of continuing health care including skilled nursing. This past year we were able to
establish a relationship with some outstanding local nursing facilities thereby

Of course, no Senior community would be complete without a full
schedule of activities. During the 1994-95 period we introduced numerous
activities which kept our resident stimulated no matter what their personal
preference. Microwave cooking classes, bingo night, concerts in the park, ceramic
classes, computer training classes, and grandparents dinner with our children are
but a few of the many activities available to our Senior residents.
In addition to the new activities mentioned here, many old activities
continued to bring joy to our Seniors' lives at Covina. The most enjoyable of these
time-tested activities is the inclusion of our residents in lodge affiars which take
place regularly on our beautiful campus. Virtually every weekend our residents are
invited to participate with their fellow lodge brothers in an array of campus-based
fun. Of particular appeal to our residents are the many barbecues which take place
in the southeast comer of the campus overlooking our expansive lawn area.
Residents not only enjoy the food and good conversation associated with such
events, but they also enjoy helping out whenever the opportunity presents itself.
On the children' s side of our campus we were equally busy serving those
in need. The total population of children residents increased 40% during the fiscal
year, which necessitated the hiring of many new personnel. Despite this explosion
of growth, we believe we provided a comfortable and loving home to children who
otherwise might have been at serious risk.
The growth of our child population and subsequent growth of staff did
bring to light the need to begin a formalized process of house parent training. As
a result, we have engaged the services of a firm which specializes in the creation
of learning material for that purpose. This new material coupled with information
gained through visits to homes similar to ours will allow us to develop a training
program which maximizes the potential offered by our high caliber personnel.
One program which the Covina Home successfully participated in
launching in 1994-95 was the Masonic Model Student Assistance Training
Program. Although this program was largely developed and administered by the
California Masonic Foundation, the Covina Home accepted responsibility for all
site development and program logistics for the five sessions conducted on our
campus during this past year. Over 250 educators throughout the State of
California were provided free food and housing accommodations as they
participated in this " investment in America' s youth." Because of the importance

385

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of the subject matter addressed in this program as well as its increasing relevance
to our own youth, all house parents at our facility were required to attend.
The Masonic Model Student Assistance Training Program was but a first
step in identifying the needs of the youth who reside at the Covina Home. During
1994-95 we re-assessed our own methods of dealing with the problems confronting
our youth and concluded steps had to be taken to better address our residents'
needs. We came to the realization that today's child resident is no longer just a
victim of economic circumstances. Unfortunately abuse and neglect are now the
nonn, with many of our children suffering from Attention Deficit Disorder or
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder.
In response to our youth's increasing psychological/sociological needs,
we have increased the use of psychological consultants to help our children
improve their mental health. Jn addition, we are beginning to work closely with
our psychology professionals in developing programs which pennit our house
parents to meaningfully participate in our children's development.
On a more upbeat note, I am extremely pleased to report five of our youth
graduated high school this past June with four deciding to continue their education
at local junior colleges. Attendance at college was made possible by the continuing
availability of monies accumulated within the Foundation's Scholarship Trust
Fund. Scholarships and loans provided by this Fund allow our college-bound
youth the opportunity to attend the colleges of their choice. This program has
become increasingly important to our children as entry into the job market demands
higher levels of education. Fortunately, our youth are recognizing this reality as
evidenced by the fact one of our former residents recently applied and was granted
a scholarship to attend a prestigious graduate school.
An important step taken this past year to improve our children's academic
perfonnance was the establishment of a computer laboratory adjacent to the study
hall/library. Four Power Mac computers are now available to our children to be
used as tools in the perfonnance of their school work. We are also working with
various educators to determine the appropriate educational software to be included
on these powerful machines for learning. Capacity of the computers is such that
we will be able to load recommended software for every age group on our campus.

neatness, loyalty, obedience, courtesy, dependability and a sence of responsibility
for their shipmates. Both attended a mock " Boot Camp" conducted at NAS
Miramar and one of the youth actually served a two week hitch on a Coast Guard
vessel stationed at the Long Beach Naval Shipyard.
These are but a small representation of the many activities to which our
youth are exposed throughout the year. It is our plan to continue these programs
and develop additional opportunities which allow our children to become
successful contributors to our society as they reach the age of maturity.

384

In addition to the many educational issues addressed throughout the year,
we also continued the tradition of exposing our children to experiences which
provide them with entertainment, while developing a sense of responsibility. For
instance, ten of our thirty-four children were participants in DeMolay, Rainbow for
Girls, or Job's Daughters. Those who participate in these Masonic organizations
do so enthusiastically and have benefited greatly from the experience.
Two of our youth participated in the United States Naval Sea Cadet Corps
programs which are designed to teach young cadets the virtues of personal

On behalf of all of the residents and staff at the Masonic Home at Covina,
we thank you for the opportunity to continue the good work which has been carried
out here for the past eight decades. We are honored by the responsibilities for
which we have been entrusted and we look forward to exceeding your expectations
as we move forward into the 21st century.
Respectfully submitted,
Dale Ankney, Administrator

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand Lodge,
Brethren:
I am pleased to present to you a summary report of the activities of the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board for the year 1994/95.
Total contributions from the brethren of the Grand Lodge for the fiscal
year beginning July l, 1994 and ending June 30, 1995 amounted to $1,246,912.57.
I am proud to report that this dollar figure represents an increase of $31, 790.5 1, or
2.6 percent, over the results for 1993/94. In recognizing this fact we must give
credit to one brother who made a major contribution of over $90,000. That
significant donation was responsible, in large measure, for the increase over last
year.
The average gift received this year was $26. 74, as compared to $22.82 last
year. In addition, the average donation per member throughout the Grand Lodge
was $10.70, an increase of about seven and one-half percent over the $9.94 average
last year. This average of $10/.70 per member is an all-time high in the recorded
history of the Endowment Fund.
Of the 448 lodges in the Grand Lodge, 197 (or 44%) achieved the Honor
Roll with an average gift of $9.94. Unfortunately, th is is fewer lodges and a
smaller percentage than the previous year.
Other gifts to the Endowment Fund were as follows:
Bequests . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . $2,292,070.66
General Undesignated .. . . .. ....... ... 11 ,852.37
Memorials ............. . .. ... ... ... . 3,202.00
Royalties ............ .... .... ........ 200.31
The Grand Total is ..... . ..... . ... $3,554,237.83
Over the past years we have witnessed a continual decline in membership,
which certainly effects the amount of money added to the permanent endowment
fund. In addition to the membership decline, however, we have also witnessed a
decline in the percentage of brethren who make any contribution at all. Last year
we reported a 43.5% participation; this year it appears that the number is only 40%.
However, we have recent information which brings that percentage into question.

394

It appears that some lodges are not reporting the numbers of brethren who make
contributions. Without this information , we cannot completely report to you the
fu II scope of Masonic Homes support being given by the brethren of the Grand
Lodge. We certainly hope to see an improvement in lodge reports in the future.
I want to hasten to add a sincere note of appreciation to those hardworking lodge secretaries who do so much to help this program. Without their
dedication, we could not be nearly as successful as we are. They are asked to
submit contributions on a timely basis, report numbers of contributors, and include
the name of any brother giving over $50. This information is critical to monitoring
the progress of the Endowment Board program. To those who do that job I say
"Thank you!"
The members of your Masonic Homes Endowment Board have spent an
extremely busy year, promoting the fund and encouraging the brethren to make
contributions. We continue to present the Masonic Homes history book entitled,
"The Greatest of These is Charity," to newly-initiated Entered Apprentice Masons.
The only limitation in that program is that the board members are sometimes not
apprised of a planned initiation. We also continue to give talks and reports, make
slide presentations, and in as many ways as possible support the lodges in their
Masonic Homes programs.
We welcomed three new members to the board during the past year:
Richard Haggerty, Robert Catalano and Willie Deforest Mock. Brother Catalano
replaced Brother Kenneth E. Patterson who gave approximately six years of service
to the Homes. One of our members, Brother William Gershon, completed nine
years of outstanding service, and will retire with our most sincere thanks. Three
others have found it necessary to resign: Clarence L. Lambing, William C.
Temple, and A. Bruce Ivie. They will be replaced respectively by Alan Palmer,
Donald Franke and Billy N. Bowles.
May I close with another reminder that the income from the Endowment
for a significant amount of the resources needed to keep our homes
accounts
Fund
in operation. With the combination of continued inflation and declining
membership, it is more critical than ever that every brother do his part in building
the Endowment Fund. I encourage every Master, Warden, Secretary and Lodge
Masonic Homes Chairman to re-dedicate himself to communicating this message
to the brethren of his lodge. We must not disappoint our brethren, sweethearts and
children who live in the Homes. They are counting on us.
Most Worshipful, on behalf of the 33 members of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board, I thank you for the opportunity of serving you and the Grand
Lodge in this capacity.

Nob Hill is charged with renting the auditorium and exhibit hall for p ublic
and private concerts, seminars, stockholder meetings, examinations, individual
performances, shows, exhibits and the like. It also operates the parking garage
through a professional parking corporation and rents and maintains four apartment
buildings on Pine Street south of the Temple with direct supervision by a
professional property manager.

87

_J

LL.

Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc. Is a "for profit" corporatio n who lly
owned by the Grand Lodge of California. It operates the California Masonic
Memorial Temple properties on Nob Hill as a general lessee of the Temple and
does business as Nob Hill Masonic Center.

The business and corporate powers of Nob Hill are managed by or under
the direction of a five person Board of Directors, four of whom are elected by the
Grand Master with the fifth serving by virtue of his office as Junior Grand Warden.
The Grand Treasurer is the Chief Financial Officer of the corporation and the
Grand Secretary is its Secretary.
The day-to-day operation of the business of Nob Hill is directed by Mr.
Ray W. Ward, a Certified Facilities Executive who formerly served as President of
the International A~sociation of Auditorium Managers and who is highly esteemed
as a lecturer and consultant in that profession. Nob Hill is fortunate to have the
multitude affairs of its business under the highly capable direction of Mr. Ward.
He and his very diligent and cooperative staff have met and exceeded the goals set
out by the Board of Directors as well as the aspirations of this Grand Lodge.
During the three plus years under the direction of Nob Hill there has been
full compliance with the very complex and extensive regulations of the Americans
With Disabilities Act so that our auditorium, exhibit hall and parking facilities are
certified for use by those persons who come under the protection of the Act.
Moreover, we have complied with recommendations of our insurance carrier fo r
public safety and have rehabilitated much equipment in this thirty-seven year old
Temple, while improving its appearance.
We would be remiss in not paying tribute to President Frank Russell and
the Board of Trustees of tile California Masonic Memorial Temple, not only for
footing the million dollar plus cost of all of the work of improvement that has been
accomplished to date, but also for giving us their complete support and cooperation
in decision making as to the timing and need for expenditures. Chief Financial
Officer of the Grand Lodge, Brother Doug Scott, has served as a liaison for both
Boards and his diligence and expertise have been of great value to us.

404

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We are pleased that from a financial standpoint our goals have also been
met. In prior Reports we told you that when we assumed the stewardship of Nob
Hill, the previous year had shown an operating loss of $74, 146. In the three years
since May of 1992, Nob Hill has paid the Memorial Temple $961,655 in rent while
assuming all of the expenses of its Temple operation. In addition, we have repaid
our initial capital borrowing of $187 ,500 plus interest of $25,804 and we are free
of debt with a comfortable cash reserve.
Moreover, of interest to you, our stockholders, we have paid the Grand
Lodge $100,000 by way of dividends, including $25,000 on the first day of this
month. This has accomplished the return to the Grand Lodge of the initial $62,500
it invested in us together with interest, plus $25,000 for its operations in these
difficult times of declining membership.
Nob Hill does not intend to sit on its laurels. Rather, our auditorium and
exhibit hall bookings for this fiscal year are up substantially and include the highly
prestigious State of the World Forum in which George Bush, Margaret Thatcher
and Mikhail Gorbachev participated on Sunday, October 1st. Their discussion was
televised live nationally and relayed world-wide by CNN. Our parking garage net
income, which is averaging over $52,000 per month this fiscal year, compares to
about $20,000 per month when we commenced business. This result is directly
related to our marketing of the auditorium and exhibit hall and it is our goal to
continue improvement in this area.
The Board extends its thanks to Grand Master Stovall, a founding Director
of Nob Hill, for his encouragement and cooperation and to Grand Treasurer
Wilkins and Grand Secretary Cooper as well as their staff for their continuous
support. It is truly a team effort that makes Nob Hill a successful enterprise.
Respectfully subrn itted,
Donald B. McCaw, PGM, President

ON FINANCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the relative legislation referred
to it for the 1995 Annual Communication as follows:
Recommendations No. 10, 13, 14 and 17 have no financial impact on
Grand Lodge finances.
Resolution No. 95-01 has no significant impact on Grand Lodge finances.
Resolution No. 95-03: this resolution would result in the current Temple
building in San Francisco being sold and the offices being moved to Fresno.
This would result in an aggregate additional expenditure of $250,000
annually by the Grand Lodge of California. The Grand Lodge would not be a
beneficiary of the proceeds of the sale of the building either by tax code or by the
by-laws of the California Masonic Memorial Temple. Also, Nob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc., as operator of the current building, would cease to exist and
Grand Lodge, as its sole stockholder, would lose its dividend estimated to be
$40,000 annually. Other major factors in this extra expenditure are assuming
financial responsibility for the library/museum and historical sites and a significant
increase in rent.
Additionally, the Grand Lodge would incur one time moving costs of
$175,000 at a minimum. Quite commonly, actual moving costs materially exceed
original estimates.
Resolutions No. 95-09 and 95-10 have no financial impact on Grand
Lodge finances.
Resolution No. 95-11: this resolution would result in lodges not paying
per capita on Master Masons who maintain plural memberships.
This would result in Grand Lodge receiving approximately $75,000 less
annually in per capita, based on membership at June 30, 1995 and the 1995/96 per
capita rate.
Resolutions No. 95-12 and 95-13 have no financial impact on Grand
Lodge finances.
Resolution No. 95-14 has minimal to no financial impact on Grand Lodge
finances.
Resolution No. 95-15 was withdrawn.
Resolution No.95-16: this resolution would increase the contributions to
Masonic Homes of California required for Lodges for the degrees.

Resolutions No. 95-18 and 95-19 have no financial impact on Grand
Lodge finances.
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the monthly accounting reports
and financial statements prepared by the accounting staff of our Grand Lodge
which covered data for the fiscal year ending October 31, 1995.
The Grand Lodge Finance and Executive Committees recommend a
Budget which covers the period November I, 1995 to October 31, 1996.
The proposed Budget for the next Grand Lodge year continues the current
level of expenditures with several major differences:
I.

The Endowment Fund contributions by Grand Lodge 1s

ON INVESTMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:

The lnvesnnent c~~mittee has the responsibility of reporting annually to
Gr~~d Lodge on the cond1t10n of the various funds of Grand Lodge and those
entities.
During the year quarterly meetings are held by the committee with its
inv~stment counselors. At each meeting an independent analytical consulting firm
reviews the performance of the various funds as compared with similar funds, ie.,
Endowment, Non-Profit and Trust Funds in the United States.
i:ie primary concern of the committee is the preservation of the principal
of the various funds together with the highest rate of return commensurate with
safety and good invesnnent practice.
Three funds, Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes General
Fund and the Hugo M. Loerber Union City Fund constitute 91 % of the total
investments.
Among other funds supervised by the committee are the General Fund of
Grand Lodge, the funds of the Ca"lifornia Masonic Memorial Temple, California's
Masonic Foundation Pooled Income, and several restricted-use funds of Masonic
Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1995 was
$378,086,000 compared to $324,922,000 a year earlier, an increase of 16.4%. The
approximate 1994-1995 cash yield on the total invested funds was 3 .5%.
Fixed income securities, including government and corporate bonds
composed 40% of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common stocks
and cash equivalents.
The rewarding accumulation of assets in the various funds of Grand Lodge
has been the result of the efforts of Masons and their friends. The operation of the
Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are financed almost entirely from the
Endowment and the General Fund investments. The expansion at Union City in
the last several years was funded entirely from the Hugo M. Loerber Fund. Other
revenues furnish support for the charitable activities and educational grants from
the Grand Lodge of California.
The funds invesnnents rm1k among the highest in quality because the
Investment Committee exercises the utmost prudence and care in their overseeing
of the management of the funds. During the past year the committee replaced two
of the funds equity managers with three new managers. The cash yield and the

Respectfully submitted,
