PROCEEDTNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

During the summer months the committee continued regular visits to
lodges across the state. At the same time efforts were being made to find a way to
reprint the four volume set entitled "One Hundred Years of Freemasonry in
California''. This was finally accomplished in time for the present Communication,
and the sets were displayed and sold at the History Booth this year. The profit from
these sales will enable us to comfortably finance the "One Hundred Fifty Years"
publication.
Planning continues with regard to lodge visits and committee members
were active throughout helping lodges establish at least one "Lodge History Night"
per year and include it as an on-going annual lodge event. The suggestion was to
have the senior members of a given lodge attend that evening and give them an
opportunity to just sit around and tell stories about the ·good old days. These
moments of golden memories could ten be recorded on either video or sound tape,
and later these wonderful stories could be used as material in writing that lodge's
history. This is important to each lodge, since the older members are the brethren
who usually have the interesting tidbits and stories, and unfortunately it is precisely
these brothers who will be passing membership to the eternal Grand Lodge above
very soon. Once they go, we lose their wonderful contributions and stories forever.

as by volunteer committee assistants such as brother Irv Cohen. In fact, it is just
this kind of effort which shows the need for additional manpower support for the
committee membership. It will also be recalled that during 1995 the suggestion of
establishing a History Committee Assistant Corps of ten men for each member of
the committee was made. The need has not expired to date.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F. & A.M of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit the
following data as its Annual Report for the Fiscal Year ending June 30, 1995. The
Committee is in its 68th year.
The Committee takes its directive to supervise the operations of the
several Masonic Service Bureaus in the State of California very seriously. Th.ese
Bureaus, which number 12, extend from the San Diego in the South, to Sacramento
in the North, assist in rendering Relief to Distressed Worthy Brothers and their
families residing in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge F & AM of California.
Sojourners as well as California Masons receive assistance when the situation
requires it. The Committee also assists the Masonic Service Association in the
continuing development of its "Hospital Visitation Program" at several of the
Veterans Administration Facilities in California. Members of the Committee in
conjunction with Executive Secretaries of the Bureaus also participate in the work
of the Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada.
Committee Members
The 1993-1994 Committee consists of Wor. Paul E. Brown of San Diego,
Wor. Robert W. Meier of Los Angeles, Wor. William H. Murphy of Fresno, Wor.
George C. Hesse of San Jose and Howard J. Dumont of Elverta, serving as
Committee Chainnan.
Executive Secretaries

R. Stephen Doan
Stephen Pritsker

Kenneth N. Cooper
Ralph H. Head

419

There currently is a vacancy in the Santa Clara Valley Bureau. There is
an aggressive search being made by Wor. Hesse and the officers of that Bureau to
fill the vacancy.
Committee Meetings
The customary four Committee meetings were not held during the
preceding year. It was decided by members of the Committee (with the consent of
Most Worshipful William F. Stovall) that the final meeting of the year was not
necessary. The first was held during the Annual Communication of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California, reviewed and discussed several
problems of the various Bureaus. Wor. A. Bruce Ivie past Committee President

acted as chairman for this meeting. The infonnation booth on the "G" floor was
manned by members of this Committee and several of the Executive Secretaries.
It was operated from Sunday through Tuesday.
The Southern regional meeting was held at the Scottish Rite Temple in
Pasadena on Saturday, March 25, 1995. All of the Southern Bureaus were
represented. The meeting was held to review the report form s required by this
Committee and to answer questions about them. Ample time was given over to the
discussion of problem areas. The afternoon session, which was closed to all but the
members of this Committee, was for the purpose of review of the closing of the
Santa Monica Bay Masonic Service Bureau. The several member Lodges of the
Santa Monica Bureau voiced no objection to consolidation with the Los Angeles
Bureau. The vote was unanimous for closure of the Bureau on the last day of June
1995.
The Committee again met on April 21, 1995 at the Oakland Scottish Rite
Temple. Former Committeeman, Ray Rookard, acted as our host. This, like our
previous meeting of March 25, 1994, was for review of the forms required by this
Committee. The Very Worshipful, John L. Cooper III, Grand Secretary, attended
this meeting for a question and answer session. The informational session was
overwhelmingly favorable. The Committee, having completed its' business at the
morning session, did not hold a closed session.

Changes in the Bureaus
The Fresno Service Bureau is undergoing some expansion with the
addition of some Lodges in the TulareNisalia/Hanford area. They have requested
to change the name to THE CENTRAL VALLEY MASONIC SERVICE
BUREAU. This is due to Warren C. Carr, Executive Secretary, going the extra
mile to bring the neighboring Lodges into this Bureau.
The Santa Monica Bay Service Bureau consolidated with the Los Angeles
Bureau on July 1, 1995. This was with the approval of the Most Worshipful,
William F. Stovall, and the consent of the member Lodges. The anticipated
savings to the Bush Mansonic Relief Fund Inc., is in excess of $3 ,600.00.
Bureau Operating Expenses
A quick review of the "Recapitulation of Service Bureau Operating
Expenses" shows that care is taken by the Executive Secretaries to keep
expenditures to a minimum. This year $177,5 12.5 1 was expended by the several
Bureaus. It should be of interest to the reader that $184,486.55 was the total
amount budgeted. for all Bureaus.

Bush Masonic Relief, Inc.
Bush Masonic Relief, lnc. was the primary source of funding for the four
Service Bureaus in Los Angeles County. This is a unique situation as no "per
capita" tax is collected from the member Lodges. The generous support of these
Bureaus by the Bush Fund is greatly appreciated by those cognizant of it and of
course those who were assisted by it.
Blood Banks
The following Service Bureaus maintain operative Blood Bank services:
Bakersfield (provides this service for all Masonic Bodies in its area), East Bay,
Central Valley (Fresno), Sacramento, San Francisco and Southern Alameda
County.
Uniform Compacts
Uniform Compacts which act as an agreement between a Masonic Lodge
and the local Masonic Service Bureau were finalized for the following Lodges:

Conclusion
This Committee sincerely appreciates the support given it by the Most
Worshipful, William F. Stovall; his elected as well as appointed corps of officers
and the staff of the Grand Lodge Office in San Francisco. Recognition is also to
be given to those special Masons who give of their time to act as Officers of the
Masonic Service Bureaus. Last, but certainly not least, this Committee extend its
appreciation to those twelve Masons who serve this Fraternity as Executive
Secretary of their respective Service Bureaus.
Respectfully submitted,
Howard J. Dumont, Chairman

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
PRINCE HALL RECOGNITION STUDY

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M., of California:
The Prince Hall Recognition Study Committee is pleased to report that the
special relationship which has developed between our Grand Lodge and the Most
Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii, Inc., since 1990,
is moving swiftly toward the establishment of complete fraternal relations between
these two grand lodges. Last year Grand Lodge approved legislation which took
the first step toward such mutual recognition, and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge
took a similar step in this direction in July of this year. Grand Master William F.
Stovall has further advanced this process by placing before you his
Recommendation No. 6, which would establish full and unconditional recognition
of their grand lodge, while providing a clear statement that our grand lodge will not
interfere in the proper internal jurisdiction of any other grand lodge with which we
are in fraternal communication.
The committee met twice during the past Grand Lodge year with our
counterparts from the Prince Hall Grand Lodge. Through all these deliberations
we continued to be impressed with the quality, depth, and sincerity of the
commitment of the representatives of their grand lodge. On the eve of mutual
recognition, we wish to pay tribute to the members of the Most Worshipful Prince
Hall Grand Lodge of California and Hawai i, Inc .. whose dedication to the
principles of Freemasonry and to the working out of our joint future, was
unparalleled. Without their diligence and patience, it could not have happened.
The history of how this came about is short, but significant. In 1990 our
Grand Lodge had before it a resolution which, if adopted, would have granted
unilateral recognition to the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California. Recognizing
that any such step should invo lve discussion with the leaders of the Prince Hall
Grand Lodge, the proponent withdrew his resolution in favor of the establishment
of the Prince Hall Recognition Study Committee. T hat committee was appointed
by Most Worshipful Ronald A. Sherod in 1990, and has functioned under four
other Grand Masters since.
The Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California responded
to our invitation by appointing leaders of stature within their organization to meet
with us. After defining our joint mission, and sening forth our initia l goals, we
were able to make significant progress in working out the means by which mutual
recognition could take place . While California was not the first grand lodge to
move toward recognition of another grand lodge within its own state boundaries,
it must be recognized that there were problems unique to California which had to

427

be addressed. Not the least of these was the multi-state jurisdictional problem, for
the Prince Hall Grand Lodge has lodges in Hawaii as well as in Califom~a .. Our
Grand Master, Most Worshipful William F. Stovall, has addressed this 1ssu.e
through his Recommendation No. 6, and our committee strongly endorses th.is
solution. Put simply, it states that we will abide by the law of the grand lodges ~
that jurisdiction that are recognized by that particular jurisdiction .. California
Masons would therefore only visit lodges in Hawaii that are recognized by the
Grand Lodge of Hawaii itself. This proposal has resolved any potential conflict
between our full and complete recognition of the Most Worshipful Prince Hall
Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii, without infringing upon the rights of the
Grand Lodge of Hawaii to the proper governance of its own jurisdiction: T~e
solution is consistent with our current law on visitation, which states that Cahforn1a
Masons are expected to follow the law of the jurisdiction they visit with reference
to issues of Masonic recognition. It is a timely solution, and one that is supported
by both the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii,
and by the Grand Lodge of Hawaii itself.
During early September, Most Worshipful Stovall authorized committee
member, Frank Russell, to make a trip to Hawaii to meet with their Grand Master,
Most Worshipful Richard M .W. Dang, and the recognition com~~ttee he ha~
appointed. That committee had only met once prior to his amvmg so their
deliberations had been few . They were very receptive to what he had to say and
made the decision to begin dia logue with the Prince Hall Grand Lodge to start their
own recognition process. In so doing that decision prevents any misunderstanding
between the two Grand Lodges of California and Hawaii . We have a copy of that
Jener and I will read it to you now. DONE! So with the successful passage of
Most Worshipful Stovall's recommendation #6, The Most Worshipful Prine~. H~ll
Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii, Inc. and the Grand Lodge of Hawa11 will
start the recognition process. That action will help accomplish our common
objectives so all 3 jurisdictions may dwell together, as Brethren, as it was meant to
be.
When the two committees jointly began their deliberations our comminees
were convinced that recognition could not be mandated, it had to evolve. Brethren,
your comminees biggest compliment has been your asking "What .i~ tak.ing so
long." The time has come. It has evolved, and the road to recognition 1s now
before us.
If you, Grand Lodge, approve this next step toward ful.I and compl~te
recognition, this comminee expects to have a key role in th~ ~plem~~tat~on
process. There is muc h yet to be done. The procedures by which mt~rv1s1~at1on
wiJl take place must be worked out in detail, and worked out to the sat1sfact1on of
both grand lodges. But we are confident that the future is a bright one for both the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Pipeline to the Senate
Our committee is fortunate in having a direct contact with the California
State Legislature, Senator Ralph Dills, a member of our fraternity who is also a
long-time member of our committee. His interest in and support for our Public
Schools is well known. Because of this interest and support we are kept informed
of all pending legislation whose passage would affect our schools.
His most recent contribution to our committee is his annual Resolution
adopting one week in April as Public Schools Week. Senator Dills' input is always
valuable.
Proclamations
We have long been aware of the publicity value of Public Schools Week
Proclamations. This year, as in all previous years, we urged lodges to obtain such
proclamations from local city and county officials. Our committee sets a good
example by obtaining similar proclamations from the State Governor and the State
Legislature. In addition we drafted a proclamation for our Deputy Grand Master
to use as his Public Schools Week Proclamation during his year as Grand Master
in 1996. After editing, it was accepted.
Pamphlets
This year we printed 10,000 pamphlets extolling the achievements of our
Public Schools and expressing Masonry's interest in their welfare. Although these
pamphlets were intended ~or distribution throughout the year, they were especially
effective at Public Schools Week Observances, Public School Cornerstone
Ceremonies, or used as part of table settings at dinner meetings.

431

SCHOOLS". The jackets are being sold for $20.00, the shirts for $15.00 and the
hats for $6.00. Hats and shirts are the best selling items. This last year we have
found that only a few individuals purchased these items. Currently we are not
reordering these items.
Masons on Campus
It has taken almost a year of ground work to finally allow the Masons to
attempt to visit a campus and work with the students and staff. The Los Angeles
Unified School District Board of Education has allowed the Masons on Campus
program to be a part of the Volunteer Programs Options and Service Concepts (preschool through adult school) program. Volunteer opportunities include:

Classroom Volunteers
Schools Volunteers
Community Resource Volunteers
Volunteers for the Handicapped
Volunteers with Special Skills
Due to the number of Masons available, the number of schools, and the
diversity of the students, people of all influences are encouraged to participate. At
this time we have a fine working relationship with the School Board of Education,
the Prince Hall. Masons, the citizens in the area and the students and staff.
Information packets are available for each lodge from your Grand Lodge Public
Schools committeeman. It is highly encouraged that each lodge adopt a Masons
on Campus program.
California Masonic Foundation

Fillers
Many Masters have difficulty in filling out their lodge bulletins. As a
service to these Masters we supplied them with what we call "fillers" to fill in the
gaps in their trestleboards. These fillers contain interesting information about
Public Schools and were written with the Master in mind. It is pleasing to note that
many Masters used them as part, or all, of their Master's message.
Jackets, Shirts and Hats
We are always on the lookout for new ways to "develop and promote
methods of increasing interest in and support for Public Schools". To this end we
laid in a supply of white jackets, white shirts and white hats, each bearing the Little
Red School House and the message in bold letters: "SUPPORT PUBLIC

The California Masonic Foundation has invited the Public Schools
Chairman to the quarterly meetings of the Foundation. This has proven to be an
effective path of communication between the Foundation and the Public Schools
Committee.
California Masonic Model Student Assistance Program
The California Masonic Model Student Assistance Training Program is
up and running. For more information about the Program please refer to the
California Masonic Foundation Board of Trustees Report. The Public Schools
Committee is taking an active role in the implementation of this program.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Conclusion

Respectfully submitted,

Several words of thanks are in order. The first is to Brother Clyde M.
Stine (494) (my ghost writer), and his wife Audley for their untiring efforts for over
two decades on the Public Schools Committee.

Dare] N. Reynolds, Chairman

To Brother Don Pollock (721) and all the brothers who are working so
hard to promote Public Schools in the Los Angeles Unified School District.
To Brother Ray Young ( 499) for his many hours of dedicated service in
the acquiring of our State' s Public Schools Proclamations and the hours in the
developing of our newsletters.

To my wife Elizabeth and all the other wives whoever husbands have
served on this committee with diligence and honor since its inception in 1920.
Without their support and understanding we would not be able to carry on our
m1ss10n.
A special thank you to all who have participated in the logistics of the
School Box program.
It is evident from the foregoing that membership on the Public Schools
Committee is no sinecure; we are a hard working committee. In reality this report
has no closing date. Ours is not a committee that winds up its business at the end
of the year, closes up shop and goes home. Even as this is being written our
members are still working.

Our notable projects are still under way and will not be completed until
future Masonic years. Our assignments include: implementation of the California
Masonic Model Student Assistance Training Program; the task of spreading our
Public Schools Committee experiences with other Masonic jurisdictions; and lastly
is the sincere efforts to expand our Masons on Campus Program and promote
Public Schools not only in the Los Angeles Unified School District but in all school
districts.
We have had a very successful year but as this report draws to a close we
are planning for an even more successful 1995-1996!
I have served on the Public Schools Committee for nine years. Under
Article VI, Section 6010 of the California Masonic Code, I am ineligible for
reappointment. It has been my pleasure to serve the Grand Lodge and associate
with you fine brothers. May we always remember to "SUPPORT PUBLIC
SCHOOLS".

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

Your Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation continued its
dedication to its guiding principles during this Grand Lodge Year. These principles
are:

1.

Each local temple association and lodge is responsible for and
knows best how to operate its real estate.

2.

The Committee may help the temple association by providing
access to talent in several business specialties which may be
partially lacking on their board of directors.

J.

By fully documenting their intent, reasoning and decisions in
each major project, the temple board of directors helps both the

Your Committe e emphasiz ed administr ative decentral ization during the
year. Using our guiding principle of placing decision- making closer to the local
level, our committe emen were empower ed to provide greater access by lodge
members and greater freedom of decision when critical matters were at hand.

A Masonic Lodge is a benefit to the communi ty. The Temple should
re~ect the high s~dards of the work of the lodge. By promoting and maintaini ng
a higher communi ty standard of conduct, we set an example for and thereby invite
others to join us upon a higher plateau.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE .

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
TOURNAMENT OF ROSES PARA DE FLOAT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The Tournament of Roses Parade Float Committee has the responsibility
of arranging all of the details necessary to enter a Masonic Float in the Rose Parade
in Pasadena on New Year's Day.
The scope of the committee's tasks includes the selection of the float
theme, design of the float, negotiation of a contract with the float builder, fund
raising from members of the Masonic Fraternity on a voluntary basis, liaison with
the Tournament of Roses Committee and the float builder, selection of float riders,
publicity, float decoration, food service for the decorators, costumes,
accommodation and transportation for riders, photography and videography, design
and sales of merchandise relating to the float, and many other details.
The 1995 float was titled "SERVICE THROUGH SPORTS" in keeping
with the Parade theme "SPORTS - QUEST FOR EXCELLENCE". This provided
the opportunity to display some of the key leaders of the Family of Freemasonry
and the Shrine East/West Football Game which supports the Shrine Hospitals. The
script provided to the TV commentators also mentioned the role of the Job's
Daughters in their support of sports.
As the year 1995 is the 75th Anniversary of the International Order of
Job's Daughters, they were honored on the front of the float where they formed a
living triangle of three young ladies - Kay Louise Weber, Miss International Job's
Daughter from Spokane, Washington; Shannon Galagan, Supreme Bethel Honored
Queen from Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada; and Karen Boerwinkle, California
Grand Bethel Honored Queen. These young ladies were situated behind the Holy
Bible symbolically opened at the Book of Job and they were flanked by two large
diamonds representing 75 years.
In the center of the float the Grand Master of Masons in California,
William F. Stovall, stood between the pillars of the Lodge, symbolically greeting
new members. He was joined by C. Fred Kleinknecht, Sovereign Grand
Commander, Supreme Council, Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction of the United
States and Blair C. Mayford, Grand Master of the Grand Encampment of Knights
Templar.
The rear portion of the float was built as a representation of a football
stadium with the goal posts spelling out SHRINERS HOSPITALS. In front of the
goal posts, the Imperial Potentate of the Shrine of North America, Burton E.
Ravellette, Jr. was accompanied by two football players, Napoleon Kaufman, then

437

all-American running back at the University of Washington and now on the Raiders
team, and Jerrott Willard, star running back and Most Valuable Player at the
University of California. Two children from the Shriners Hospital in Los Angeles
also rode on the flat on each side of the Imperial Potentate. A delightful young
lady, I I-year only Jennifer Gray from Lompoc, California has been a patient at the
Hospital for a period of eight years. A brave young man, 15-year old James Brown
from Oceanside has also undergone numerous surgeries at the Hospital. Both have
served as poster children for the Shrine East/West Football Game.
In addition to the dedicated work of the Float Committee members, special
thanks are due to a number of people or organizations for the assistance they
provided. In particular, the 1,000 or so members of the Masonic Youth Groups and
their advisors who decora ted the float did an outstanding job and also acted as
ambassadors for Freemasonry by assisting on other floats as well. Again this year,
our float was the first one completed prior to the judging on the day before the
Parade. Members of the Shrine and York Rite performed the almost impossible
task of providing hot, wholesome meals for the decorators for several days.
Four members of Al Malaikah Shrine Travel Club, Nobles Robert Pierce,
John Kocheim, George Stone and Maury Shapiro provided their motor homes at
the start of the Parade to keep the riders warm until it was time for them to board
the float for the 5 mile journey down the Parade route. Two mortuaries, Inglewood
Mortuary and Douglass Family Mortuaries, provided limousine services for the
riders. South Pasadena Masonic Temple and Lodge made their facilities available
for the riders to change clothes and also provided lunch after the Parade. Pasadena
Temple was also made available for the New Year's Eve Party organized for the
youth decorators.·
The committee also appreciates the devoted services of Vernon and
Margaret Dandridge and Melissa Cronin who coordinated some of the float
decorators and Saundra Coe and Michelle Brown who manned the decorator signin table and merchandise sales during the decoration period.
The 1995 float was well received by the viewing public and was
fi nancially successful also, even though the committee was very concerned in
September when donations were far below the needs to meet expenses. We are
indebted to the Grand Lodges from several other jurisdictions, California Lodges
and other Masonic organizations for their contributions. We are especially grateful
to the Job 's Daughters, Eastern Star, Imperial Shrine and Scottish Rite Foundation
for their generous support. Fortunately, contributions in the last three months
before the Parade enabled the committee to meet its obligations with very little to
spare. Actual net expenditures were $90,007, including $75,000 for the float itself.
Other expenses included the float entry fee, publicity, correspondence,

photography, video editing, accommodation, food for decorators, costume rental
and other non-recoverable miscellaneous expenses.
The television coverage on the 1995 float was significantly better than in
previous years, partly due to the commentators having generally followed a script
provided to them by the committee. In addition, being the ninth float in the Parade,
our float was in a favorable position to be included in the pre-Parade TV
interviews. Channel 5 interviewed the Committee Chairman at the decorating
pavilion and Channel 11 interviewed the Grand Master and other Masonic leaders,
as well as Jennifer Gray, during the pre-Parade TV coverage.
As in past years, a 29 minute videotape was produced from footage
provided by several members of the committee, as well as published materials
relating to Freemasonry. This tape described the structure of the Family of
Freemasonry, information about the charities supported by the Family of
Freemasonry, the activities of the International Order of Job's Daughters and the
backgrounds of the football players and the children from the Shrine Hospital. It
also showed the decorators applying the floral arrangements to the float and the TV
coverage by all TV stations. Complimentary copies of this video were provided
to all riders, all Grand Lodges and the concordant organizations which contributed
financially to the float program. Copies are also available for purchase by
individuals and organizations who wish to use the video as a means of informing
friends and neighbors about Freemasonry.
An 8x I 0 color photograph of the float was also sent to individual lodges
which contributed $100 or more to the float and to every Grand Lodge and
concordant organization.
Since January 2, 199 5, our attention has been focused on the 1996 float.
The Parade theme is "KIDS - LAUGHTFR AND DREAMS". With the
concurrence of our Deputy Grand Master, we chose a design proposed by the float
designer and builder, Phoenix Decorating Co. This float will not be an obvious
Masonic float but well be an eye-catching design which is expected to attract the
attention of children and adults. This flat, a large figure of Humpty Dumpty on a
wall, will be slightly smaller than previous floats but, for the first time, we will
have some automation to make Humpty Dumpty rock and wink. Riding on the flat
will be seven children from the Masonic Home at Covina dressed in costumes
made by residents of the Homes at Covina and Union City. The float will be titled
"WE SUPPORT YOUTH". The TV narration will highlight the various ways in
which children are supported by the Family of Freemasonry, through scholarships,
youth organizations and activities, medical services, etc.
Based on previous float costs, the budget for the 1996 float is $83,000.
The float is somewhat smaller than the previous floats. The cost of the float itself
is $66,500 ($8,500 less than previous floats). Other expenses amounting to about

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

439

$16,500 are for the float entry fee, correspondence, telephone, publicity fl yers,
mailings, photography and videography, costumes, food for the decorators during
the decoration period, refreshments for the decorators' New Year's Eve Party and
other miscellaneous expenses. The committee has attempted to keep the costs as
low as possible and still provide a first class product to represent Freemasonry. We
are very proud of the fact that we have one of the least expensive floats in the
Parade.

\

The committee receives no Grand Lodge appropriation for the
performance of its obligations. The committee members have absorbed most of
their out-of-pocket expenses associated with the tasks involved in the float
program. No contributed funds are used for the benefit of any of the committee
members. The committee has no luncheon or dinner meetings in the course of its
work. Several weeks after the Rose Parade, the committee members and their
spouses gather for a social " Dutch-treat" dinner to celebrate the end of another
successful year.
As you are awa.re, the financial support for the float program is derived
from voluntary contributions. ln the past four years, we have attempted to broaden
the support of the float to Masonic organizations worldwide but with limited
success. We are very grateful for the contributions by several other Grand Lodges,
especially those which have provided support every year. We have also made
appeals at the Grand Masters' conference each year, most recently suggesting that
a contribution of$ I per member throughout the United States and Canada would
provide an endowment fund of$2,500,000 from which the interest only could be
used to provide a float in the Rose Parade every year for an indefinite period. No
further solicitation of funds would ever be needed. To date, this suggestion has not
been adopted.
Jn spite of our continual appeals, contributions are again lagging seriously
and the Float Committee is again concerned. The income from contributions at the
time of writing this report is $29,000. We still need $54,000 to complete our
financial obligations for the 1996 float from this year's income. Fortunately, we
have some funds remaining from previous years which may have to be used to
meet some of these obligations.
The most difficult task facing the Rose Parade Float Committee is fund
raising. We have considered many options and we have kept our Grand Masters
fully informed of these deliberations. We are very concerned that the support of
the float is not spread more evenly throughout our fraternity. Although we have
enjoyed support from many of the other Grand Lodges and concordant
organizations in North America, most of the support comes from California Lodges
and other organizations in California. Some California Lodges have been very
generous in their financial support each year. However, the Lodge participation

441

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

has dropped to less than 15 percent so far this year. We do not think it is fair for
the burden to be carried by just a few Lodges.
For our part, we cannot rely on the voluntary contributions satisfying the
need for the funds. Any shortfall has to be paid by the Grand Lodge of California
with whom the contract for the float has been made. While we may be able to meet
our obligations for the 1996 float by tapping our small reserves from the previous
years, we are very concerned about being able to raise enough funds for the 1997
float when we hope to showcase the Rainbow Girls on their 75th Anniversary. We
therefore felt that we had no alternative but to seek your support through the
assessment of $1 for the 1996-1997 per capita year. Accordingly, we have
reluctantly submitted Resolution 95-18 for your approval at this Annual
Communication so that it can be included in the assessment of Lodges in the I 99697 period.
On occasion, we have been asked whether the float provides any tangible
benefit to the fraternity and whether it is worth the money being spent on it. While
we would like to be able to provide evidence of increased membership, we do not
have such information available-to us. It must be realized that a tum-around in our
membership statistics may take several years to accomplish and may be the result
of several factors. We believe that the float program would be a major contributor
to such a result.
In terms of advertising value, the Rose Parade reaches a very large
viewing audience worldwide. Commercial organizations pay at least $250,000 for
a few seconds of air time. Our float is on camera for an average of 50-60 seconds,
depending on the TV channel. As stated by the Imperial Potentate of the Shrine of
North America who rode on the float last year, "We could not buy this publicity for
the money that the float is costing us."
We believe that there are some very positive results from this program, as
follows:
We are putting Freemasonry before the public in a positive
I.
manner, by highlighting some of our principles and
accomplishments, especially our charitable programs. It is our
hope that this exposure will offset the criticisms of Freemasonry
by our adversaries.
We are showcasing the Masonic Youth Groups in two ways.
2.
First, as responsible young people decorating our float and other
floats. Second, by presenting these wholesome groups as role
models while riding on the floats.

We are educating the public that Shriners are also Masons, and
that the Family of Freemasonry consists of many related
organizations working together for a better world.
Through the float videos, we are providing information about
4.
Freemasonry in an entertaining manner. In small doses, we are
answering the question often asked- "What Do Masons Do?"
In closing, I am pleased to report that the members of the committee have
enjoyed working on one of the most positive activities in Freemasonry and we
thank the Grand Master and other officers and Lodges for the support that they
have given us during the year. We are also grateful to the Pasadena Scottish Rite
and the Southern California DeMolay for the use of their meeting facilities.

Trial Record No. 2355
In this case a member of Sacramento Lodge No. 40 was charged with
misappropriation of funds. The charges were filed in 1993. When the matter
came before Grand Lodge in October, 1993, the proceedings were found to contain

Elk Grove Lodge, No. 173, was determined to be an appropriate other
Lodge. ~harges were refiled September 8, 1994. Service of the charges and
proper notice was made September 9, 1994. The matter could not be completed
by the 1994 session of Grand Lodge and was put over to 1995.
So far as can be seen in the file, no response was made by the accused
Brother_ to the refiled charges. Before the original charges were filed, the accused
ha~ wntten a letter admit-tir.g certain things and giving an explanation for his
action. When no response was made to the re-filed charges the matter falls within
the provisions of CMC Sec. 32150. Under the provisions of that sections of our
Code, ~ Trial Master is appointed, he alone makes a complete investigation.
determmes whether the charge and specifications are true, makes a finding and
When an accused brother enters a plea of Not Guilty, our
fixes the p~nalty.
procedure ts under the provisions of CMC Sec. 32160. Under CMC 32160 a
Co~miss~on is elected, hears the evidence, makes findings on the charge and
spec1ficat1ons, and fixes the penalty.
. ~n this case, a Commission was elected. A trial was held. Only six
co~m1ss1on~rs were present for the trial. Those six commissioners apparently
dehberated m the presence of the Trial Master and the Secretary of the Lodge.
(Secretary's report.) CMC Sec. 32350 says only the commissioners may be
present during deliberations.
No verdict was prepared or signed by the Commissioners. CMC Sec.
32350 says the v~te shall be recorded, giving the number of votes, both aye and no,
upon each question. (See Form Nine of Grand Lodge Fonns for Trial which is
fumi~hed by the ?rand Secretary.) In this case the Lodge secretary says that it was
unan.1mously decided by the six commissioners present that the accused was g uilty
of mismanagement of funds entrusted to his care, but that since he had returned the
money, he should only be reprimanded in open Lodge.
In the absence of any response to the amended charges, the election of a
commission, and its use in a trial, was not necessary. The proceedings should have
been held under CMC Sec. 32 150, not 32160.

The Trial Master did make a report. He found that this was a matter
between the accused and the members of the bowling league. He found the
acc~sed Not Guilty of the specification and Not Guilty of the charge. Despite
fin~~g th~ ~c~used Not Guilty, he fixed the penalty at reprimand in open Lodge.
.It is 1mphc1t m our law that if the accused is Not Gui lty, no punishment shall be
unposed.

444

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Trial Master gave the basis of facts for his decision. While brothers
may have differing opinions regarding the facts, we place in the hands of the Trial
Master the authority to investigate and make findings. Our law (CMC Sec 33030)
says a judgment of acquittal should not be reversed or disturbed except in a case
of gross violation of Masonic law by the Trial Commission or by the Lodge
acquitting the accused. Here the trial commission was unnecessary and, in fact,
improper. Even so, it was used. And evidence was taken in the presence of
commissioners and the Trial Master. We have no record of the proceedings, so
we cannot review what was said .. Therefore, the findings of the Trial Master should
be affirmed.

California Masonic Code Section 32020, subsection C2 says that a
declaration by a member that he does not believe in a Supreme Being is a Masonic
offense committed by the member against his Lodge of the Master thereof.
Subsection CZ says that attempted resignation from or renunc iation of Masonry is
also an offense against his Lodge or the Master thereof.
The Trial Master found that the member had not requested a dim it, that his
desire to separate himself from Masonry was fixed and permanent. We concur
with the Trial Master that the request for removal constituted an attempted
resignation, and thus constituted a Masonic offense.
However, we do not concur with the recommendation of the Trial Master
for suspension. The Trial Master discussed one difference between suspension and
expulsion, that is that a member suspended can be restored by his Lodge, while one
who is expelled can only be reinstated by a vote of the Grand Lodge. We believe
that the difference is more than just a question of which body can restore or
reinstate. We think there is a difference in the finality of the result.

When we affirm the findings of the Trial Master, we are finding that the
accused was acquitted of the charge and specification against him. When that is
true, there can be no penalty.
We feel we should note that this is the second acquittal of this brother on
this charge.
Under the circumstances of this case, we submit the following resolution:

Here the member has stated his disagreement with a basic requirement for
membership. He has also said he has a desire to permanently separate himself from
Masonry.

RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2355, the findings of Not Guilty of
the charge and specification be ratified, confirmed and approved, that
these findings constitute an acquittal of the charge and specification, that
there should be no penalty imposed and that the penalty recommended be
stricken.

We believe this requires the greatest penalty and recommend that the
penalty be raised to expulsion.
Your Committee therefore submits the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2376 the findings of the Trial
Master be affirmed and approved except that the penalty is raised to
expulsion.

Trial Record No. 2376
A member of Palmdale Lodge No. 769 was charged with unmasonic
conduct in two specifications. The specifications alleged that, by a letter to the
Lodge, he had disavowed a belief in a Supreme Being, and that he wished to be
removed from the rolls of the Lodge.
The accused was properly served with the charges and notice of the
charges on December 14, 1994. By a letter written October 11, 1994, the accused
informed the Lodge that he was "not a believer'' and had not been for many years.
He explained that in his view God was a myth invented by humankind. He also
asked that his name be removed from the Lodge rolls. The properly appointed
Trial Master spoke to the accused in June, 1995. He reiterated his disbelief in a
Supreme Being, and stated that because of his self-examination and personal
philosophy, he could not change his belief or his desire to resign.

WARDENS' MANAGEMENT RETREATS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The Wardens Weekend Management Retreat Program continues to be one
of the most successful programs in our Grand Lodge. This y~ar we trained a total
of224 Senior Wardens and 161 of their ladies, and 212 Junior Wardens and 14~
of their ladies. These numbers are approximately the same as the 1994 Warden~
Retreats attendance. We continue to reach over fifty (50) percent of the Lodges m
our Grand Jurisdiction. The following is a breakdown of the Retreats:
Senior Wardens Retreat, North - 107 Wardens and 80 Ladies, March 3-5,
1995, San Ramon Marriott Hotel
Senior Wardens Retreat, South - 117 Wardens and 81 Ladies, March 1012, 1995, Holiday Inn Crowne Plaza, LAX Airport
Junior Wardens Retreat, South - 112 Wardens and 75 Ladies, May 5-7,
J995, Holiday Inn Crowne Plaza, LAX Airport
Junior Wardens Retreat, North- JOO Wardens and 65 Ladies, May 19-21,
1995, San Ramon Marriott Hotel

\
I

The Junior Wardens Retreats were under the direction of our Senior Grand
Warden, Allen B. Gresham, and his wife Clara. These Retreats were built around
Allen's theme "QUALITY IS THE KEY TO SUCCESS - YOU CAN MAK E A
DIFFERENCE" . Subjects covered in these Retreats included, "In Search of
Excellence", "Discovering the Future'', " Passion for the Membership'', " Planning
Your Year as Master", " Preparing for Change", " Masonic Protocol", "How to Get
Things Done", " Be a Leader: The Evolution of Responsibility", "The Secretary as
Support", and many more. In addition, the ladies received training in the history
of Freemasonry and the role of the Master' s wife. This training was reinforced
with Team Building E·ercises and Group Reports. The Junior Wardens and their
ladies left these Retreats with a better understanding of Freemasonry, their
leadership role in the Lodge and how to make their Lodges successful.
Speakers used in these sessions included Charles Alexander, Allen
Gresham, Tony Wordlow, Mel Nahin, Victor Howard, Stanley Cazneaux, Loyal
Stark, Robert Winterton and Rodger Page. Each did an outstanding job and were
well received by those in attendance. The ladies speakers included Greta
Alexander, Clara Gresham, Marilyn Wordlow, Gloria Cazneaux and Jorene Page.

Staff Clinical Psychologist, for his outstanding contributions to the success of these
Retreats. His excellent presentations are well accepted by those in attendance. He
is responsible for the development of the Work Exercises used in the Breakout
Sessions. His knowledge in Management Organization and Leadership Skills have
been a major reason for the success of the Retreat.
Once again this year I want to thank Roben Winterton, Sr., Inspector of
the 497th Masonic District, for his significant contribution to the Wardens Retreats
Program. Brother Bob has been involved in these Retreats since their inception and

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON YOUTH ORDERS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
As I am sure you already know, the Youth Orders Committee of your
Grand Lodge has recently changed in fonn and function . Our primary function is
(if the local parties feel that an independent moderator can be helpful) now to assist
Lodges and Temple Associations, as well as any of our three Masonic Youth
Orders, in the resolution of any disagreements which may arise between them. A
local Youth Group may request our participation through their Executive Officer,
Grand Guardian, or Supreme Deputy, as may be the case. A Lodge or Temple
Association may request our participation through their Division Assistant Grand
Lecturer via their District Inspector. The Youth Orders Committee Chainnan will
then assign a member of the committee who will schedule, and serve as moderator
of, a meeting with aH the parties. Although the committeeman has no authority to
impose any solution, all of the parties will be aware that a complete report of the
meeting, its outcome, and the moderator's recommendations, will be sent to not

451

only the participants actually attending the meeting, but also to the Assistant Grand
Lectur~r and Principle Ad~lt Leader of the Youth Order; to any Grand Lodge
Committee deemed appropriate; and to all members of the Grand Lodge Executive
Committee. This Committee will also include details of any such ''formal
interventions" in its Annual Report to the Grand Lodge. Alt hough situations
req.uirin~ such intervention are relatively rare, this committee has in the past
assisted m the successful resolution of what seemed, at the time, to be insoluble
problems. Your Youth Orders Committee will be available should you desire our
participation.
I am very pleased to tell you that no ''formal interventions" were
necessary during this last Grand Lodge year. All assistance which was requested
of the Committee was satisfactorily resolved by simple telephone conversations.
!11i~ is the type of report which the Youth Orders Committee sincerely hopes that
1t will always be able to present to this Grand Lodge.
It is interesting (and in a strange way somewhat disturbing) to note that
only one of the requests for assistance came to us from an Inspector (and that
Inspector happens to be a Brother with whom your Committee Chainnan served
as a Grand Officer in 1990-1991.) The balance of the requests came from one of
the various leaders of the Youth Orders. Your Committee urges the members of
the Ritual Committee to make certain that all Inspectors, and through them all of
the Lodges and Temple Associations of our Jurisdiction, are aware that this
Com~i~ee stai:ids. ready, _willing, and able to serve any Lodge or Temple
Assoc1at1on which may destre the Committee's assistance.
One new and particularly exciting development has occurred this year.
Through the efforts of our Grand Master, Most Worshipful William F. Stovall, and
of the Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation
Worshipful Brother David Decker, the California Masonic Foundation has decided
to fund the publication of your Youth Orders Committee' s Scholarship Manual
on a continuing basis. The Youth Orders Committee will research and validate the
infonnation, and the Foundation will cover both the costs of preparation by the
Grand Lodge staff, and of the publication each year of an updated listing of the
educational financial assistance available to our Masonic Youth. Sufficie nt copies
will be prepared for each Lodge Secretary and Inspecto r as well as for each Bethel,
Chapter and Assembly, throughout the Jurisdiction of California. A limited
number of copies will also be available for the use o f th e various other concordant
and appendant bodies. It was planned that the fi rst of these new annual
Scholarship Manuals would be available for distribution at this Annual
~ommunication, or very shortly thereafter. The continuing availability of this
important document should be of great assistance to our Masonic Youth in the
years to come.

Your Committee Chairman (and all of the Members of the Youth Orders
Committee) extend their sincere thanks to Most Worshipful Brother Stovall for
pennitting us to, in this small but important way, serve our Grand Lodge. A special
thank you is also given to Very Worshipful John L. Cooper, our Grand Secretary,
and to his very competent staff, who have always given every Member of this
Committee any support which has been requested, while tolerating and minimizing
the effect of any procrastination on the part of this Committee's Chainnan. The
most heartfelt thanks, however, go to the Members of our three Masonic Youth
Orders. It is these young men and women who always make our service such a joy.
